questions.understand_first:
A ship has always produced information about herself - the noon report, the engine log, the sounding book, the survey record. What changed is that the instruments started reporting continuously and automatically instead of once a day by hand, and the quantity that arrives is now far beyond what a person can read. That is the whole idea: not that the information is new, but that there is so much of it, arriving so fast and in so many different forms, that the old way of handling it - a human reading a page and forming a judgement - stops working. So you need machines to do the reading, and the interesting question becomes what you ask them to find.

The second idea is that there is a ladder of usefulness. At the bottom you are simply describing what happened, which is what a noon report always did. A step up, you ask why it happened. Higher again, you predict what will happen next - this bearing is running warmer each week and will fail in about two months. At the top, the system recommends what to do about it. Most of the commercial value people talk about lives on the upper rungs, and most of the difficulty in getting there is not clever mathematics but ordinary data that turns out to be wrong.

The third idea, and the one that makes this an examination question in 2023 rather than a magazine article, is that the regulator had just started asking for the data too. Once a ship's compliance depends on a number calculated from her own reported consumption, the quality of that reporting stops being a commercial nicety and becomes a legal exposure.

blocks.h: 1. The principles of Big Data - the brief introduction the stem asks for

blocks.p: The stem asks for this briefly, and that is an instruction rather than a courtesy. Two things need to be established before either limb can be answered: what makes data big, and what one actually does with it once it is.

Big Data is not simply a large quantity of data. The working definition is that data becomes big when it can no longer be handled by the methods that were adequate for it before - when the volume, the rate of arrival or the mixture of formats defeats a spreadsheet and a human reader. It is conventionally described by a set of properties beginning with V:

ul: Volume - a modern main engine and its auxiliaries may carry several thousand instrumented points logged continuously. A single ship generates more data in a day than her noon reports produced in a year.
Velocity - the data arrives continuously and in some applications must be acted on immediately, rather than being reviewed at the end of a voyage.

Variety - it is not one kind of thing. Structured sensor readings, free-text defect reports, survey photographs, AIS tracks, weather fields and noon reports are all different in form and must be brought together to be useful.
Veracity - whether the data is true. This is the property that matters most at sea and is discussed at section 3.
Value - whether analysing it changes a decision. Data that changes no decision has no value however much of it there is.

blocks.p: The second half of the introduction is what is done with the data, because the four functions in limb (b) each need a different level of it. Analytics is conventionally described as a ladder, and each rung is harder and worth more than the one below:

rows: Descriptive
What happened?
This voyage burned 412 tonnes
Diagnostic
Why did it happen?
Consumption rose because hull fouling increased shaft power at the same speed
Predictive
What will happen next?
At the present fouling rate the ship will miss her charter speed warranty within seven weeks
Prescriptive
What should be done?
Clean the propeller at the next port call rather than waiting for drydock

blocks.p: That ladder is the frame for the rest of the answer. The regulatory limb below lives mostly on the first two rungs, because a regulator wants an accurate account of what happened. The commercial limb lives on the upper two, because an owner wants to know what to do.

blocks.h: 2. Limb (a), opportunities - the regulations coming at this sitting had just become data-dependent

blocks.p: The opportunity is best understood by seeing what had changed in the eight weeks before this paper was sat. The revised MARPOL Annex VI adopted by resolution MEPC.328(76) came into force on 1 November 2022, and its chapter 4 requirements on carbon intensity became applicable on 1 January 2023. That is six weeks before this examination. The consequence is precise and it is the hinge of the whole limb:
Compliance itself became a calculation performed on the ship's own reported data. It is no longer a matter of holding a certificate and passing a survey. Three requirements make the point:

ul: Regulation 27 requires ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above to collect and report fuel oil consumption data for each calendar year, which is then aggregated by the Administration and submitted to the Organization. That reporting stream was already running before this sitting.

Regulation 28 requires the ship's operational carbon intensity to be determined against a required value, and the ship to be rated. The rating is computed from the consumption and distance data the ship herself reports.

Regulation 25 requires the attained EEXI of an existing ship to be not greater than the required EEXI, verified at the first periodical survey on or after 1 January 2023 - so at this sitting the fleet was in the middle of being verified.

blocks.p: The opportunities that follow are then straightforward to state, and each is a scoring point:

ul: The same data serves compliance and management. A consumption and distance record accurate enough to be reported is accurate enough to be optimised against. An operator who instruments the ship properly gets the regulatory return and the operational improvement from one investment.

Compliance moves from reactive to predictive. Because the carbon intensity metric is computed over a whole calendar year, a ship that waits until December to look at it has lost the year. Analytics allows the year-end position to be forecast in February and the trading pattern adjusted while there is still time to change the outcome. This is the single most valuable opportunity at this particular sitting.
Verification becomes cheaper and less disputable. A continuous, timestamped record is easier to present to a verifier and to an Administration than a reconstructed one.

Technical decisions acquire evidence. Whether a particular energy-saving device or coating actually delivered what was claimed becomes measurable on the operating fleet, rather than a matter of the maker's brochure.

Fleet-level allocation. Where an operator controls several ships, analytics allows the trading pattern to be arranged so that each ship's carbon intensity stays where it is wanted - matching ships to trades rather than accepting the allocation that arises by accident.

blocks.h: 3. Limb (a), challenges - and the marks are in the ones peculiar to ships

blocks.p: Generic difficulties - the cost of software, the shortage of data scientists - will be written by every candidate and score little. The marks are in the challenges that arise because this is a ship:

headers: Why it is a shipping problem specifically
rows: Connectivity

Bandwidth at sea is limited and charged by volume. Sending every sensor reading ashore continuously is not affordable, so processing has to be split between ship and shore, and the split has to be designed.
Veracity and sensor drift

A flow meter, a torsion meter or a draught gauge drifts, fouls or fails, and it does so silently. A fouled log gives a plausible speed that is simply wrong. Bad data that looks reasonable is more dangerous than no data, because it is acted on.
Granularity of the legacy record

The noon report is one observation a day, manually entered, and it remains the baseline for many performance claims. Reconciling continuous automatic data against a daily manual record produces disagreements that have commercial consequences.
Split ownership of the data

On one ship the owner, the technical manager, the charterer, the engine maker and the equipment suppliers each generate and claim data. Who owns it, who may see it and who may sell it is frequently unsettled, and it is a contractual question rather than a technical one.
Cyber exposure

Once compliance depends on a data pipeline, an attack on that pipeline is a compliance failure as well as a security incident. Connecting previously isolated machinery systems to a shore network to collect data is exactly what creates the exposure.
Standardisation

Equipment from different makers reports different quantities under different names at different intervals. A great deal of the effort in any real project is spent making the data comparable before any analysis begins.
Competence and trust
A system that recommends an action is only useful if the engineer believes it. An alert that is wrong three times is ignored the fourth time, when it is right.

blocks.p: Two of these deserve emphasis because they are the ones a well-prepared candidate can develop into real marks. The first is veracity: analytics amplifies whatever it is given, so a systematic error in a sensor becomes a systematic error in every decision taken downstream of it, and the discipline of validating instruments does not disappear with automation - it becomes more important. The second is data ownership, because it is the challenge that no amount of engineering solves. It is settled, if at all, in the charter party and the management agreement.

blocks.h: 4. Limb (a), the future transformation of the industry

blocks.p: The stem prints 'future transformation or the shipping industry'. That is a keystroke error for 'of', and it is answered as of.
The transformation to describe is a change in the nature of assurance:

ul: From periodic to continuous. Shipping has always assured itself by inspection at intervals - the annual survey, the vetting inspection, the drydocking. Continuous data makes it possible to know the condition of a ship between those events, and in time to let the evidence rather than the calendar determine when intervention is needed.
From documents to records. The unit of proof shifts from a certificate asserting a condition on a date to a dataset showing the condition over time.
From experience to evidence in technical decisions. Judgements that were made on the basis of what had worked before become measurable across a fleet.

New commercial questions. Once a ship's operational efficiency is a published, comparable number, it becomes a term of trade - it affects what she can be chartered for and by whom. The technical department's performance becomes commercially visible in a way it was not.

blocks.p: The honest qualification, which is worth a mark because most candidates omit it: this transformation was at its beginning at this sitting and not complete. The regulatory data stream had just started, no ship yet had a carbon intensity rating, and much of the industry was still assembling the instrumentation. An answer that describes the transformation as accomplished overstates the position at February 2023.

blocks.h: 5. Limb (b), chartering

blocks.p: Chartering is where the ship's measured performance meets a contractual promise, and analytics operates on both sides of that meeting.

ul: Performance warranties. A time charter typically warrants a speed at a stated consumption in stated weather. Whether the warranty was met, and if not by how much, is a data question that generates real money. Continuous data allows the owner to demonstrate compliance and the charterer to test it.

Speed and consumption claims. The classical dispute is whether an underperformance was the ship's fault or the weather's. Analytics settles it by combining the ship's own logged data with independent weather hindcast fields for the same position and time, and the resulting analysis is far harder to dispute than a noon report.
Weather routeing and good weather periods. Whether a period qualifies as 'good weather' under the charter definition determines whether it counts in the performance analysis at all. Data decides it.

Voyage estimation. Before fixing, the expected consumption and duration for a specific ship on a specific route in a specific season can be estimated from what that ship actually did, rather than from her design figures. This is a direct commercial advantage in setting a rate.

Position and market intelligence. AIS data analysed at fleet scale shows where competing tonnage is, how long ships are waiting at load ports, and how much tonnage is effectively out of the market - all of which inform the rate at which one is willing to fix.

blocks.p: The point to make explicitly, because it is the examinable one: the charter party is a contract about performance, and analytics changes the evidence available to prove performance. That is why it matters to chartering rather than merely being interesting.

blocks.h: 6. Limb (b), operations

blocks.p: Operations is where the upper rungs of the ladder earn their keep.

ul: Voyage optimisation. Speed, trim and route are chosen together against the forecast weather and the arrival requirement. The largest single operational saving available to most ships is avoiding a fast passage followed by waiting at anchor, and identifying that opportunity is a data problem.

Hull and propeller performance monitoring. Fouling is a gradual loss that is invisible day to day and large over a docking cycle. Normalising the ship's power-speed relationship for draught, trim, weather and current isolates the fouling component and shows what it is costing. That converts the decision to clean the propeller from a calendar decision into an economic one - clean when the cost of fouling exceeds the cost of cleaning.

Machinery condition monitoring. Continuously logged temperatures, pressures, vibration and performance parameters allow a developing fault to be recognised as a trend rather than as an alarm. A bearing running progressively warmer is a maintenance decision; the same bearing at its alarm point is a breakdown.

Condition-based maintenance. Overhauls driven by measured condition rather than running hours, which reduces both unnecessary opening-up and unexpected failure. This is the operational form of the same shift from periodic to continuous described at section 4.

The regulatory reporting stream. The regulation 27 data collection and the regulation 28 carbon intensity calculation are themselves operational analytics tasks, and doing them well is a compliance requirement rather than an option.

blocks.h: 7. Limb (b), vetting

blocks.p: Vetting here means the commercial inspection regimes - the tanker and dry bulk inspection schemes under which a charterer satisfies itself about a ship before fixing her - and not class or statutory survey, which is a different thing.
What analytics changes:

ul: The inspection is a snapshot; the data is a record. A vetting inspection observes a ship on one day. Continuous operational and safety-management data lets an operator demonstrate what the ship is like on the other three hundred and sixty-four, which is a stronger case than the snapshot alone.

Preparation and self-assessment. An operator can analyse its own observation history across the fleet, identify the deficiency categories that recur, and correct them before an inspector finds them. Recurring observations are the ones that damage a record.

Trend analysis across the fleet. Where the same observation appears on several ships it is a management-system failing rather than a ship failing, and only fleet-level analysis distinguishes the two. That distinction is exactly what the management self-assessment element of these regimes is aimed at.

Near-miss and incident analysis. Free-text near-miss reports are the classic under-used data source. Analysed at scale they reveal the precursor patterns that precede incidents, which is what a vetting regime is ultimately trying to assess.

Screening before the inspection. Charterers increasingly screen candidate ships against port State control history, age, incident record and inspection outcome before an inspection is even sought, so a ship's data record affects whether she is considered at all.

blocks.h: 8. Limb (b), design of the vessel

blocks.p: The connection between operating data and design is a feedback loop, and describing that loop is the answer to this limb.

ul: Designing for the operating profile actually observed. Ships have traditionally been optimised around a contract speed and design draught that many never operate at. Fleet data shows the speed, draught and trim distribution a ship of that type in that trade genuinely experiences, and the hull and propeller can be optimised for that instead. This is the single largest design consequence.
Sizing machinery to real demand. Measured electrical and auxiliary loads across a fleet inform the number and rating of generators, pumps and compressors, instead of accumulated design margins.
Evidence on energy-saving devices. Whether a duct, a fin or a coating delivered its predicted saving is measurable across sister ships, and that evidence feeds the next specification.
Structural and maintenance feedback. Recurring defect and repair data identifies details that fail in service, which is design information that only the operating fleet can supply.

The digital twin. A calibrated model of the ship maintained against her live data allows a proposed modification - a bulbous bow retrofit, a propeller change, a power limitation - to be evaluated numerically before it is bought. At this sitting that was the direct route to demonstrating an EEXI compliance option.

Retrofit as the near-term case. With the EEXI requirement biting on the existing fleet from 1 January 2023, the immediate design application was not the newbuilding but deciding which modification to make to a ship already trading, and data determined which option actually met the requirement.

blocks.p: The closing point, which ties the whole answer together: the four functions in limb (b) are the same loop seen at four different timescales. Operations acts on data in days, chartering in weeks, vetting over a year, and design over the life of the next ship. What makes the data valuable is that the loop closes at all.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks and three demands, one of which is unnumbered. The stem says 'with brief introduction on the principles of Big Data explain the following', so the introduction is marked work and not scene-setting. Candidates lose marks at both ends: some omit the introduction entirely and go straight to limb (a), and others write two pages on the four Vs and run out of time before reaching limb (b)'s four functions. Brief means brief.

The larger structural risk is treating the question as one essay about how useful data is. Limb (a) is regulatory and strategic; limb (b) is commercial and technical across four named functions. Four functions are named, so there should be four visible answers. An examiner marking limb (b) is looking for chartering, operations, vetting and design, and will not hunt for them inside a continuous discussion.

blocks.h: The temporal trap, and it is a real one

blocks.p: Limb (a) asks about upcoming regulations. It is February 2023. The regulations that are upcoming are the ones in MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4: the fuel oil consumption data collection under regulation 27, which was already running, and the operational carbon intensity rating under regulation 28, whose first rating year had begun six weeks earlier. Nobody had a rating yet. The EEXI verification under regulation 25 was happening at first annual surveys during that year.

What is not upcoming, and must not appear: the EU Emissions Trading System extension to shipping, which applied from 1 January 2024; FuelEU Maritime; the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted 7 July 2023, five months after this paper; and everything later. A candidate who writes about emissions trading in a February 2023 answer is describing a scheme that had not begun.

blocks.h: The four Vs, and which two actually matter at sea

blocks.p: Volume, velocity and variety are the standard three and can be given in a sentence each. The two worth developing are veracity and value.

Veracity is the marine-specific one. Sensors on a ship drift, foul and fail, and they do it silently. A speed log reading two per cent low gives a plausible number that is wrong, and every efficiency calculation downstream of it is then wrong in the same direction. The engineer's discipline of checking instruments against each other does not disappear when the data becomes automatic - it becomes the foundation of the whole edifice. Plausible bad data is more dangerous than obviously missing data, because it gets used.

Value is the disciplining question: does analysing this change a decision? A great many shipping data projects have collected impressive quantities of information that changed nothing, because no one identified in advance which decision the analysis was supposed to inform.

blocks.h: The ladder, and why limb (b) needs it

blocks.p: Descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive. The reason this belongs in the introduction rather than being decoration is that the four functions in limb (b) sit at different rungs, and saying so is a mark:

rows: Chartering
Diagnostic
The question is usually why did the ship underperform - her fault or the weather's
Operations
Predictive and prescriptive
The value is in acting before the loss occurs, not in recording it
Vetting
Descriptive and diagnostic
The regime asks what the record actually shows, and whether a fault is a ship fault or a system fault
Design
Descriptive at fleet scale
What the operating profile genuinely is, across many ships and years

blocks.h: Hull and propeller performance - the technical core of the operations limb

blocks.p: This is the one place in the answer where an engineer can show real technical understanding, and it is worth doing properly. The problem is that a ship's fuel consumption at a given speed varies with draught, trim, wind, sea state, current and water temperature, and the fouling signal is buried under all of them. Isolating it requires normalising the observed power-speed relationship to a reference condition, so that measurements taken in different conditions become comparable.

Once that is done, the slow upward drift in normalised power at constant speed is the fouling, and it can be costed. The decision to clean the propeller or the hull then stops being a docking-cycle habit and becomes an economic calculation: clean when the accumulated cost of the added power exceeds the cost and off-hire of cleaning. That sentence is worth a mark on its own because it converts a technical measurement into a management decision, which is what this subject is examining.

blocks.h: Data ownership - the challenge that engineering cannot solve

blocks.p: Worth a short paragraph because few candidates raise it. On a single ship the owner, the technical manager, the time charterer, the engine builder and several equipment suppliers all generate or receive data. Who owns it, who may use it, who may sell an aggregated version of it, and whether the charterer may see the owner's machinery data are contractual questions. They are settled in the management agreement and the charter party, or they are not settled at all. This matters practically because performance disputes turn on access to the data, and a party who controls the data controls the argument.

blocks.h: Cyber risk belongs in this answer

blocks.p: The link to make is precise: collecting machinery data means connecting machinery systems that were previously isolated. That connection is the exposure. And because compliance now depends on the data pipeline, a successful attack on it is not only a security incident but a compliance failure - the ship cannot demonstrate what she is required to demonstrate. The ISM Code's safety management system is the vehicle through which cyber risk is managed, which connects this answer to Q5 on the same paper.

blocks.h: Vetting is commercial, not statutory

blocks.p: A common error is to answer the vetting limb with class and statutory survey. Vetting in this context is the charterer's satisfaction that a ship is acceptable - the tanker and dry-bulk inspection regimes and the associated management self-assessment. The distinction to draw is between the ship inspection, which is a snapshot, and the management assessment, which is about systems. Analytics helps most with the second, because a deficiency appearing on one ship is a ship problem and the same deficiency appearing on six is a system problem, and only fleet-level analysis tells them apart.

blocks.h: Design - lead with the retrofit case, not the newbuilding

blocks.p: The instinct is to talk about optimising a new hull. At February 2023 the live design question in the industry was not the newbuilding but the existing ship, because EEXI had just become applicable to the trading fleet. The immediate design application of data was deciding which compliance option - engine or shaft power limitation, a propeller modification, a bulbous bow retrofit, an energy-saving device - would actually bring a particular ship into compliance without destroying her commercial usefulness. Leading with that shows the candidate knows what year it is.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Do not quote a figure for the volume of data a ship generates, the size of the market, or the percentage saving from any measure. Published figures vary enormously with assumptions and an invented one is worse than none.
Do not name commercial platforms or vendors. The question is about the technique, not the products.
Do not describe artificial intelligence in general terms. The question asks about data and its use, and a general essay on machine learning answers neither limb.
Do not write about emissions trading, FuelEU Maritime, or the 2023 GHG Strategy. None of them applied at this sitting.
Do not treat the transformation as complete. At February 2023 the regulatory data stream was weeks old and no ship had a rating.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Which regulations are the upcoming ones at this sitting?" The CII rating cycle whose first year has just begun, and the DCS reporting stream that feeds it. NOT the EU ETS, NOT the 2023 GHG Strategy, NOT any Net-Zero Framework - all three are future here.
"Has any ship been rated yet?" No. The first rating year is six weeks old and the rating is determined after the calendar year ends.
"Give me the four Vs." Volume, velocity, variety, veracity - and say at once that veracity is the one that decides whether any of it is usable at sea.
"Whose data is it?" The question the industry has not settled. Owner, charterer, manager, maker and platform all claim it, and engineering cannot resolve a commercial question.
"What does big data have to do with cyber risk?" Everything - the connectivity that moves the data is the attack surface, and it is managed through the ISM safety management system.
"Is vetting statutory?" No. It is commercial, and that is exactly why data moves the needle there faster than regulation does.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What data does your ship already send ashore every day, and who reads it?
Your noon report and your automated log disagree. Which do you trust, and what do you do?
How would you demonstrate that a hull cleaning actually paid for itself?
What would you need to measure before you could tell an owner whether to derate the engine?
Who owns the engine performance data on a time-chartered ship?
What is the first thing you would do if the ship's performance-monitoring PC would not boot?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Principles, then the two limbs. PRINCIPLES (1): the four Vs, and the ladder - descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive. LIMB (a) in three moves: OPPORTUNITIES (2) - compliance has just become data-dependent; CHALLENGES (3) - the ones peculiar to ships, bandwidth, sensor drift, crew workload, ownership, cyber; TRANSFORMATION (4). LIMB (b) is four words in the stem's own order: CHARTERING (5), OPERATIONS (6), VETTING (7), DESIGN (8). If nothing else survives, keep four Vs, four rungs, four applications.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of what is asserted

blocks.p: No figure of any kind is offered for a data or analytics claim. No fuel saving percentage, no sensor accuracy, no bandwidth number, no market size and no adoption rate appears anywhere. Figures of that kind are vendor-sourced, ship-specific and move faster than any examination syllabus, and none could be supported from a held source.

No product, platform, class notation or software is named, and no claim is made about how many ships carry any capability. The answer is written on the mechanism - what the data is, what it is used for, and what limits its usefulness - rather than on the market.

The temporal boundary is the live risk on this question and it is stated rather than assumed. Limb (a) asks about 'upcoming regulations', and what is upcoming depends entirely on the sitting date. At February 2023 the answer is the CII rating cycle and its reporting stream. A donor written in 2025 reaches for the EU ETS, the 2023 GHG Strategy and the Net-Zero Framework, and all three are future here and are excluded by name.

questions.short_title: IMO Instruments Implementation Code - Objectives, Flag State Strategy, KPIs and the Three State Roles
questions.text_verbatim: Referring to the IMO Instruments Implementation Code. a) Briefly Discuss the objectives of the code and strategy recommended to flag state to achieve the objective. Which all IMO instruments covered in the code. b) What are the key performance indicators for evaluation of Flag state performance as per the code. c) Briefly discuss the Flag state, coastal state, and Port state responsibilities.

decomposition: Limb a) first demand: the OBJECTIVE of the Code, stated close to the Code's own words
Limb a) second demand: the STRATEGY the Code recommends to a State to achieve that objective
Limb a) third demand: WHICH IMO INSTRUMENTS the Code covers - and the answer must be the list operative at THIS sitting
Limb b): the key performance indicators for evaluating flag State performance
Limb c) first: flag State responsibilities - implementation, delegation, enforcement, surveyors, investigation
Limb c) second: coastal State responsibilities - the services a coastal State provides
Limb c) third: port State responsibilities - control, no more favourable treatment, and officer independence
The framing the stem assumes but does not ask: what made the Code MANDATORY, which is what makes any of this enforceable

Not read from any frozen field. Every candidate above threshold was adjudicated by reading both printed stems in full.

WHAT IS REUSED: the donor's PARAGRAPH-LEVEL READING of A.1070(28) - objective at annex paragraph 1, the three-part strategy at paragraph 3, the six subject areas at paragraph 6, the nine policy areas at paragraph 7, flag State implementation from paragraph 15, delegation at 18 to 21, enforcement at 22 to 27, surveyors at 28 to 37, investigation at 38 to 41, KPIs at 42 to 44, coastal State at 45 to 51 and port State at 52 to 63. That structural map is the donor's real value and it is unaffected by the passage of time, because A.1070(28) is unamended between the two sittings.

See question_delta and temporal_review.

questions.question_delta: THE PRINTED STEMS ARE CHARACTER-IDENTICAL SAVE FOR ONE PRINTED MARK FIGURE. QP2510-Q7 prints (6) against limb a); this paper prints no mark figure at all, here or anywhere else on the paper, so the 16 is derived from the rubric. All three exact instances - March 2024, December 2024 and October 2025 - print the same sentence, the same three limbs, the same elision 'Which all IMO instruments covered in the code', and the same inconsistent capitalisation. THERE IS NO QUESTION DELTA. THE TEMPORAL DELTA IS THE ENTIRE STORY, AND IT IS THE SHARPEST DONOR TRAP ON THIS PAPER. The donor sits thirty-two months later and answers the third demand of limb a) - which instruments the Code covers - by reference to RESOLUTION A.1187(33), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code. That resolution was adopted by the THIRTY-THIRD ASSEMBLY on 6 DECEMBER 2023, ten months after this sitting, and its own operative text REVOKES A.1157(32). At February 2023 the revocation has not happened and A.1157(32), adopted by the thirty-second Assembly in December 2021, is the operative list. Carrying the donor's citation across would import an instrument that did not exist for another ten months and would simultaneously delete the one that did. THE CITATION IS REVERSED TO A.1157(32). The same reversal applies to the port State control procedures, which are A.1155(32) at this sitting and not A.1185(33). The III CODE ITSELF IS UNAMENDED between the sittings - A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013 - so the whole of the donor's paragraph-level structural reading transfers without qualification, and it is only the ASSEMBLY LAYER SITTING ON TOP OF IT that moves.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: FIVE DEMANDS ACROSS THREE PRINTED LIMBS, and the commonest failure is to answer three. Limb a) alone contains three separate instructions - the objectives, the strategy recommended to the flag State, and which instruments the Code covers - and the third of these is routinely dropped because it reads like an afterthought. Limb b) asks for KPIs, which is a definite thing in the Code and not an invitation to invent management metrics. Limb c) asks for THREE state roles, and candidates habitually write at length on flag and port State and give coastal State a single line, when the Code treats it as a full third part. The intent is to see whether the candidate has actually read the Code as a structured document rather than absorbed a general impression that flag States should implement conventions properly.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 by rubric. NO MARKS ARE PRINTED against this question or any limb, and none is printed anywhere on this paper - the exact donor prints (6) against limb a) and this paper prints nothing. The derivation is recorded rather than concealed: instruction 2 states all questions carry equal marks, six answered questions are required, and the paper prints Total Marks - 100. Internally: limb a) is weighted heaviest at about 7 because it carries three demands, limb b) about 4, limb c) about 5 split across three roles.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The objective stated close to the Code's own words, including the point that a State is bound only for the instruments to which it is actually a Party; the three-part strategy given as three parts and not paraphrased into one; a correct account of which instruments the Code covers, WITH THE RIGHT ASSEMBLY RESOLUTION FOR THIS SITTING; the KPIs given as the Code's own evaluation criteria rather than as invented indicators; and three visibly separate state roles, with coastal State given real content. Recognition that the Code became MANDATORY and how, because that is what turns it from advice into an audited obligation.
primary_source_plan: Read the III Code A.1070(28) structure from the MIW verification record that read the resolution in full, and use its paragraph-level map rather than re-deriving it.

ESTABLISH INDEPENDENTLY which Assembly resolution carries the non-exhaustive instrument list AT FEBRUARY 2023, and do not take the donor's citation. The donor cites A.1187(33), adopted after this sitting.
Confirm from the anchor that the 33rd Assembly adopted on 6 December 2023 and is therefore future, and that the 32nd Assembly of December 2021 is the operative one.
Give the instrument list BY SUBSTANCE - the treaty families the Code reaches - rather than by reciting a resolution annex whose exact contents at this sitting are not held.

Do NOT assert the number of treaty instruments audited under IMSAS as a bare figure without saying what is being counted; the donor's own record flags that the commonly-quoted number depends on whether protocols are counted separately.
Do NOT assert the IMSAS audit cycle length or the number of audits completed at this sitting; no held source fixes either for February 2023.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - and precisely localised. The Code itself is unamended and carries no freshness risk at all. The ENTIRE risk sits on one citation in limb a) - the Assembly resolution carrying the instrument list - where the donor is ten months wrong for this sitting. Once that is reversed there is nothing else on the question that moves.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The Code is an IMO instrument and the question sets no Indian limb. India's role appears only as an example of a State that is simultaneously flag, coastal and port State, and no Indian instrument is asserted.
technical_ambiguities: Whether 'Which all IMO instruments covered in the code' asks for a list of conventions or for the subject areas the Code addresses. It asks for the instruments - the Indian-English elision is of 'are', so the demand is 'which IMO instruments are covered'. Both are given, because the subject areas at annex paragraph 6 are the natural way to organise the instrument list, but the instruments are named.

Whether the KPIs in limb b) are the Code's own evaluation criteria or general management indicators. They are the Code's own, at annex paragraphs 42 to 44, and answering with invented management metrics answers nothing.

Whether coastal State responsibilities under the Code mean UNCLOS jurisdictional rights. They do not. The Code addresses what a coastal State should PROVIDE and DO - navigational services, hydrographic and meteorological information, casualty response - not the extent of its maritime zones. Confusing the two is the standard error on limb c).
Whether the Code binds a State in respect of instruments it has not ratified. It does not, and the Code says so expressly at annex paragraph 2. This is a scoring point that most candidates miss.

Whether to describe the Code as mandatory. It is - through the amendments that brought the III Code and the audit scheme into the mandatory instruments - and saying how it became mandatory is worth a mark. The date and mechanism are stated at the level the held sources support.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Seven numbered sections. Section 1 frames the Code and what made it mandatory. Sections 2, 3 and 4 answer limb a)'s three demands in the printed order - objective, strategy, instruments. Section 5 answers limb b). Sections 6 and 7 answer limb c), with flag State in section 6 and coastal and port State together in section 7, because the coastal and port roles are shorter and are better contrasted side by side than separated.

steps.title: What the Code is, and what makes it bite
points: Resolution A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013; revoked A.1054(27)
Made mandatory through amendments to the treaty instruments, audited under IMSAS from 1 January 2016
It is the audit standard - the yardstick against which a Member State is measured

steps.title: Limb a), first demand - the objective of the Code
points: To enhance global safety and protection of the environment and to enable States to implement the instruments they are Party to
Annex ¶2 - a State is bound only for the instruments to which it is a Contracting Government or Party

steps.title: Limb a), second demand - the strategy recommended to the State
points: Three parts - promulgate the law, enforce it, and continuously improve against measured performance

steps.title: Limb a), third demand - which IMO instruments the Code covers
points: The mandatory treaty families - SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, LL, COLREG, TONNAGE, and their Protocols
At this sitting the non-exhaustive list is A.1157(32) - NOT A.1187(33), which is ten months future

steps.title: Limb b) - key performance indicators for flag State performance
points: The Code's own evaluation criteria - casualty and detention record, survey and certification performance, RO oversight, investigation completion, reporting to the Organization

steps.title: Limb c), first role - flag State responsibilities
points: Implementation, the minimum programme, delegation to ROs and oversight of them, enforcement, surveyor qualification, casualty investigation, reporting

steps.title: Limb c), second and third roles - coastal State and port State
points: Coastal - the services a State provides to shipping off its coast
Port - control, no more favourable treatment, PSCO qualification and independence

questions.understand_first: A convention is only words until some government makes it real. The Organization that writes the conventions has no ships, no surveyors and no courts; everything it agrees has to be turned into national law and then actually enforced by the individual States that signed it. For most of the twentieth century there was no way of checking whether a State was doing that well, badly or at all. Some States ran serious administrations; others sold the right to fly their flag and did very little else, and the ships suffered for it. This Code is the answer to that problem. It sets out, in ordinary administrative terms, what a government has to have in place if it is going to be taken seriously - laws that actually reproduce what it agreed to, people competent to inspect, a way of dealing with those it delegates work to, a way of investigating when something goes wrong, and a way of knowing whether any of it is working. Crucially, it then became something a State can be audited against, so the question of whether a flag is doing its job stopped being a matter of reputation and became a matter of findings. The second idea is that a State wears three hats and the Code addresses all three. The same country is the flag of the ships on its register, the coastal State off whose shore other people's ships pass, and the port State whose harbours those ships enter. Each hat carries different work: as a flag you are responsible for your own ships wherever they are; as a coastal State you owe services and a response to what happens off your coast; as a port State you check other people's ships when they come to you. Keeping those three apart is most of what this question is testing.
questions.memory_cue: FIVE DEMANDS IN THREE LIMBS - limb a) hides three. Code = A.1070(28), 2013, revoked A.1054(27), MANDATORY under IMSAS from 1 Jan 2016. Limb a): OBJECTIVE (implement what you are Party to - and only what you are Party to), STRATEGY (promulgate, enforce, improve), INSTRUMENTS (SOLAS MARPOL STCW LL COLREG TONNAGE + protocols; list is A.1157(32) at this sitting, NOT A.1187(33) which is ten months future). Limb b): the Code's own evaluation criteria, not invented metrics. Limb c): THREE hats - FLAG owns its ships, COASTAL provides services, PORT checks others under no more favourable treatment.

blocks.h: 1. What the Code is, and what makes it bite

blocks.p: The IMO Instruments Implementation Code - the III Code - was adopted by the Assembly as resolution A.1070(28) on 4 December 2013, and it revoked its predecessor, the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments of 2011. It is a statement of what a Member State must have in place in order to give proper effect to the IMO instruments it has accepted.
The point that turns this from an administrative document into an examinable obligation is the next one, and it should be made early because everything else depends on it:

The Code is mandatory, and compliance with it is audited. The Code was made mandatory through amendments to the principal treaty instruments, and it is the standard against which Member States are audited under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme, which became mandatory on 1 January 2016. A State is therefore not merely encouraged to organise its administration in this way - it is measured against the Code, and the findings are real.
Two structural features of the Code should be stated at the outset because they shape every later answer:

ul: The Code is organised in three parts by role - common areas, then flag States, then coastal States, then port States - which is precisely the division limb c) asks about.
The Code repeatedly requires a State not simply to have arrangements but to evaluate and improve them. That built-in review requirement is what generates the performance indicators in limb b).

blocks.h: 2. Limb a), first demand - the objective of the Code

blocks.p: Stated close to the Code's own terms, the objective is to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment by assisting States to implement the IMO instruments to which they are Party, and by supporting the development of a State's own administrative capability. It is aimed at implementation and enforcement, not at making new technical rules.
Three elements of that objective are worth stating separately because each is a scoring point:

ul: It is about giving effect to existing obligations. The Code adds no substantive safety or pollution requirement. It is about whether the requirements already agreed are actually delivered.
It applies according to each State's own circumstances. The Code acknowledges that States differ in size, fleet and capability, and asks each to view the Code in the light of its own position.

A State is bound only in respect of instruments to which it is a Contracting Government or Party. This is expressly said and it is the point most candidates miss. The Code does not oblige a State to implement a convention it has not accepted; it obliges it to implement properly the ones it has.

blocks.p: The last of these deserves a sentence of its own in an answer, because it disposes of a common misconception that the Code somehow universalises IMO obligations. It does not. It universalises the standard of administration, not the substantive conventions.

blocks.h: 3. Limb a), second demand - the strategy recommended to the State

blocks.p: The Code recommends a strategy in three parts, and giving them as three parts rather than as one paraphrase is what earns the marks:

headers: What the State must actually do
rows: 1. Promulgate

Enact national legislation and administrative instruments that give effect to the instruments it is Party to - and give effect to them fully and completely, not selectively. This means the national law must actually reproduce the obligation, not gesture at it.
2. Enforce

Establish the administrative machinery to implement and enforce what it has enacted - the surveyors, the inspectors, the records, the sanctions, the delegation arrangements and the oversight of anyone the work is delegated to.
3. Evaluate and improve
Continuously assess its own performance against measured results, identify shortcomings, and correct them. The Code makes review a standing obligation rather than an occasional exercise.

blocks.p: Two further duties sit alongside the strategy and are worth adding:

ul: The State must promulgate laws and regulations and take the other steps necessary to give the instruments full and complete effect, so that safety of life at sea and protection of the environment are assured.
The Code carries the no-transfer-of-pollution principle - in giving effect to environmental obligations, a State must not simply move the harm from one medium or place to another.

blocks.p: The Code also sets out what a State should do when a new or amended instrument enters into force: review and update the national law, notify those affected, provide the administrative arrangements to implement it, and train the people who will apply it. That is the strategy in operation rather than in principle, and mentioning it shows the Code has been read.

blocks.h: 4. Limb a), third demand - which IMO instruments the Code covers

blocks.p: This is the demand candidates drop, and at this sitting it is also the one where the citation matters.

The Code applies to the mandatory IMO instruments - the treaty instruments that are subject to the audit scheme. In substance they are the following families, together with their Protocols where those are separate instruments:

rows: SOLAS 1974 and the 1988 Protocol
Safety of life at sea - construction, equipment, operation
MARPOL and the 1997 Protocol
Prevention of pollution from ships, all annexes as accepted
STCW 1978 and the STCW Code
Training, certification and watchkeeping of seafarers
Load Lines 1966 and the 1988 Protocol
Assignment of freeboard and conditions of assignment
COLREG 1972
Collision regulations
TONNAGE 1969
Measurement of tonnage

blocks.p: The Organization also maintains a non-exhaustive list of the obligations arising under those instruments, so that a State and an auditor can see what is actually being audited. At this sitting that list is the one adopted by the thirty-second Assembly.

A caution on the count. The number of instruments is commonly given as nine, but that figure depends on whether the Protocols are counted as separate instruments from their parent conventions. It is safer to name the families and note the Protocols than to assert a bare number, and an answer that does so is more accurate rather than less.

blocks.h: 5. Limb b) - key performance indicators for flag State performance

blocks.p: The Code requires a flag State to evaluate and review its own performance, and it sets out the criteria by which that evaluation is to be made. These are the key performance indicators the question asks for, and they are the Code's own - not general management metrics.
The State should measure itself on:

ul: Casualty record - the frequency and severity of casualties involving its ships, so that trends can be detected rather than incidents merely counted.

Port State control detention and deficiency record - the rate at which its ships are detained and the deficiencies found on them abroad. This is the most externally visible indicator a flag has, because it is measured by other States.
Survey and certification performance - whether statutory surveys are carried out when due and whether certificates are issued properly and on a sound basis.
Performance of recognized organizations - the results of the oversight programme over the ROs to which work has been delegated, since a flag remains responsible for what its ROs do in its name.
Casualty investigation performance - whether investigations are carried out where required, completed, and reported to the Organization.
Reporting to the Organization - whether the State submits the information the instruments require of it, on time and completely.
Legislation currency - whether national law has been kept up to date with amendments to the instruments.
Resources and training - whether the administration has, and maintains, sufficient qualified people for the size and nature of its fleet.

blocks.p: The Code's point about these indicators is as important as the list: they exist so the State can identify shortcomings and act on them. An indicator that is measured and not acted upon does not satisfy the Code, because the third part of the strategy is improvement and not merely measurement.

blocks.h: 6. Limb c), first role - flag State responsibilities

blocks.p: This is the longest part of the Code and the answer should reflect that, but it organises cleanly under six heads:

rows: Implementation

Give full and complete effect in national law to the instruments the State is Party to, and establish a programme to ensure its ships comply - the minimum safety and environmental protection programme covering survey, certification, manning, casualty investigation and enforcement.
Resources and organisation
Maintain an administration with sufficient competent people, defined responsibilities and documented procedures, appropriate to the size and nature of the fleet.
Delegation to recognized organizations

Where survey and certification work is delegated, the RO must be formally authorised under a written agreement, the scope of the delegation must be defined, and the flag must oversee the RO's performance. Responsibility is not transferred with the work.
Enforcement

Investigate non-compliance, take action against its ships and their operators, provide adequate sanctions of sufficient severity to be a deterrent, and detain a ship where necessary until she can proceed without unreasonable danger.
Surveyors
Flag State surveyors must be qualified, trained, subject to documented procedures, and identifiable - the Code addresses their qualification, their authority and their identification at length.
Casualty investigation and reporting

Investigate marine casualties involving its ships in accordance with the applicable requirements, and report the results to the Organization. Investigation is for the purpose of preventing recurrence, not for apportioning blame.

blocks.p: The delegation head is the one to develop if time allows, because it is where flag States most often fail an audit. The Code's position is unambiguous: a State may delegate the work to a recognized organization, but it retains the responsibility, and it must therefore have an oversight programme capable of telling it whether the delegated work is being done properly.

blocks.h: 7. Limb c), second and third roles - coastal State and port State

blocks.p: These are shorter than the flag State part and are best contrasted directly, because the distinction between them is what the limb is testing.
Coastal State. The Code addresses what a coastal State should provide to shipping off its coast - it is a question of services and response, not of jurisdictional zones. A coastal State should:

ul: provide and maintain aids to navigation, and vessel traffic services where the traffic warrants them;
provide hydrographic services and up-to-date charts, and promulgate navigational warnings;
provide meteorological services and weather warnings;
provide a search and rescue capability, and arrangements for responding to casualties and to pollution incidents in the waters for which it is responsible;
provide places of refuge arrangements and the means to respond to a ship in need of assistance;
conduct casualty investigation where a casualty occurs in its waters, and cooperate with other substantially interested States;
report to the Organization as required, and evaluate and improve its own performance in these services.

blocks.p: The error to avoid is answering this limb with the UNCLOS maritime zones. The Code is not about how far a coastal State's jurisdiction extends; it is about what the State does with it.
Port State. The Code addresses the State's control over other people's ships entering its ports:

ul: establish and maintain a port State control capability, with procedures and trained officers, to verify that visiting ships comply with the applicable instruments;

apply the no more favourable treatment principle - a ship whose flag State is not Party to an instrument is not to be treated more favourably than a ship whose flag State is. Without this, non-ratification would be an advantage, and the whole convention system would leak;

ensure port State control officers are qualified, trained, authorised and independent - independent of commercial interests in the port and in the ships they inspect, which the Code addresses expressly;

take appropriate action where deficiencies are found, up to and including detention where the ship is unfit to proceed to sea without danger, and inform the flag State and the recognized organization concerned;
avoid undue delay to the ship, and provide for compensation where a ship is unduly detained;
report inspections and detentions, including through the regional port State control arrangements, and evaluate and improve its own performance.

blocks.p: The closing observation that ties limb c) together: the three roles are held by the same State at the same time, and the Code expects each to be discharged independently of the others. A State's failures as a flag are not excused by its diligence as a port State, and the audit looks at all three.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks and five demands hidden inside three printed limbs. Limb a) alone asks three things - objectives, strategy, and which instruments are covered - and the third is dropped by most candidates because it reads like a trailing afterthought. Count the demands before writing: objective, strategy, instruments, KPIs, three state roles. That is five things, and the answer should have five visible places where each is dealt with.

The second structural failure is limb c). Candidates write a page on flag State, half a page on port State, and one line on coastal State. The Code gives coastal State a full part of its own, and an examiner marking that limb has three boxes to tick.

blocks.h: The citation that decides this question at this sitting

blocks.p: This is a February 2023 paper. The Organization maintains a non-exhaustive list of the obligations under the instruments relevant to the III Code, and that list is periodically replaced by a new Assembly resolution.

At this sitting the operative list is the one adopted by the thirty-second Assembly in December 2021. The thirty-third Assembly met and adopted its resolutions on 6 December 2023 - ten months after this paper was sat - and the list it adopted expressly revoked its predecessor. A candidate who cites the 2023 list in a February 2023 answer is citing an instrument that did not yet exist and, worse, has deleted the one that did.

The same trap catches port State control procedures, which belong to the thirty-second Assembly at this sitting and not to the thirty-third. An Assembly boundary is the adoption date, not the meeting month, and December 2023 is after February 2023.

blocks.h: The point about ratification that most candidates miss

blocks.p: The Code says expressly that a State views the Code according to its own circumstances and is bound only in respect of the instruments to which it is a Contracting Government or Party. This is worth a mark on its own because it corrects a natural misunderstanding: the Code does not oblige every State to implement every IMO convention. It obliges a State to implement properly the ones it has actually accepted. The Code standardises the quality of administration, not the list of ratifications.

blocks.h: What 'mandatory' means here, and why it matters

blocks.p: The Code began life as guidance. It became mandatory through amendments to the principal treaty instruments, and it is the standard against which Member States are audited under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme, mandatory from 1 January 2016. Saying this early frames the whole answer, because it explains why any of these administrative arrangements are enforceable at all. Before the audit scheme, a State that ran a poor administration faced reputational consequences at most; after it, there are findings, corrective action plans and a follow-up.

blocks.h: Be careful with the number of instruments

blocks.p: The figure of nine is commonly quoted for the instruments subject to audit, but it depends entirely on whether Protocols are counted separately from their parent conventions - SOLAS and the 1988 SOLAS Protocol, MARPOL and the 1997 Protocol, Load Lines and the 1988 LL Protocol. Name the families and mention the Protocols rather than asserting a bare number. An answer that explains why the count is ambiguous is stronger than one that states a figure and is marked against a different counting convention.

blocks.h: The delegation point - where flags actually fail

blocks.p: If there is time to develop one part of the flag State limb, develop this one. A flag State may authorise a recognized organization to carry out survey and certification on its behalf. The Code requires a formal written agreement, a defined scope of what is delegated, and an oversight programme to verify the RO is doing it properly.

The principle to state is: the work may be delegated; the responsibility may not. A flag State that authorises an RO and then never checks on it has not discharged its obligation, and this is one of the commonest audit findings in practice. It also connects to the port State limb, because when a port State detains a ship it informs both the flag and the RO that certified her.

blocks.h: No more favourable treatment - say why it exists

blocks.p: Most candidates state the principle. The mark is in explaining the purpose: if a ship flying the flag of a non-Party State could claim exemption from port State inspection on the ground that its flag never agreed to the convention, then not ratifying would be a commercial advantage and the whole treaty system would be undermined. No more favourable treatment closes that hole. It is the reason a convention can be effective against ships whose flags have not accepted it.

blocks.h: Coastal State is about services, not zones

blocks.p: The standard error is to answer the coastal State limb with UNCLOS - territorial sea, contiguous zone, EEZ, and the rights that attach to each. That is a different subject. The III Code asks what the coastal State does: aids to navigation, hydrographic and chart services, meteorological warnings, traffic services, search and rescue, pollution response, places of refuge, and casualty investigation in its waters. Provision and response, not jurisdiction.

blocks.h: The KPIs are the Code's, not yours

blocks.p: Limb b) invites invention, and invention scores nothing. The indicators are the Code's own evaluation criteria and they cluster around externally visible outcomes - casualties, detentions, survey and certification performance, RO oversight results, investigation completion, and reporting compliance. The detention record is worth singling out because it is the one measured by other States rather than self-reported, which makes it the hardest for a weak administration to flatter.

blocks.h: A useful closing line

blocks.p: If the answer needs a conclusion, the strongest one is structural: the same State is flag, coastal and port State simultaneously, and the Code expects each role to be discharged on its own terms. Diligence in one does not excuse failure in another, and the audit examines all three. That sentence demonstrates that the three limbs have been understood as one system rather than as three lists.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Citing A.1187(33) for the list of instruments the Code covers. That resolution was adopted on 6 December 2023, ten months after this sitting, and it revokes the one that was operative. The answer here is A.1157(32).
Citing A.1185(33) for port State control procedures. At this sitting it is A.1155(32).
Saying the III Code is voluntary. It became mandatory through the IMSAS amendments to the instruments themselves, and that is what makes it bite.
Confusing the Code with the audit. The Code is the standard; IMSAS is the audit scheme that checks a State against it.
Giving a precise count of the instruments the Code covers. State the families and say the list is maintained by Assembly resolution.
Treating the coastal State role as a matter of maritime zones. It is about services - aids to navigation, hydrography, meteorology, search and rescue, casualty response.
Inventing key performance indicators. The Code has its own; give those.
Forgetting that the flag State remains responsible for what it delegates to a recognized organization.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Which Assembly resolution lists the instruments at this sitting?" A.1157(32), from the 32nd Assembly of December 2021. Anything numbered (33) is ten months in the future.
"Is the Code mandatory?" Yes - by amendment to the parent instruments, not by its own force.
"What is the objective in one sentence?" To enhance global safety and environmental protection by helping States implement the instruments they have ratified.

"Name three flag State KPIs." Casualty and detention rates, the completeness and timeliness of reporting, the currency of implementing legislation, and the effectiveness of oversight of recognized organizations.
"Can a flag State delegate to class?" It may authorise a recognized organization - and it remains responsible.
"What does the port State role add?" A second line of defence against a flag State that has not done its job.
"Which State role is not about ships at all?" The coastal State - it is about the services a State provides to shipping in its waters.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your flag State audits your company next month. What will they ask to see?
What is the difference between a class surveyor and a flag State inspector on your ship?
Who issues your Safety Management Certificate, and on whose authority?
If your flag has delegated everything to class, who is answerable at IMO?
What does a port State inspector do that a flag State inspector does not?
Give me one thing a coastal State owes you that has nothing to do with inspecting your ship.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: What it is, then a) b) c) in the printed order. WHAT IT IS (1): A.1070(28), made mandatory through IMSAS, audited rather than certified. LIMB a) in three demands: OBJECTIVE (2), STRATEGY (3) - legislation, resources, oversight, review - and INSTRUMENTS (4), listed by A.1157(32) and not by anything numbered (33). LIMB b) KPIs (5). LIMB c) THREE ROLES: FLAG (6), then COASTAL and PORT (7). Anchor phrase: implement, enforce, audit - and the single date that decides the question is the 32nd Assembly, not the 33rd.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the Assembly boundary

blocks.p: The single largest risk on this question is a citation, and it has been reversed deliberately. All three exact donors for this stem sit after December 2023 and cite A.1187(33). That resolution did not exist at this sitting and revokes the one that did. A.1157(32) is used throughout, and the reversal is recorded in the paper anchor at sections 2.4 and 4.

No number of instruments is asserted and no ratification count is given. The families the Code covers are named; the count is not, because the list is maintained by Assembly resolution and any figure would be a snapshot.

The III Code text was not read at source this session. Its content is carried at INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED provenance from the MIW record that read it in full, and the paragraph addresses within the annex are cited only so far as that record establishes them. No provision is quoted verbatim.

quick_revision.recall_15s: III Code = A.1070(28), adopted 4 Dec 2013, revoked A.1054(27). MANDATORY, audited under IMSAS from 1 Jan 2016. Limb a) THREE demands: OBJECTIVE - implement the instruments you are Party to, and only those; STRATEGY - promulgate, enforce, evaluate-and-improve; INSTRUMENTS - SOLAS+88 Prot, MARPOL+97 Prot, STCW, LL+88 Prot, COLREG, TONNAGE, list at A.1157(32) (32nd Assembly) NOT A.1187(33) which is +10 months. Limb b) KPIs - casualties, PSC detentions, survey/certification, RO oversight, investigation completion, reporting, legislation currency. Limb c) THREE hats: FLAG - implement, delegate-but-oversee, enforce, surveyors, investigate; COASTAL - services: nav aids, charts, met, SAR, pollution response, places of refuge; PORT - PSC, no more favourable treatment, officer independence, detention, no undue delay.
critical_numbers: A.1070(28) adopted 4 December 2013 - the III Code itself, UNAMENDED at this sitting
IMSAS mandatory from 1 January 2016
A.1157(32) - the operative non-exhaustive obligations list at February 2023, adopted by the 32nd Assembly, December 2021
33rd Assembly adopted 6 December 2023 - TEN MONTHS AFTER this sitting. A.1187(33) and A.1185(33) are PROHIBITED here
The count of audited instruments is commonly given as nine BUT depends on whether Protocols are counted separately - name the families instead
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Resolution A.1070(28), the IMO Instruments Implementation Code. Annex paragraph 1 the objective; paragraph 2 that a State is bound only for instruments it is Party to; paragraph 3 the three-part strategy; paragraph 6 the subject areas; paragraphs 42 to 44 the evaluation of flag State performance; paragraphs 45 to 51 coastal State; paragraphs 52 to 63 port State, including no more favourable treatment and PSCO independence.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing A.1187(33), the 2023 non-exhaustive list of obligations, for the instruments limb. It was adopted on 6 December 2023 - ten months after this sitting - and it revokes the list that WAS operative. The correct citation here is A.1157(32). The same boundary makes PSC procedures A.1155(32), not A.1185(33). The second trap is answering the coastal State limb with UNCLOS maritime zones instead of the services the Code actually requires.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the III Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what the Code is and what made it mandatory. Limb a): 2 objective, 3 the three-part strategy, 4 which instruments. 5 limb b) KPIs. Limb c): 6 flag State, 7 coastal and port State contrasted.
retrieval_cards.why: Five demands hide inside three printed limbs and the instruments demand is the one dropped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the III Code and when was it adopted?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013, revoking A.1054(27). Mandatory, and the standard against which States are audited under IMSAS from 1 January 2016.
retrieval_cards.why: Framing the Code as the audit standard explains why any of it is enforceable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Assembly resolution carries the obligations list at February 2023?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1157(32), adopted by the 32nd Assembly in December 2021. NOT A.1187(33), which was adopted 6 December 2023 - ten months after this sitting - and which revokes A.1157(32).
retrieval_cards.why: This is the sharpest donor trap on the paper; all three exact donors sit after the 33rd Assembly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a State bound by the Code for conventions it has not ratified?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Code says expressly that a State is bound only in respect of instruments to which it is a Contracting Government or Party. The Code standardises the quality of administration, not the list of ratifications.
retrieval_cards.why: Most candidates miss it and it corrects a natural misunderstanding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The three-part strategy.
retrieval_cards.answer: Promulgate - enact national law giving full and complete effect. Enforce - establish the administrative machinery, surveyors, records and sanctions. Evaluate and improve - measure performance, find shortcomings, correct them.
retrieval_cards.why: Giving three parts as three parts is where the marks are; paraphrasing into one loses two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instruments does the Code cover?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS 1974 and the 1988 Protocol; MARPOL and the 1997 Protocol; STCW 1978 and the STCW Code; Load Lines 1966 and the 1988 Protocol; COLREG 1972; TONNAGE 1969.
retrieval_cards.why: Name the families and the Protocols rather than asserting a count of nine, which depends on the counting convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The flag State performance indicators.
retrieval_cards.answer: Casualty record; port State control detention and deficiency record; survey and certification performance; results of RO oversight; casualty investigation completion and reporting; reporting to the Organization; currency of legislation; resources and training.
retrieval_cards.why: These are the Code's own criteria; invented management metrics score nothing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can a flag State delegate its responsibility to an RO?
retrieval_cards.answer: It may delegate the work under a formal written agreement with a defined scope, but not the responsibility. It must operate an oversight programme over the RO's performance.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest real audit finding, and it links to the port State limb where detentions are notified to the RO.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does no more favourable treatment exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: So that a ship flying the flag of a non-Party State cannot claim exemption from port State inspection. Without it, not ratifying would be a commercial advantage and the treaty system would leak.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the principle is common; explaining its purpose is the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the coastal State limb ask for?
retrieval_cards.answer: The services the coastal State provides - aids to navigation, hydrographic and chart services, meteorological warnings, traffic services, SAR, pollution response, places of refuge, casualty investigation in its waters. NOT the UNCLOS maritime zones.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering with jurisdictional zones answers a different question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The closing observation on limb c).
retrieval_cards.answer: The same State holds all three roles at once and the Code expects each to be discharged on its own terms. Diligence as a port State does not excuse failure as a flag, and the audit examines all three.
retrieval_cards.why: Shows the three limbs understood as one system rather than three lists.

notes: RISK IS MEDIUM AND IT IS LOCALISED TO ONE CITATION. The III Code itself carries no temporal risk whatever: A.1070(28) was adopted 4 December 2013 and is unamended between this sitting and all three of its exact donors. The entire risk sits on the Assembly layer above it.

THE REVERSAL. All three exact donors - QP2403-Q7 (March 2024), QP2412-Q9 (December 2024) and QP2510-Q7 (October 2025) - sit AFTER the thirty-third Assembly. QP2510-Q7, the preferred donor, answers limb a)'s instruments demand from RESOLUTION A.1187(33), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code. THAT RESOLUTION WAS ADOPTED 6 DECEMBER 2023, TEN MONTHS AFTER THIS SITTING, and its own text REVOKES A.1157(32).

AT FEBRUARY 2023 THE OPERATIVE LIST IS A.1157(32), adopted by the thirty-second Assembly in December 2021. The citation has been reversed accordingly. This is recorded rather than silently applied because it is the single most consequential donor decision on the paper.

THE SAME BOUNDARY REACHES THE PSC LAYER. Procedures for port State control at this sitting are A.1155(32), not A.1185(33). The answer's port State limb is written to the Code itself rather than to the PSC procedures resolution, so the exposure is small, but the boundary is recorded because a candidate reaching for a PSC citation would reach for the wrong one.

AN ASSEMBLY BOUNDARY IS THE ADOPTION DATE, NOT THE MEETING MONTH. The thirty-third Assembly adopted on 6 December 2023. February 2023 is before it by ten months and there is no ambiguity of the kind that affects a month-only sitting adjacent to a boundary - this sitting is nowhere near it.

OPERATIVE AND UNCHANGED: the IMO Member State Audit Scheme became mandatory on 1 January 2016, seven years before this sitting, so the Code's status as the audit standard is settled and carries no risk.

NOT ASSERTED: the number of IMSAS audits completed, or the audit cycle length, as at February 2023. The donor's own record flags the instrument count as depending on the counting convention, and no held source fixes the audit progress figures for this date. Neither is needed by any limb.

DONOR AUDIT COMPLETED: all three exact donor records were read line by line against this sitting. Apart from the A.1187(33) citation and the associated PSC resolution edition, NOTHING in their content required reversal - the paragraph-level reading of A.1070(28), the strategy, the KPIs and the three state roles all transfer intact. Expected yield was one finding and actual yield was one finding, which is recorded as the result rather than presented as a clean sweep.
NO SITTING-RELATIVE PROSE IS CARRIED FROM ANY DONOR. All prose is authored fresh.

questions.short_title: EEXI Design Compliance Measures, and the CII Rating with AER and EEOI
questions.text_verbatim: a) IMO has introduced the EEXI requirements under MARPOL Annex VI Chapter IV for existing vessels from 2023 as a measure towards reduction of C02 emissions from shipping. Explain the various design features adopted in the existing vessels to comply with the present EEXI which meets the EEXI framework under Phase 2 ( f 20% - 30% reduction). b) Explain the concept of CII rating and critically discuss the role of measuring metrics of AER and EEOI. What are the measures required to be taken by the vessel to improve its CII ratings.

subparts.text: IMO has introduced the EEXI requirements under MARPOL Annex VI Chapter IV for existing vessels from 2023 as a measure towards reduction of C02 emissions from shipping. Explain the various design features adopted in the existing vessels to comply with the present EEXI which meets the EEXI framework under Phase 2 ( f 20% - 30% reduction).
Explain the concept of CII rating and critically discuss the role of measuring metrics of AER and EEOI. What are the measures required to be taken by the vessel to improve its CII ratings.

questions.subpart_marks_note: No mark figure is printed against this question or against either limb, and none is printed anywhere on this paper. questions.recurrence_adjudication: The host prints only its own self-reference and no backward chain. That is unsurprising rather than informative: EEXI and CII applied for the first time on 1 January 2023, six weeks before this sitting, so there COULD be no earlier instance for the host to point to. This is the clearest example on the paper of why a host annotation is not evidence of anything - its emptiness here reflects the age of the regulation, not the state of MIW's corpus. MIW's own derivation finds a near-character-identical later instance, QP2410-Q8 (October 2024), which prints the same opening sentence including the same 'C02' zero-for-O misprint. Tier A on the printed stems, read in full.
decomposition: Limb a) framing: where EEXI sits in law, and what the printed 'Phase 2 (20% - 30% reduction)' actually refers to - because as printed it conflates two different schemes
Limb a) main demand: the DESIGN features adopted in EXISTING vessels to reduce the attained EEXI
Limb a) the measure most ships actually took - power limitation - and why it is a design measure at all
Limb b) first demand: the concept of the CII rating - what is measured, against what, and how the grade arises
Limb b) second demand: AER and EEOI compared CRITICALLY - not merely defined
Limb b) third demand: the measures a vessel takes to improve its rating, and the distinction between operational and technical measures
The SEEMP as the instrument through which improvement is administered
The state of the world at this sitting - the first rating year six weeks old and no ship yet rated

AN EXACT QUESTION IS NOT AN EXACT ANSWER, AND ON THIS QUESTION THAT IS TRUE IN THE STRONGEST FORM ON THE PAPER. The donor sits twenty months later and on the FAR SIDE of the first CII rating cycle. QP2410-Q8 (October 2024) prints the same opening sentence including the same C02 zero-for-O misprint, and asks the same two things. TWO PRINTED DIVERGENCES were found on re-diffing: first, the donor prints mark figures against its limbs while THIS PAPER PRINTS NO MARK FIGURE ANYWHERE, so the 16 is derived from the rubric; second, the donor sub-letters limb a) into a) and b) while this paper runs limb a) as one continuous instruction and reserves b) for the CII limb.
