Regulation 28 determines the operational carbon intensity AFTER THE END of each calendar year. The first rating year was 2023. In October 2024 the donor stands after the first ratings were assigned and can describe ships as having been rated A to E and can treat the regulation 28.2 reporting deadline as passed. AT FEBRUARY 2023 THE FIRST RATING YEAR IS SIX WEEKS OLD AND NO SHIP IN THE WORLD HOLDS A CII RATING. Everything in limb b) is therefore written FORWARD-LOOKING - what the mechanism will produce - rather than descriptively. A SECOND REVERSAL follows from the same distance: the donor could not resolve which SEEMP guideline edition was in force on its examination day because MEPC.395(82) was adopted inside its sitting month. That difficulty does not arise here at all - MEPC.395(82) is October 2024 and simply future - and the operative guidelines are MEPC.346(78) of 2022. A THIRD REVERSAL is the entry into force of the revised Annex VI itself: see temporal_review and the paper anchor section 2.3.

The word 'critically' is an instruction - it requires the weaknesses of each metric to be stated, not merely their definitions. The discriminator across the whole question is whether the candidate can keep the DESIGN index apart from the OPERATIONAL index: EEXI is a one-off technical characteristic of the ship, CII is an annual measure of how she is actually run, and a great many candidates blur them into a single account of decarbonisation.

technical_ambiguities: THE PRINTED 'PHASE 2 ( f 20% - 30% reduction)' IS SUBSTANTIVELY WRONG AND NOT MERELY MISPRINTED. The stray 'f' is a typographic error for 'of' and is preserved. But the underlying framing conflates two schemes: the PHASED Phase 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 structure belongs to the REQUIRED EEDI table at regulation 24 Table 1, which applies to NEW ships by delivery date. EEXI takes its required reduction factor from REGULATION 25 TABLE 3, which is banded by ship type and size and is NOT phased. The answer states the framing as printed, then distinguishes the two, because a candidate who simply adopts the printed framing will describe the wrong table.

Whether 'design features' excludes operational measures. It does. Limb a) asks about design, and operational measures belong in limb b) where improvement of the CII is asked. Keeping them apart is part of what is being tested, and putting slow steaming under limb a) is the standard error.

Whether power limitation is a 'design feature'. It is treated as one, because it is a permanent, verified, certified modification to the ship recorded in her technical file, and because it is what the fleet overwhelmingly did. But the answer says plainly what it is - a limitation on the ship rather than an improvement to her - because that honesty is itself examinable.

Whether AER and EEOI are alternatives for regulatory purposes. They are not. AER is the metric used for the regulatory rating of most ship types; EEOI is a voluntary and more meaningful commercial measure. Presenting them as interchangeable misses the whole point of the critical comparison.

Whether the CII applies to all ships. It does not - the regulation 28 obligation attaches at 5,000 gross tonnage and above, matching the data collection threshold, and certain ship types are outside it. The threshold is stated; a full type-by-type applicability list is not.

questions.understand_first:
There are two quite different ways of asking whether a ship is efficient, and this question asks about both. The first is a question about the ship as an object: given her size, her engine and her hull, how much carbon does she inherently produce to move a tonne of cargo a mile? That is a property she has when she is built or modified, and you can calculate it from her particulars without her ever leaving the berth. The second is a question about how she is actually run over a year: how much fuel did she really burn, and how much useful work did she really do? Two identical sister ships have the same answer to the first question and can have very different answers to the second, because one is driven hard and the other is not.

The first idea gave rise to a design index. For new ships it had been in place for years; the obvious gap was the enormous existing fleet, built before the requirement, which was never going to be caught by a rule aimed at newbuildings. So the same calculation was applied backwards to ships already trading, and each was required to demonstrate that her figure was no worse than a limit set for her type and size. A ship that fails can be modified - and, because the calculation contains the engine power, she can also simply be prevented from using all of it, which is the cheap route and the one most ships took.

The second idea gave rise to an annual rating. Each year the ship's actual fuel consumption and distance are used to compute a number, that number is compared with what is expected of her, and she is graded on a five-point scale. Grades slip over time because the expected value tightens each year, so standing still means falling behind. The important thing to see is that the two schemes pull in different directions on one point: limiting a ship's power satisfies the design index without necessarily changing anything about how much fuel she burns, and the annual rating is unmoved by anything that does not actually reduce consumption.

blocks.h: 1. Where EEXI sits in law - and what the printed Phase 2 framing refers to

blocks.p: The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index is part of chapter 4 of MARPOL Annex VI, in the revised Annex adopted by resolution MEPC.328(76). That revised Annex entered into force on 1 November 2022, and its chapter 4 carbon intensity requirements applied from 1 January 2023 - six weeks before this examination.
The structure is the same as the design index for new ships, applied to a ship that already exists:

ul: Regulation 23 requires an attained EEXI to be calculated for each ship in the applicable categories. It is a calculated figure in grammes of CO₂ per tonne-mile, derived from the ship's installed power, her specific fuel consumption, her capacity and her reference speed.
Regulation 25 sets the required EEXI, and the obligation is simply that attained EEXI shall not exceed required EEXI.
Compliance is verified once, at the first periodical survey on or after 1 January 2023, and recorded in the ship's technical file and on her IEE Certificate.

blocks.p: A point of accuracy on the stem, and it is worth a mark. The question prints 'the EEXI framework under Phase 2 ( f 20% - 30% reduction)'. Two things need separating:

ul: The phased structure - Phase 0, Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3, tightening by delivery date - belongs to the required EEDI at regulation 24 and its Table 1, and applies to new ships.

EEXI takes its required value from regulation 25 and Table 3, where the reduction factor is set by ship type and size band. It is not phased: an existing ship has one required EEXI, not a series of them.

blocks.p: The reduction factors in the EEXI table do broadly fall in the range the question quotes for the larger conventional cargo types, which is presumably why the framing was written that way. But the correct statement is that the required reduction is read from the EEXI table by type and size, not that EEXI has phases. An answer that says so is more accurate than the question.

The rest of limb a) then follows from the formula. The attained EEXI is, in essence, emitted CO₂ divided by transport capacity, so anything that reduces the numerator or increases the denominator improves it. Since the denominator is fixed by the ship's capacity, in practice every measure attacks the numerator - and the numerator contains the installed power, the specific fuel consumption, and the carbon factor of the fuel. Those three terms organise the whole of the answer.

blocks.h: 2. Hull and propulsive design measures

headers: Practical note on an existing ship
rows: Bulbous bow retrofit

The original bulb was optimised for a design speed and draught the ship no longer operates at. Reshaping it for the actual operating profile reduces wave-making resistance and therefore the power needed at the reference speed.
A drydock job requiring hull modification. Justified where the ship's real operating speed has fallen well below her design speed - which after years of slow steaming is common.
Advanced hull coating
Reduces frictional resistance and, as importantly, resists fouling so the resistance stays low.
Applied at a scheduled drydocking. Its EEXI credit is limited because the index uses a reference condition, but its real-world benefit is substantial.
Propeller retrofit or modification
A propeller matched to the current operating point rather than the original design point. Larger diameter and lower rpm, improved blade section, or a new propeller altogether.
One of the most effective single retrofits, because the original propeller is frequently mismatched to how the ship is now run.
Propeller boss cap fins and hub vortex devices
Recover rotational energy from the hub vortex downstream of the propeller.
Fitted with the propeller, comparatively inexpensive.
Pre-swirl and post-swirl devices - ducts, stators, fins
Condition the flow into or out of the propeller so it works in a more uniform wake, improving propulsive efficiency.
Effectiveness is strongly hull-form dependent and requires CFD or model verification for the particular ship.
Rudder improvements - bulb, twisted leading edge, fins
Recover rotational energy in the propeller slipstream and reduce rudder drag.
Often combined with a propeller change as a package.
Air lubrication
A layer of air bubbles or a cavity beneath the flat of bottom reduces frictional resistance.
Significant installation, needs compressor power which partly offsets the gain, and suits ships with a large flat bottom.
Wind assistance - rotors, rigid sails, kites
Provides thrust independent of the main engine, reducing the power the engine must deliver.
Treated in the index through the innovative energy efficient technology provisions. Structural and cargo-access implications are the practical obstacle.

blocks.h: 3. Machinery and energy-recovery measures

ul: Waste heat recovery. An exhaust gas economiser raising steam, or a power turbine and turbogenerator, converts exhaust heat into useful work and displaces auxiliary generator load. It reduces total fuel burned for the same propulsion.

Engine derating and retuning. Re-optimising the engine for the lower power at which it now actually operates improves the specific fuel consumption at that operating point. Slide-fuel valves, adjusted injection timing and turbocharger cut-out are the usual measures.
Shaft generator. Taking electrical load from the main engine, which is more efficient per unit of energy than a small auxiliary diesel, reduces total consumption.
Efficient auxiliaries. Variable-frequency drives on pumps and fans, and demand-based rather than continuous running, cut electrical load.

Low-carbon and alternative fuels. This is the one measure that attacks a different term: the carbon factor CF, the mass of CO₂ per unit mass of fuel. Switching to LNG, LPG, methanol or a biofuel reduces the numerator without touching the machinery's efficiency at all. On an existing ship it usually requires conversion of the fuel system and tanks, which is why it was the least-used route at this sitting.

blocks.h: 4. Power limitation - what most existing ships actually did

blocks.p: This deserves its own section because it is the honest answer to what the fleet did, and because it shows understanding of the formula rather than a list of hardware.

The attained EEXI contains the installed main engine power. Reduce the power that may be used and the attained figure falls, without altering the ship physically in any other way. Two forms are recognised:

ul: Engine Power Limitation (EPL) - a limitation applied to the engine itself, typically through the control system and mechanical or software stops, so that it cannot exceed a stated output.
Shaft Power Limitation (ShaPoLi) - the shaft power is monitored and limited, leaving the engine itself unaltered.

blocks.p: In each case the limitation must be verifiable, recorded in an onboard management manual, and capable of being overridden in an emergency to restore full power where the safety of the ship demands it - with the override recorded. Class and the Administration verify the arrangement.

The critical observation, and it is the one that distinguishes a good answer: power limitation makes the ship compliant without making her efficient. It reduces the maximum speed available to her, and therefore her commercial flexibility, but it does not by itself reduce the fuel she burns on any voyage she was already performing at a lower power. It has no effect on her CII rating unless the limitation actually forces her to sail more slowly than she otherwise would. That is precisely the tension between the two schemes in limb a) and limb b), and stating it links the two halves of the answer.

blocks.h: 5. Limb b) - the concept of the CII rating

blocks.p: Where EEXI is a property of the ship, the Carbon Intensity Indicator measures how she is actually operated over a calendar year. The mechanism has four steps:

ol: Data in. Under regulation 27, ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above collect fuel oil consumption data, together with distance travelled and hours under way, for each calendar year and report it to the Administration, which submits it to the Organization.

Attained CII. Under regulation 28, the ship's attained annual operational CII is calculated from that data - the CO₂ emitted, derived from fuel consumed and its carbon factor, divided by a measure of transport work.

Required CII. The attained value is compared with a required value, obtained from a reference line for the ship's type and size and then tightened by an annual reduction factor relative to a 2019 baseline. The reduction factor increases year on year, so the required value becomes progressively harder to meet.
Rating. The ratio of attained to required places the ship in one of five bands, A to E, where A is the best. The band boundaries are set for each ship type.

blocks.p: The consequence is what gives the scheme teeth: a ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year, must develop a plan of corrective actions as part of her SEEMP, to be approved and implemented. There is no direct financial penalty in the regulation itself - the pressure is regulatory and, increasingly, commercial, because charterers see the rating.

The state of the scheme at this sitting must be stated correctly. Regulation 28 determines the rating after the end of the calendar year. The first year to which it applies is 2023, which began six weeks before this examination. No ship therefore held a CII rating at the date of this paper. The first ratings could not be assigned until 2024. An answer describing the distribution of ratings across the fleet, or describing ships as having been rated, is describing a state of affairs that did not yet exist.

blocks.h: 6. AER and EEOI critically compared - the denominator is the whole argument

blocks.p: Both metrics have the same form - CO₂ emitted divided by transport work - and both are expressed in grammes of CO₂ per tonne-mile. They differ only in what they count as transport work, and the entire critical discussion lives in that difference.

rows: Denominator
Deadweight capacity × distance sailed
Cargo actually carried × distance sailed
What it therefore measures
Carbon per unit of capacity offered
Carbon per unit of transport work actually done
Data needed
Fuel, distance, and the ship's deadweight - all readily available and already reported
Fuel, distance and cargo carried on every leg - which the ship does not always hold reliably
Ballast voyages
Counted in full - distance is distance, and the deadweight denominator does not care whether cargo is aboard
A ballast leg has zero transport work, so it worsens the figure sharply and correctly
Comparability
Good. Two ships of the same type and size are compared on the same basis regardless of trade
Poor. A ship in a short-sea trade with frequent port calls cannot be fairly compared with one on long ocean legs
Regulatory role
The metric used for the CII rating of most ship types
Voluntary, and long-established as a management tool
Principal weakness
It rewards behaviour that is genuinely wasteful. A ship sailing empty at full speed still divides by her full deadweight, so her figure can look respectable while she does no useful work at all
It is volatile and can be worsened by commercial decisions entirely outside the ship's control - a part cargo, a repositioning leg, a waiting period

blocks.p: The critical judgement to state explicitly is this. EEOI is the better measure of what the industry actually cares about, because carbon per tonne of cargo actually moved is the real environmental performance of a transport operation. AER is the better measure to regulate with, because it can be computed from data that is already reported, verified and hard to manipulate, and because it produces figures that are comparable between ships. The regulator chose administrability over meaning, and did so deliberately.

The cost of that choice is a real perverse incentive, and saying so is what makes the discussion critical rather than descriptive. Because the AER denominator is capacity rather than cargo, a ship can improve her rating by sailing longer distances - including in ballast - since distance appears in the denominator. A ship that sits idle at anchor burning auxiliary fuel accrues emissions with no distance at all and is penalised heavily, whereas the same ship steaming a pointless ballast leg is treated more kindly. That is the opposite of the intended incentive, and it is the standing criticism of the metric.

Two further limitations worth a line each: neither metric accounts for the cargo's own characteristics - a full cargo of a light commodity that fills the ship by volume before reaching her deadweight is invisible to AER - and both are annual, so a single unrepresentative year can determine a rating.

blocks.h: 7. Measures to improve the rating - operational

blocks.p: Because the CII is driven by fuel actually burned, only measures that reduce real consumption or increase real transport work will move it. The operational measures are the fastest-acting and the most powerful:

ul: Speed reduction. The single largest lever available. Propulsive power varies approximately with the cube of the speed, so a modest reduction in speed produces a disproportionate reduction in consumption. This is why it dominates every other operational measure.
Voyage optimisation and weather routeing. Choosing the route and speed profile that minimises consumption against the forecast, rather than steaming the shortest line at full speed.

Just-in-time arrival. The classic waste is a fast passage followed by days at anchor. Arriving when the berth is actually available allows the whole passage to be run at lower speed for the same arrival time - the largest easily-available saving on many trades, and it requires cooperation with the port and the charterer rather than any engineering.
Trim and draught optimisation. Operating at the trim that minimises resistance for the actual draught and speed, established by trials or by a validated model.
Hull and propeller cleaning. In-water cleaning between drydockings, timed on measured performance rather than on the calendar.
Reducing auxiliary and boiler load. Shutting down unnecessary machinery, managing cargo heating and tank cleaning, avoiding unnecessary boiler running in port.
Improving utilisation. Reducing ballast legs and carrying fuller cargoes improves the real efficiency, and improves EEOI directly - though, as section 6 explains, AER responds to this only weakly.

blocks.h: 8. Measures to improve the rating - technical, and the SEEMP as the instrument

blocks.p: The technical measures are the same family as limb a), but the test they must pass is different: they improve the CII only if they reduce fuel actually consumed in service. So hull coating, propeller retrofit, energy-saving devices, waste heat recovery, shaft generators, variable-speed auxiliaries and air lubrication all help. Power limitation, as noted at section 4, does not, unless it forces a genuinely lower operating speed.
A change of fuel to one with a lower carbon factor reduces the attained CII directly, because the emitted CO₂ falls even if the energy consumed does not.

All of this is administered through the SEEMP. Under regulation 26 every ship carries a ship-specific Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan. With effect from 1 January 2023 - again, six weeks before this sitting - the SEEMP for ships subject to the CII must include an enhanced part containing:

ul: the required CII values for the next three years;
an implementation plan setting out how the ship intends to achieve them;
a procedure for self-evaluation and improvement;
and, where the ship has been rated D three years running or E once, the plan of corrective actions.

blocks.p: The operative guidance at this sitting is the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, resolution MEPC.346(78), together with the CII guideline set covering the reference lines, the reduction factors, the rating boundaries and the correction factors.

The closing point, which answers the question as a whole: limb a) and limb b) can be satisfied by different actions, and only some actions satisfy both. Power limitation satisfies EEXI and does nothing for CII. Just-in-time arrival improves CII and does nothing for EEXI. A propeller retrofit, a hull coating or a waste heat recovery system improves both. Recognising which measures do which is the practical substance of managing a ship under chapter 4.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks and five demands: the design measures; the concept of the CII rating; a critical comparison of AER and EEOI; the improvement measures; and, implicitly, the correct legal framing of EEXI. The single biggest structural failure is blurring the two indices into one essay about decarbonisation. They are different in kind and the question is testing whether the candidate knows that.

blocks.p: That last row is the most examinable single fact in the whole subject, and it is where the two limbs of this question meet.

blocks.h: The stem is wrong about Phase 2 - handle it, do not adopt it

blocks.p: The question says EEXI has a Phase 2 with a 20 to 30 per cent reduction. The phased structure - Phase 0, 1, 2, 3, tightening by delivery date - belongs to the required EEDI for new ships, at regulation 24 and Table 1. EEXI takes its reduction factor from regulation 25 and Table 3, banded by ship type and size, and is not phased at all. An existing ship has one required EEXI, not a sequence of them.

The factors in the EEXI table do largely fall in that range for the bigger conventional cargo types, so the framing is not absurd - but it is not correct either. Say the framing as printed, then distinguish the two tables. A candidate who adopts the framing uncritically will start describing the wrong table. Do not, incidentally, attempt to reproduce the tables. They are ship-type and size specific and cannot be recalled reliably; describing how the factor is obtained is worth more than a half-remembered number.

blocks.h: Organise limb a) by the formula, not as a shopping list

blocks.p: The attained EEXI is emitted CO₂ over transport capacity, and the numerator contains three things you can attack: installed power, specific fuel consumption, and the carbon factor of the fuel. Every measure in the answer belongs to one of those three, and saying so organises the list into an argument:

ul: Reduce the power needed - hull, coating, bulb, propeller, energy-saving devices, air lubrication, wind assistance.
Reduce the fuel per unit of power - derating and retuning, waste heat recovery, shaft generator, efficient auxiliaries.
Reduce the carbon per unit of fuel - alternative fuels, through CF.
Or simply reduce the power term in the formula - power limitation.

blocks.h: Be honest about power limitation

blocks.p: It is what the overwhelming majority of existing ships actually did, because it is cheap, quick and requires no drydocking. An answer that omits it is describing a world that did not happen. But the examinable insight is the criticism: it makes the ship compliant without making her efficient. It removes speed she may have needed commercially, and it does nothing at all for her CII unless she is thereby forced to sail slower than she otherwise would.

Get the safety point in too: the limitation must be overridable to recover full power where the safety of the ship requires it, and the override must be recorded. That detail shows the arrangement has been understood as a real installation rather than as a paper exercise.

blocks.h: AER against EEOI - argue about the denominator

blocks.p: Both are CO₂ per tonne-mile. The only difference is what the tonnes are. AER divides by deadweight - the capacity the ship offers. EEOI divides by the cargo she actually carried. Everything follows from that one distinction and the answer should be built on it rather than on two separate definitions.

The trade-off to state: EEOI is more meaningful, AER is more administrable. EEOI measures what we actually care about - carbon per tonne of cargo genuinely moved - but it needs cargo data the ship may not hold reliably, it is volatile, and it cannot fairly compare a short-sea trader with an ocean voyager. AER needs only fuel, distance and a number from the ship's particulars, all of which are already reported and verified, and it compares like with like. The regulator chose administrability, deliberately.

Then deliver the criticism, because the question says critically: AER rewards a ship for sailing empty. The denominator is deadweight times distance and it does not ask whether there was any cargo aboard. A ship steaming a long ballast leg at speed can post a respectable AER while performing no transport work whatever, and a ship waiting at anchor burning auxiliary fuel accumulates emissions with no distance in the denominator at all and is punished. That is the wrong way round, and it is the standing objection to the metric.

blocks.h: Speed is the answer to the improvement limb

blocks.p: If only one improvement measure could be given, it would be speed reduction, because propulsive power goes approximately as the cube of speed. Nothing else available to a ship's staff comes close. Build the improvement limb outward from that: speed, then the things that let you take speed out without losing the fixture - weather routeing, and above all just-in-time arrival, which converts waiting time at anchor into slower steaming at sea for the same arrival.

Then trim, hull and propeller cleaning, auxiliary and boiler load, and utilisation. Then the technical measures, with the test stated: does it reduce fuel actually burned in service? If not, it does not improve the CII.

blocks.h: Know what year it is

blocks.p: This paper was sat in February 2023. The revised Annex VI had been in force since 1 November 2022 - three months. Chapter 4 had applied since 1 January 2023 - six weeks. The first CII rating year had just begun and no ship anywhere held a rating; the first ratings could not exist until 2024. EEXI verification was happening at first annual surveys through that year, so much of the fleet had not yet been verified either.

Write the CII limb forward-looking - what the mechanism will produce - and not as a description of ratings the fleet already had. And do not import anything later: the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted on 7 July 2023, five months after this paper, and the EU Emissions Trading System did not reach shipping until 1 January 2024.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Do not quote a percentage saving for any measure. Published figures vary enormously with ship type, baseline and assumptions, and an invented one is worse than none.
Do not attempt to reproduce the CII rating boundary values or the reference line coefficients. Explain how they are obtained instead.
Do not put slow steaming under limb a). It is operational and belongs in limb b).
Do not present AER and EEOI as interchangeable. One is the regulatory metric; the other is voluntary.
Do not say ships were rated A to E at this sitting. None was.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Is the revised Annex VI in force at this sitting?" Yes - since 1 November 2022. The corpus amendment register says 2023-11-01 and it is wrong by a year; the resolution's own operative paragraph 3 settles it.

"The stem says Phase 2, 20 to 30 per cent. Is that right?" No, and handling it is the question. The phased Phase 0/1/2/3 structure belongs to the required EEDI table for new ships. EEXI takes its reduction factor from a table banded by ship type and size, and it is not phased.
"How many ships hold a CII rating today?" None. The first rating year began six weeks ago and the rating is determined after the year ends.
"Which strategy is operative?" The Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018. The 2023 Strategy is five months future.

"AER or EEOI - which is the regulatory metric?" AER, because its denominator is deadweight × distance and needs no cargo data. EEOI uses actual cargo carried and is the better operational measure - and it is the one that cannot be audited from mandatory reported data.
"What did most existing ships actually do for EEXI?" Engine or shaft power limitation - because it is cheap, reversible and verifiable, not because it makes the ship efficient.
"Does power limitation improve the CII?" Only if the ship actually slows down. EEXI is a design index; CII is measured in service.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Show me where the EEXI Technical File is kept and what is in it.
Your ship has an overridable power limitation. Who may break the seal, and what must you record?
Your CII is trending towards D. What would you do first, and what would it cost?
Why does a slower ship have a better AER but perhaps a worse EEOI?
What is in Part III of your SEEMP that was not in Parts I and II?
What would you change on this ship if you had one drydocking and a fixed budget?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Law first, then the design measures, then the rating. LAW (1): revised Annex VI in force 1 November 2022, EEXI and CII applicable 1 January 2023 - and the printed Phase 2 framing belongs to EEDI, not EEXI. DESIGN MEASURES in three groups: HULL AND PROPULSIVE (2), MACHINERY AND ENERGY RECOVERY (3), POWER LIMITATION (4) - the one most ships used. RATING: the CII concept (5), AER against EEOI - the argument is the denominator (6), then improvement measures OPERATIONAL (7) and TECHNICAL with the SEEMP as the instrument (8). Anchor pair: EEXI is design, CII is service.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the corpus correction this question depends on

blocks.p: This is the first MIW paper whose answer depends on an open corpus correction rather than merely referencing one. The corpus amendment register records the entry into force of MEPC.328(76) as 2023-11-01. The correct date, taken from the resolution's own operative paragraph 3 read at source, is 1 November 2022. The correction request TSCR-3 is carried, not re-raised, and the corpus was not modified. Without the correction this question cannot be answered at all: a February 2023 sitting reading the register would conclude the revised Annex VI was not yet in force and would then have to explain EEXI and CII - which the paper states are in force - under a superseded Annex.

No numerical reduction factor, size band, rating boundary or reference-line constant is asserted. The regulation records establish the structure of the tables; the values are not reproduced, and no worked EEXI or CII calculation appears.
No percentage saving is claimed for any design measure, and no manufacturer, product or installed population is named. Published figures are hull-specific and largely vendor-sourced.

The forward-looking treatment of the rating is deliberate and is the paper's own finding. No ship held a CII rating at this sitting, so every statement about ships responding to their ratings has been re-authored as anticipation rather than description.

quick_revision.recall_15s: EEXI = the ship, once. CII = the year, every year. EEXI: chapter 4, revised Annex VI (MEPC.328(76), in force 1 Nov 2022, ch.4 applies 1 Jan 2023); reg 23 attained, reg 25 required, attained ≤ required, verified at first survey on/after 1 Jan 2023. Printed 'Phase 2' is the EEDI table (reg 24 T1, new ships); EEXI uses reg 25 T3, banded by type and size, NOT phased. Attack the numerator: power (hull, bulb, coating, propeller, ESDs, air lubrication, wind), SFC (derate/retune, WHR, shaft generator, VFDs), CF (alternative fuel) - or just limit the power: EPL/ShaPoLi, overridable, recorded. CII: reg 27 data (≥5,000 GT) → reg 28 rating; attained/required from a reference line with a tightening reduction factor; bands A-E; D×3 or E×1 → corrective action plan in the SEEMP. AER = deadweight×distance (capacity offered - administrable, comparable, but rewards a fast empty ship); EEOI = cargo carried×distance (real work - meaningful, but needs cargo data and is not comparable across trades). Improve: SPEED first (cube law), JIT arrival, routeing, trim, cleaning, utilisation. SEEMP Part III from 1 Jan 2023; guidelines MEPC.346(78). Feb 2023: NOBODY is rated yet.

quick_revision.major_trap: Adopting the stem's 'Phase 2 (20% - 30% reduction)' framing and then describing the EEDI table. The phased structure is regulation 24 Table 1 for NEW ships; EEXI takes its factor from regulation 25 Table 3, banded by type and size and NOT phased. retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the EEXI and CII question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb a): 1 where EEXI sits in law and what the printed Phase 2 framing really refers to; 2 hull and propulsive measures; 3 machinery and energy recovery; 4 power limitation. Limb b): 5 the rating mechanism; 6 AER against EEOI critically; 7 operational improvement; 8 technical improvement and the SEEMP.
retrieval_cards.why: Five demands across two limbs, and the two indices must be kept apart.

retrieval_cards.prompt: EEXI against CII in one line each.
retrieval_cards.answer: EEXI is a one-off calculated property of the ship - attained must not exceed required, regs 23 and 25, verified once. CII is an annual measure of how she was actually operated - regs 27 and 28, rated A to E every year.
retrieval_cards.why: Blurring them into one essay on decarbonisation is the biggest structural failure on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the stem right that EEXI has a Phase 2?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The phased Phase 0/1/2/3 structure belongs to the required EEDI at regulation 24 Table 1, for new ships. EEXI takes its reduction factor from regulation 25 Table 3, banded by ship type and size, and is not phased.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who adopts the printed framing describes the wrong table.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How should limb a) be organised?
retrieval_cards.answer: By the formula. The numerator holds installed power, specific fuel consumption and the fuel's carbon factor. Reduce power needed (hull, bulb, coating, propeller, ESDs, air lubrication, wind); reduce fuel per unit power (derate, retune, WHR, shaft generator, VFDs); reduce carbon per unit fuel (alternative fuels); or limit the power term directly.
retrieval_cards.why: Turns a shopping list into an argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the honest criticism of power limitation?
retrieval_cards.answer: It makes the ship compliant without making her efficient. It removes speed she may need commercially and does nothing for her CII unless it actually forces her to sail slower than she otherwise would.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what most ships did, and the criticism is where the two limbs of the question meet.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The four steps of the CII rating.
retrieval_cards.answer: Reg 27 data collected and reported at 5,000 GT and above; reg 28 attained annual operational CII calculated; compared with a required value from a reference line tightened by an annual reduction factor; the ratio places the ship in one of five bands A to E.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanism, not the numbers, is what is examinable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to a poorly rated ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year, requires a plan of corrective actions developed as part of the SEEMP, approved and implemented. No direct financial penalty in the regulation; the pressure is regulatory and commercial.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what gives the scheme teeth.

retrieval_cards.prompt: AER against EEOI - the one distinction.
retrieval_cards.answer: The denominator. AER divides by deadweight capacity times distance - the capacity offered. EEOI divides by cargo actually carried times distance - the work actually done.
retrieval_cards.why: Everything else follows from it; build the comparison on it rather than on two definitions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The critical objection to AER.
retrieval_cards.answer: It rewards sailing empty. Deadweight times distance does not ask whether cargo was aboard, so a fast ballast leg posts a respectable figure for no transport work, while a ship waiting at anchor burning auxiliary fuel accrues emissions with no distance in the denominator and is punished. The incentive runs the wrong way.
retrieval_cards.why: The question says 'critically'; this is the criticism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did the regulator choose AER?
retrieval_cards.answer: Administrability over meaning. AER needs only fuel, distance and deadweight - already reported, verified and hard to manipulate - and it compares like with like. EEOI is more meaningful but needs cargo data, is volatile, and is not comparable between trades.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the trade-off as a deliberate choice is the mark of a critical answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The single most powerful improvement measure.
retrieval_cards.answer: Speed reduction - propulsive power varies approximately with the cube of speed. Then just-in-time arrival, which converts waiting at anchor into slower steaming for the same arrival time.
retrieval_cards.why: Nothing else available to ship's staff comes close.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the state of the CII scheme at February 2023?
retrieval_cards.answer: The first rating year began 1 January 2023, six weeks earlier. Regulation 28 determines the rating after the end of the calendar year, so no ship anywhere held a rating; the first could not be assigned until 2024.
retrieval_cards.why: The twenty-month-later donor can describe ships as rated; this sitting cannot.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the SEEMP have to contain from 1 January 2023?
retrieval_cards.answer: For ships subject to the CII, an enhanced part carrying the required CII values for the next three years, an implementation plan, a self-evaluation and improvement procedure, and where triggered the plan of corrective actions. Operative guidance: MEPC.346(78), the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the instrument through which the whole improvement limb is administered.

notes: THIS IS THE HIGHEST-RISK QUESTION ON THE PAPER AND ALL THREE OF THE PAPER'S TEMPORAL REVERSALS LAND ON IT. The subject is six weeks old at the sitting, its governing entry-into-force date is recorded wrongly in the corpus register, and the exact donor sits on the far side of the first rating cycle.

REVERSAL 1 - THE ENTRY INTO FORCE. Resolution MEPC.328(76) was READ AT SOURCE from the text held in the corpus. Operative paragraph 2 determines the amendments deemed accepted 1 May 2022 under MARPOL article 16(2)(f)(iii); OPERATIVE PARAGRAPH 3 records that they SHALL ENTER INTO FORCE ON 1 NOVEMBER 2022 under article 16(2)(g)(ii). THE CORPUS AMENDMENT REGISTER RECORDS 2023-11-01. That value would place this sitting BEFORE entry into force and would make the question unanswerable, since the paper states as fact that EEXI applies from 2023. PRIMARY BEATS THE REGISTER. The corpus was NOT modified; TSCR-3 is carried and remains OPEN. See the paper anchor section 2.3, which records that QP2302 is the first MIW paper whose answer actually DEPENDS on this correction rather than merely referencing it.

REVERSAL 2 - THE FIRST RATING CYCLE, AND THIS IS THE ONE THE DONOR GETS WRONG FOR THIS SITTING. Regulation 28 determines the attained annual operational CII AFTER THE END of the calendar year. The first year to which it applies is 2023, which began SIX WEEKS BEFORE THIS PAPER. NO SHIP ANYWHERE HELD A CII RATING AT THIS SITTING and the first ratings could not be assigned until 2024. QP2410-Q8 sits in October 2024, after the first ratings were assigned, and can properly describe ships as rated and treat the regulation 28.2 deadline as passed. Every such statement was re-derived here and limb b) is written FORWARD-LOOKING throughout - what the mechanism will produce, not what it had produced.

REVERSAL 3 - THE SEEMP GUIDELINE EDITION. The donor's own record carries an unresolved item: it could not establish which SEEMP guideline edition was in force on its examination day, because MEPC.395(82) was adopted on 4 October 2024, inside its sitting month, and the day of the sitting is not printed. THAT DIFFICULTY DOES NOT ARISE HERE. MEPC.395(82) is twenty months future and simply prohibited. The operative guidelines at this sitting are MEPC.346(78) of 2022, unambiguously. The donor's unresolved item is therefore RESOLVED for this sitting rather than inherited.

APPLICABLE, SIX WEEKS OLD: chapter 4 of the revised Annex VI applied from 1 January 2023. EEXI verification under regulation 25 was taking place at first periodical surveys through 2023, so a substantial part of the fleet had NOT yet been verified at this sitting. The answer says so rather than describing verification as complete.
OPERATIVE: the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships of 2018, MEPC.304(72). Confirmed for this sitting from MEPC.328(76)'s own preamble, which recites it, rather than assumed.
PROHIBITED AND EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED: the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - FIVE MONTHS AFTER this sitting.

PROHIBITED AND EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED: the extension of the EU Emissions Trading System to maritime transport, applying from 1 January 2024, and FuelEU Maritime. A modern answer on carbon intensity reaches for these automatically and neither existed for shipping at this sitting.

PROHIBITED: the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the mid-term measures of October 2025; and the outcome of the regulation 25.3 and 28.11 reviews, which had not reported at this sitting and whose results are not asserted.

NO SITTING-RELATIVE PROSE IS CARRIED FROM THE DONOR. All prose is authored fresh. The donor's EVIDENTIAL DISCIPLINE is inherited - no percentage savings, no rating boundary values, no reference line coefficients - and that discipline is the reason the twenty-month distance could be crossed safely at all.

technical_ambiguities: Whether 'maritime salvage' means salvage under the general maritime law as opposed to salvage under contract, or whether it means salvage of maritime property as opposed to something else. It means the former - pure or common-law salvage, arising from the act itself without prior agreement - and the stem's later phrase 'salvage of maritime property' confirms that maritime property is a separate concept it uses elsewhere. The answer states which reading it takes.

Whether contractual salvage is therefore NOT salvage in the legal sense. It is. The distinction is about how the entitlement arises, not about whether the service is salvage. A LOF service is contractual AND is salvage, which is exactly why the Convention's criteria are used to fix the award under it. Treating the two as mutually exclusive categories is the standard error.

Whether towage is contractual salvage. It is not - ordinary towage under a towage contract is a service for an agreed price and carries no salvage element unless the tow encounters danger beyond the scope of the contract, at which point a salvage claim can arise. The distinction is worth stating because it is the clearest illustration of the boundary.
Whether the printed '.JS per this form' is anything other than a typographic corruption of 'as per this form'. It is not; it is read as 'as' and the anomaly is preserved.

Whether special compensation and SCOPIC are within scope. They are, briefly, because the stem asks who is responsible for paying and how the award is calculated, and both answers are modified where environmental damage is threatened - special compensation is paid by the SHIPOWNER alone, not by the property interests, which is a genuine exception to the answer given to demand 3.

questions.understand_first: Someone who saves property at sea from real danger is entitled to be rewarded, even though nobody asked them to and nobody promised them anything. That is unusual - in almost every other area of law you get paid only if somebody agreed to pay you - and the reason for the exception is straightforward policy. Ships in trouble are often a long way from help, the people best placed to assist are strangers with their own commercial interests, and a legal system that offered them nothing would leave a great deal of property, and often lives, unnecessarily lost. So the law creates the reward itself, out of the act of saving. The reward is deliberately generous and it is deliberately conditional. It is conditional in that you get nothing at all if you fail; a heroic and expensive attempt that ends with the ship on the bottom earns no reward. It is generous because the size of the award takes account not just of what you spent but of the skill you showed, the risk you ran, and the value of what you saved. The point of that generosity is to make it worth a professional's while to keep expensive equipment standing by for casualties that may never come. The second idea is that this whole scheme can also be operated by agreement, and usually is. A master with a serious casualty does not want to argue about terms while the ship is going aground, and a salvor does not want to work with no idea whether he will be paid at all. So a standard form exists that settles the question in one signature - the salvor will be paid on the same 'no cure, no pay' basis, and how much will be decided afterwards by an arbitrator. That is the whole of the difference the question asks about: not whether money is involved, but whether the parties agreed anything before the work began. The third idea is the one candidates most often get wrong. The reward is not paid by the person who was rescued in some general sense. It is paid by the property that was saved - and if a laden ship is saved, the cargo was saved too, so the cargo owners pay their share alongside the shipowner.

blocks.h: 1. The three preconditions - what makes any claim a salvage claim

blocks.p: Nothing in this question can be explained without these, so they come first. Under the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, a salvage claim requires three things, and all three must be present:

ol: A recognised subject in danger. There must be a vessel or other property in peril. The danger must be real, though it need not be immediate or absolute - a ship that will be in serious trouble if the weather deteriorates is in danger.

A voluntary service. The salvor must be under no pre-existing legal or official duty to render the service. A crew member saving his own ship is doing his job; a tug performing what her towage contract already requires is doing what she was hired for; a public authority acting under a statutory duty is not volunteering.
Success. The service must have contributed to a useful result. This is the 'no cure, no pay' principle - an unsuccessful attempt, however skilful and however costly, earns nothing.

blocks.p: The point to appreciate about 'voluntary' is that it does not mean unpaid or unagreed. A professional salvage company operating commercially under a signed contract is still volunteering in the required sense, because it was under no prior duty to attend this casualty. That is exactly why contractual salvage remains salvage, which is the substance of the first demand.

blocks.h: 2. Demand 1 - the difference between maritime salvage and contractual salvage

blocks.p: Maritime salvage - also called pure salvage - is salvage arising by operation of the maritime law itself. No agreement is made before the service, and the salvor's entitlement to a reward arises from the act of successfully saving property in danger. The amount is fixed afterwards, by agreement between the parties or, failing that, by a court.

Contractual salvage is salvage rendered under an agreement made before or during the service. The parties settle in advance the basis on which the salvor will work and how the reward will be determined.

The test is the presence of a prior agreement, and nothing else. That must be said plainly, because the natural but wrong assumption is that the distinction is between an unpaid rescue and a paid one. It is not. Both are paid. The difference is where the obligation to pay comes from:

rows: Source of the entitlement
The general maritime law, operating on the facts
The agreement between the parties
When terms are settled
Afterwards, by agreement or by a court
Before or during the service
Is it still salvage?
Yes
Yes - the agreement governs how the reward is fixed, not whether the service is salvage
No cure, no pay?
Always
Usually - the standard form preserves it, but the parties may agree otherwise, for instance a daily hire rate
How the amount is determined
By a court applying the Convention's criteria
By the machinery the contract provides - typically arbitration applying the same criteria
Typical circumstance
An unplanned rescue by whoever is present
A professional salvor engaged for a serious casualty

blocks.p: Two consequences are worth stating because they show the distinction has been understood rather than memorised:

ul: The Convention applies to both. It applies to salvage operations generally, and its criteria are used to fix the award whether or not there was a contract. That is why an arbitrator under the standard form applies the Convention's own criteria - the contract does not displace the law, it provides the machinery for applying it.

The parties may contract out of some of it, but not freely. The Convention permits the parties to agree otherwise, but a contract may be annulled or modified where it was entered into under undue influence or the influence of danger and its terms are inequitable, or where the payment is excessive or grossly inadequate. That protection exists precisely because contracts of this kind are signed under pressure.

blocks.h: 3. Demand 2 - simple examples

blocks.p: The stem asks for simple examples, and one clear example of each is worth more than a paragraph of qualification.

ul: Maritime (pure) salvage. A cargo ship on passage sights a small vessel disabled and drifting towards a lee shore. She closes, passes a line, and tows the casualty clear to a place of safety. Nothing is agreed - there is no time and no need. The salving ship's owners are afterwards entitled to a salvage reward, and if the amount cannot be agreed it is fixed by a court.

Contractual salvage. A laden tanker suffers a main engine failure in heavy weather and begins to drift. Her master, on the owners' instruction, signs Lloyd's Open Form with a professional salvage company, which despatches tugs, connects, and tows her to safety. The service is performed under the agreement, and the amount of the reward is settled afterwards by arbitration under that form.

By contrast - ordinary towage, which is neither. A tug engaged to move a ship from the anchorage to her berth for an agreed price is performing a contracted service, not salvage. There is no danger and the tug is under a prior duty. But if the tow encounters unforeseen danger beyond the scope of the towage contract - the ship breaks adrift in worsening weather and the tug saves her from grounding - a salvage claim can then arise, because at that point the tug is doing something she was not engaged to do.

blocks.p: That third example is the most useful of the three, because it shows exactly where the boundary lies.

blocks.h: 4. Demand 3 - who is responsible for payment of the award

blocks.p: This is the demand most often answered wrongly, and the Convention's answer is precise.
The award is payable by the owners of all the property that was saved, and each interest contributes in proportion to the saved value of its own property.
So where a laden ship is salved, the salvage award is borne by:

rows: The ship
The shipowner - the ship's proportion of the total salved value
The cargo
The cargo owners - the cargo's proportion, divided among the several cargo interests
Bunkers and stores
Their owner, which may be the charterer rather than the shipowner
Freight and hire at risk
Whoever stood to lose it
Containers and equipment
Their owners, if separately owned

blocks.p: Three points follow, and each is a scoring point:

ul: The shipowner is not liable for the whole award. He is liable for the ship's share. Where a fully laden ship is saved the cargo's share may be by far the larger part. Saying 'the shipowner pays' is the standard wrong answer.

Liability is proportionate, not joint for the whole. Each interest's exposure is limited by the saved value of its own property, and the total award can never exceed the total salved value. A salvor cannot recover more than he saved.

No salvage is payable for saving life alone. Life salvage carries no reward against the persons saved. A salvor of life who takes part in the operation is entitled to a fair share of the award payable for saving the property - but the reward still comes out of the property, not out of the people.

blocks.p: How the salvor actually secures payment. Because the award is owed by many parties whose property is aboard one ship, the practical machinery matters:

ul: The salvor has a maritime lien on the salved property, and may arrest it. That is his real security.

The property is therefore not released until salvage security is provided by or on behalf of each interest - guarantees from the hull underwriters for the ship and from cargo underwriters for the cargo.

Who ultimately bears the cost, as distinct from who is liable. The shipowner's share falls on the hull and machinery underwriters under the policy; the cargo's share falls on the cargo underwriters. Where the salvage was incurred for the common safety of the adventure it may also be brought into general average and adjusted between the interests on that basis. These are indemnity arrangements behind the liability, not the liability itself - the question asks who is responsible, and that is the property owners.

blocks.h: 5. Demand 4 - the form popularly used

blocks.p: The form is Lloyd's Standard Form of Salvage Agreement, universally known as Lloyd's Open Form or LOF. It is the dominant contract for emergency salvage worldwide, and at this sitting the current edition is LOF 2020. Earlier editions - LOF 1980, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2011 - remain in circulation and appear in reported cases, but the machinery has been substantially stable across editions, so an answer that understands the machinery is not at risk from naming an edition.
Two features explain why it is 'popularly used', and both are worth stating:

ul: It is 'open' because the sum to be paid is left open. Nothing has to be negotiated at the casualty. The master can sign in minutes, on the owners' authority, and work can begin.
It is short. The whole point of its design is that it can be agreed by radio or by a single signature at a moment when nobody has time to negotiate.

blocks.p: The characterisation that earns the mark: LOF is not a price. It is an agreement to arbitrate on the no cure, no pay principle. What the parties agree is the mechanism - that the salvor will work, that he is paid only on success, that the amount will be fixed later by a Lloyd's arbitrator, and that security will be provided. They agree nothing at all about the figure.

blocks.h: 6. Demand 5 - how the amount of the award is calculated under the form

blocks.p: Because LOF fixes no price, the calculation is done afterwards. The route is:

ol: The service is performed on no cure, no pay terms.
Security is provided by the salved interests; the property is then released.

If the amount cannot be agreed, it is determined by arbitration in London under Lloyd's arbitration procedure, by an arbitrator appointed by the Council of Lloyd's, with a right of appeal to an appeal arbitrator.
The arbitrator fixes the award by applying the criteria in Article 13 of the Salvage Convention - which is why an answer to this demand must go back to the Convention.
The award is then apportioned among the salvors, and where more than one salvor was involved between them, on the same criteria.

blocks.p: The Article 13 criteria. The Convention lists the matters the tribunal takes into account in fixing a reward that encourages salvage operations:

ul: the salved value of the vessel and other property;
the skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising damage to the environment;
the measure of success obtained by the salvor;
the nature and degree of the danger;
the skill and efforts of the salvors in salving the vessel, other property and life;
the time used and expenses and losses incurred by the salvors;
the risk of liability and other risks run by the salvors or their equipment;
the promptness of the services rendered;
the availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage operations;
the state of readiness and efficiency of the salvor's equipment and its value.

blocks.p: Three things must be said about that list, and they are where the marks are:

ul: The criteria are not ranked and are not a formula. They are weighed together in the round. There is no percentage of salved value, and an answer that offers one is wrong.

The salved value is a ceiling, not the basis. The reward must not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property. Salved value influences the award strongly, but the award is not a proportion of it.

Two of the criteria exist to encourage professional salvors to stay in business - the availability of purpose-built salvage equipment, and its state of readiness. The Convention deliberately rewards a salvor for having maintained an expensive capability that was standing by, not merely for the hours worked on this casualty. That is the policy behind the whole regime and noting it shows the scheme has been understood.

blocks.h: 7. The environmental exception - which qualifies the answers above

blocks.p: Pure 'no cure, no pay' produced a perverse result: a salvor attending a laden tanker aground in a sensitive area might work at great expense, prevent an enormous pollution incident, and yet recover nothing if the ship was ultimately lost. The Convention addresses this, and it changes both who pays and how much:

ul: Article 14 - special compensation. Where the salvor has carried out salvage operations in respect of a vessel which by herself or her cargo threatened damage to the environment, and has failed to earn a reward under Article 13 at least equivalent to the special compensation, he is entitled to special compensation covering his expenses, which may be increased where he actually prevented or minimised environmental damage.

And it is paid by the SHIPOWNER ALONE. This is a genuine and important exception to the answer given at section 4 - special compensation is not shared proportionately among the salved interests, because it is not a reward for saving property. In practice it falls on the shipowner's P&I club.

SCOPIC. Article 14 proved difficult and expensive to assess, so the industry produced the Special Compensation P&I Clause, a contractual alternative incorporated into LOF by agreement. The salvor may invoke SCOPIC at any time and regardless of whether there is any threat to the environment, which removes the argument about whether the threat existed. Remuneration is then assessed on an agreed tariff of rates for personnel, tugs and equipment, plus an uplift, and the shipowner provides security through the P&I club. If SCOPIC exceeds the Article 13 award, the shipowner pays the difference; if the Article 13 award is greater, the salvor takes that instead, subject to a discount for having invoked SCOPIC.

blocks.p: The closing observation that ties the answer to the question as asked: the two demands the stem separates - who pays, and how much - are answered differently depending on which limb of the regime is engaged. For an ordinary property salvage the answer is the salved interests, proportionately, on the Article 13 criteria. Where the environment was threatened, a second and quite different payer appears - the shipowner alone - assessed on expenses rather than on salved value.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks and five separate interrogatives printed as one unbroken paragraph with no lettering. That layout is the trap. On a question printed as a), b), c) the candidate has a checklist; here there is nothing to count against, and the commonest failure is to write at length on the first demand, give the examples, and then run out of paragraph before the last three.

Before writing anything, number the demands in the margin: (1) the difference, (2) examples, (3) who pays, (4) which form, (5) how calculated. Then write five visible sections. The whole of the structural risk on this question is disposed of by that one step.

blocks.h: Draw the distinction on the right basis

blocks.p: The natural assumption is that pure salvage is the unpaid rescue and contractual salvage is the paid one. That is wrong and it will cost the whole of the first demand. Both are paid. The distinction is whether the parties agreed anything before the service began.

The corollary is the point that separates a good answer: contractual salvage is still salvage. It is not a different thing that happens to look similar. The Convention applies to both, and an arbitrator under Lloyd's Open Form applies the Convention's own criteria. The contract supplies the machinery for fixing the reward; it does not displace the law that creates the entitlement.

blocks.h: 'Voluntary' does not mean unpaid

blocks.p: This is where candidates tie themselves in knots. The precondition of voluntariness means the salvor was under no pre-existing duty to render this service. A commercial salvage company that has signed a contract five minutes ago and expects a large award is still volunteering, because it was under no prior obligation to attend this casualty.

Who is not volunteering: the ship's own crew saving their own ship, because that is their duty; a tug doing what her towage contract already requires; a public body acting under a statutory duty. Getting these three examples out shows the concept is understood.

blocks.h: The towage boundary - the most useful example in the answer

blocks.p: Ordinary towage is a contracted service at an agreed price with no danger and no salvage element. But a towage can turn into a salvage. If the tow encounters danger that was not within the contemplation of the towage contract - the ship breaks adrift, the weather deteriorates beyond anything contracted for, the tug performs a service she was never engaged to perform - then a salvage claim arises from that point.
Use this as the third example. It illustrates the boundary better than either of the clean cases, and it is a real practical question that arises constantly.

blocks.h: Who pays - the answer that separates the scripts

blocks.p: The owners of all the property saved, each in proportion to the saved value of its own interest. Not the shipowner. Not the insurers. Not the master.

So on a laden ship the payers are the shipowner for the ship, the cargo owners for the cargo, the bunker owner - which may be the time charterer, not the shipowner - for the bunkers, and whoever had freight or hire at risk. Where a ship is fully laden with valuable cargo, the cargo's share can dwarf the ship's.

Then draw the distinction between liability and ultimate incidence. The property owners are liable. Behind them, hull underwriters indemnify the shipowner's share and cargo underwriters the cargo's share, and where the operation was for the common safety the whole may be brought into general average. The question asks who is responsible, and the answer is the property owners. Mentioning the insurance behind it shows commercial understanding; putting the insurers forward as the answer is wrong.

blocks.h: Two limits worth stating

ul: The award cannot exceed the total salved value. A salvor never recovers more than he saved. This is the natural ceiling on the whole regime.

No reward is payable for saving life alone. A life salvor who took part in the operation gets a fair share of the property award - but if nothing was saved but people, there is no fund to pay from. Most candidates find this counter-intuitive and it is worth a mark for stating it correctly.

blocks.h: LOF - describe the machinery, not the edition

blocks.p: Name the form: Lloyd's Open Form, and at this sitting the current edition is LOF 2020. But do not build the answer on the edition. The machinery has been stable across editions, and the mark is for understanding what the form does:

ul: It is 'open' - the sum is left open, so nothing is negotiated at the casualty.
It preserves no cure, no pay.
It is an agreement to arbitrate, in London, under Lloyd's procedure.
It provides for security, so the salvor is not left chasing many parties.

blocks.p: The single sentence that earns the mark on demand 4: LOF is not a price - it is an agreement about how the price will later be decided.

blocks.h: The Article 13 criteria - weighed, not scored

blocks.p: Ten criteria. Do not attempt to rank them and do not offer a percentage of salved value, because the Convention offers neither. They are weighed together in the round.

Three groupings help recall: what was achieved (salved value, measure of success, environmental protection); what it cost and risked (time, expenses, losses, risk of liability, danger faced); and what the salvor brought to it (skill, promptness, availability of salvage equipment, its readiness and value).

The last group is worth a sentence of commentary: the Convention deliberately rewards a professional salvor for having maintained an expensive standby capability, not merely for the hours he worked. Without that, nobody would keep salvage tugs available for casualties that may never come. Noting the policy shows the regime has been understood rather than listed.

blocks.h: Article 14 and SCOPIC - short but necessary

blocks.p: It is tempting to leave these out on a question that does not mention the environment. Include them briefly, because they change the answer to two of the five demands.

The problem they solve: a salvor who prevents a major pollution incident but ultimately fails to save the ship gets nothing under pure no cure, no pay. Article 14 special compensation fixes that - and crucially it is paid by the shipowner alone, in practice by his P&I club, not shared among the salved interests. That is a real exception to the answer at demand 3.

SCOPIC is the contractual replacement, incorporated into LOF by agreement, invoked by the salvor at any time whether or not there is an environmental threat, and assessed on an agreed tariff rather than argued about. Its practical virtue is that it removes the litigation about whether a threat to the environment existed at all.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Do not quote any Article of the Convention verbatim, or any LOF clause by number. Give the substance.
Do not cite case authority.
Do not offer a percentage of salved value as the award, or any monetary figure or SCOPIC tariff rate.
Do not say the shipowner pays the award.
Do not import the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 - at this sitting the Indian statute is the Act of 1958.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Who pays the salvage award?" The owners of ALL the property saved, each in proportion to the saved value of its own interest. Not the shipowner. Not the insurers.
"What is the difference between maritime and contractual salvage?" Whether there was a prior agreement - not whether money was paid. Both are paid.
"Is contractual salvage still salvage?" Yes. The Convention applies to both, and the arbitrator under LOF applies the Convention's own criteria.
"Does 'voluntary' mean unpaid?" No - it means under no pre-existing duty. A commercial salvor under a signed contract is still volunteering.
"When does a towage become a salvage?" When the tow meets danger beyond the scope of the towage contract and the tug does what she was never engaged to do.
"Is LOF a price?" No - it is an agreement to arbitrate on no cure, no pay.
"What percentage of salved value is the award?" There is no percentage. The criteria are weighed in the round, and the salved value is a ceiling.
"Who pays special compensation?" The shipowner alone, in practice through the P&I club - not the salved interests proportionately.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your master has signed LOF. What are the first three things you do in the engine room?
Who on board has authority to sign LOF, and on whose instruction?
Your ship is saved but the cargo is lost. Who contributes to the award?
What is a maritime lien, and why does the salvor care about it?
What is the practical difference between Article 14 and SCOPIC to a shipowner?
Your tug is towing you and the weather deteriorates badly. When does her claim change character?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Preconditions, then the five printed demands, then the exception. PRECONDITIONS (1): danger · voluntary · success. Then the stem's five, in order: DIFFERENCE (2) - prior agreement or not; EXAMPLES (3) - passing ship, signed LOF, and towage as the boundary; WHO PAYS (4) - all the property saved, in proportion to saved value; THE FORM (5) - LOF, an agreement to arbitrate; HOW CALCULATED (6) - Article 13, unranked, salved value is the ceiling. Then the EXCEPTION (7) - Article 14 special compensation, shipowner alone, or SCOPIC. Anchor: five questions in one paragraph - number them before you write.

The Salvage Convention text is not held by the corpus, which classifies this treaty family as citation and index only. quick_revision.recall_15s: FIVE demands, no lettering - number them first. Preconditions: DANGER · VOLUNTARY · SUCCESS (no cure no pay). (1) DIFFERENCE = was there a prior agreement? - not 'was there money?'. Pure salvage: entitlement from the act, by maritime law. Contractual: terms agreed first - still salvage, Convention still applies, arbitrator still uses Article 13. (2) EXAMPLES: passing ship tows a drifting vessel clear / master signs LOF with a professional salvor / ordinary towage is neither - but becomes salvage if danger arises beyond the contract. (3) WHO PAYS = owners of ALL property saved, each in proportion to its saved value - ship, cargo, bunkers, freight at risk. Shipowner pays only the ship's share. Secured by maritime lien + salvage security; H&M and cargo underwriters indemnify behind; may go into general average. Award ≤ total salved value. No reward for saving life alone. (4) FORM = Lloyd's Open Form, LOF 2020 current here - an agreement to ARBITRATE, not a price. (5) CALCULATION = London arbitration, Article 13 criteria - salved value, success, environmental efforts, danger, skill, time and expense, risk, promptness, availability and readiness of salvage equipment - unranked, weighed together, salved value is the ceiling. EXCEPTION: environmental threat → Art 14 special compensation, SHIPOWNER ALONE (P&I), or SCOPIC on an agreed tariff.
