blocks.p: Two further points on the international layer. India is not a party to the Hamburg Rules, and the Rotterdam Rules are not in force; neither governs any Indian bill at this sitting. And the Rules apply of their own force only where a bill of lading or similar document of title covers the contract - which is one more reason the choice of document at section 2 above is a substantive choice and not a clerical one.

The closing observation that ties the two limbs together. Limb (a) asks why a bill is made transferable, and limb (b) asks when it becomes the contract. They have the same answer. Both the transferability and the hardening of the document into the contract exist to serve one person - the stranger who buys or lends against a cargo he cannot see, on the faith of a piece of paper. Everything distinctive about the bill of lading follows from the decision to protect him.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks and three demands under two printed letters. Limb (a) hides two of them - the main function, and the reasons for an order bill - and limb (b) carries the third. Write three visible sections, not two, because the commonest structural failure here is to give the functions in detail and then dispose of the order bill in three lines.

Limb (b) is where the question actually lives. It recites the settled proposition that a bill is evidence of the contract and asks when it becomes the actual contract. That demand has no counterpart anywhere in the solved corpus, and it is answered by explaining the general rule first and the exceptions second.

blocks.h: Read the question properly - there are three demands, not two

blocks.p: The paper prints (a) and (b), but limb (a) contains two separate demands: the main function, and the reasons for an order bill. Answer them as two sections. A script that runs them together almost always gives the functions in detail and then disposes of the order bill in three lines, which loses about a third of the marks.
Note also the bracketed (a) (b) lettering - this is the only question on this paper that brackets its limb labels. It signals nothing; do not read anything into it.

blocks.h: Answer the singular 'main function' - do not dodge it

blocks.p: The stem says 'the main function', in the singular, and also says 'in detail'. The two together mean: give the three functions properly, then commit to an answer on which is principal.

Commit to the document of title function, and give the reason: a sea waybill is a receipt and is evidence of the contract, but it is not a document of title. So the first two functions are not distinctive of a bill of lading, and the third is. Every commercial use that makes the bill indispensable - CIF sales, string sales afloat, documentary credits, bank pledges - rests on the third function alone.
That single comparison with the sea waybill is the most efficient scoring sentence in the answer, because it disposes of the singular demand with a reason instead of an assertion.

blocks.h: Explain the mechanism before the reasons

blocks.p: The reasons for an order bill make no sense until the examiner can see that you know what one is. Three lines will do it: consigned 'to order' or 'to order of' rather than to a named person; transferred by endorsement and delivery, or by delivery alone if endorsed in blank; and the carrier delivers against presentation of an original, one accomplished original voiding the rest.
Then draw the contrast that the stem actually asks for: the straight bill names one consignee, is not transferable by endorsement, and the cargo can go to that person and to nobody else.

blocks.h: The four reasons - and the one that is usually given badly

ul: Sale afloat. Commodity cargoes are sold in strings, and at shipment the seller often does not know who the final receiver is. Only a transferable document permits it.

Financing. This is the important one and it is usually reduced to 'banks want it'. Say why: the bank advances money against goods it will never see, and its security is that it holds the bill as a pledge and can obtain and sell the cargo if it is not repaid. A bill naming the buyer as consignee gives the bank no security whatever, because the buyer can collect his cargo without it. The order form is the precondition of the credit, not a preference.

Retention of the right of disposal. The seller takes the bill to his own order, so the goods are afloat but still under his control, and he endorses only when paid. If the buyer defaults he can sell to somebody else.
Control of delivery, which protects the carrier too. The master cannot possibly know who has bought a cargo three times over. The presentation rule converts that impossible enquiry into a simple one.

blocks.p: Then add a short paragraph on the costs - the bill that arrives after the ship, the letter of indemnity that follows and the P&I cover it forfeits, mis-delivery liability, fraud with blank endorsements and switch bills, and the stale bill. An answer that presents the order bill as pure advantage reads as recited; one that prices it reads as understood.

blocks.h: Limb (b) is not a trick - explain the rule before the exception

blocks.p: The stem states that the bill is evidence of the contract. That statement is correct. Do not attack it. The question asks when the position is otherwise, and you cannot answer that without first saying why the general rule exists.

Give the three reasons: the contract was concluded before the bill existed (space booked, rate agreed, goods delivered); the bill is signed by the carrier alone; and it is issued as a consequence of the contract rather than as its formation. The consequence between carrier and shipper is that the bill is strong but not conclusive evidence, and evidence of the actual bargain is admissible.

blocks.h: The answer they want is the transfer to a third party

blocks.p: Once the bill is transferred to a consignee or endorsee, its terms are the contract between the carrier and that holder. Give the reasoning, not just the rule: the transferee was not party to the earlier bargain, has only the document, and has usually paid on the faith of it; if the carrier could prove some different agreement the document would be worthless as a trading instrument.

A high-scoring connection: this is the same movement as the one that makes the statements of quantity and apparent order and condition conclusive rather than prima facie once the bill reaches a good faith third party. Both hardenings happen at the same moment and for the same reason. Say so.

blocks.h: The charterparty bill - the best illustration available

blocks.p: Use it, because it shows the same document holding two characters at once. In the charterer's hands the bill is a mere receipt, because the contract between owner and charterer is the charterparty. In an indorsee's hands the same bill is the contract between owner and holder, since the holder is not party to the charterparty and may never have seen it. Charterparty terms bind him only so far as they are effectively incorporated.

blocks.h: Two more circumstances, quickly

ul: No antecedent agreement at all - a parcel shipped with no prior booking. There is no earlier contract for the bill to evidence, so the bill is the contract.
The parties agree it shall govern - a booking note stating that carriage is subject to the terms of the carrier's bill of lading. Unglamorous and extremely common.

blocks.h: Then land it on the statute

blocks.p: The Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 vests in the consignee or endorsee all rights of suit 'as if the contract contained in the bill of lading had been made with himself'. That statutory phrase is the best single line available for limb (b), because the legislature itself speaks of the contract being contained in the bill.

blocks.h: Get the statute book right - this is the trap on this question

blocks.p: At this sitting the Indian frame is the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856, the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993 giving effect to the Hague-Visby Rules, and the Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930 for the document-of-title characterisation, with the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 as the governing shipping statute.

Do not write the Bills of Lading Act 2025 or the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 into this answer. Both commenced on 10 September 2025 - thirty-one months after this paper was sat. They repealed the 1856 and 1925 Acts and re-enacted the Rules with modifications and with different article numbering. Material written for a 2025 or 2026 sitting on this subject is entirely wrong for this one, and this is the only question in the batch where the Indian statute book itself moved.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Do not cite any Article or rule of the Hague-Visby Rules by number. Give the substance - no held source fixes the numbering for this sitting, and the later Indian re-enactment renumbers them.
Do not cite case authority. None is held, and no case name should appear.
Do not import the donor question's limb on the obligations of shipowner, carrier and consignee. It is not asked here.
Do not quote any bill of lading clause or condition. No form is held.
Do not give any package limitation figure, SDR value or monetary amount.
Do not say the order bill is 'negotiable' without qualifying it - a transferee takes no better title than his transferor had.
Do not describe the letter of indemnity as a normal or proper commercial practice. It is universal, and it is outside the contract.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Which Act governs bills of lading in India at this sitting?" The Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993. Not the 2025 Acts - they commenced 10 September 2025, thirty-one months later.
"What is the main function?" The document of title function - because a sea waybill is also a receipt and also evidence of the contract, and is not a document of title.
"Why does a bank insist on an order bill?" Because it holds it as a pledge and can obtain and sell the cargo if it is not repaid. A bill naming the buyer gives the bank no security at all.

"Is an order bill negotiable in the same sense as a bill of exchange?" No. A transferee takes no better title than his transferor had. 'Negotiable' here means transferable by endorsement and delivery.
"When does the bill become the contract?" On transfer to a consignee or endorsee, who was not party to the antecedent bargain and has only the document.
"What is a charterparty bill in the charterer's own hands?" A mere receipt - the contract between owner and charterer is the charterparty. In an indorsee's hands the same bill is the contract.
"Is a letter of indemnity for a clean bill proper?" No. It is universal, and it asks the carrier to make an untrue statement to the world.
"What else changes at the moment of transfer?" The receipt statements harden from prima facie to conclusive - the same movement, at the same moment, for the same reason.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your cargo has arrived and the receiver has no bill of lading. What happens next?
What is a letter of indemnity, and why does your P&I club dislike it?
Who signs the bill of lading on your ship, and on whose authority?
The mate wants to clause the bill and the shipper objects. What do you do?
How many original bills are issued, and what happens when one is presented?
What is a sea waybill, and why would a shipper use one instead?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Three demands, six sections. FUNCTIONS (1): receipt · evidence of contract · document of title - and the third is the MAIN one, because a sea waybill has the first two and not the third. MECHANISM (2): 'to order', transferred by endorsement and delivery, delivered against one original presented. REASONS (3): sell afloat · finance · right of disposal · control delivery - plus the costs, LOI and mis-delivery. Then limb (b): WHY ONLY EVIDENCE (4) - the contract was made before the bill existed and the carrier signs alone. WHEN IT BECOMES THE CONTRACT (5) - on transfer, the charterparty bill, no antecedent agreement, agreement that it shall govern, and the statute. STATUTE BOOK (6): 1856 + 1925 as amended 1993, and the 2025 Acts are thirty-one months future.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, and the statute book that moved after this sitting

blocks.p: This is the only question in the 2023 batch so far on which the Indian statute book itself was replaced between the sitting and a corpus donor, and that is the live risk. The Bills of Lading Act 2025 and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 commenced on 10 September 2025 - thirty-one months after this paper - repealing the 1856 and 1925 Acts and re-enacting the Rules with modifications. The corpus's October 2025 answer to the same subject is written entirely on them, and its whole statutory layer is excluded here.

No article or rule of the Hague-Visby Rules is asserted by number anywhere, and the prohibition is substantive rather than formal. No carriage-convention text is held for this sitting - India Code publishes current law only and removed both Acts on repeal - and the two corpus donors cite the same provisions under two different numbering schemes, because the 2025 re-enactment renumbers. No held source fixes the numbering a February 2023 candidate would have found, so the substance is stated and the addresses are not.

The text of the 1856 Act is likewise not held. Its first section and the effect of that section are carried at INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED provenance, and no wording of the Act is quoted - the statutory formula given in the answer is presented as substance.

One genuinely contested practical question is recorded as unresolved rather than decided: whether a carrier may lawfully deliver against a straight bill without production of the document. The answer states only that a prudent carrier requires production in any event, and states that as practice rather than as law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the bill of lading question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the three functions and which is main. 2 what an order bill is and how it is negotiated. 3 the four reasons for choosing it over a named consignee, plus its costs. 4 why the bill is normally only evidence. 5 the five circumstances in which it becomes the contract. 6 the Indian statute book operative at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: Two printed letters conceal three demands, and the second demand in limb (a) is the one habitually compressed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The three functions of a bill of lading.
retrieval_cards.answer: A receipt for the goods - marks, quantity and apparent order and condition. Evidence of the contract of carriage. A document of title, transferable and the key to delivery.
retrieval_cards.why: Everything else on the question is built on these three.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which is the MAIN function, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: The document of title function. A sea waybill is also a receipt and also evidence of the contract, but it is not a document of title - so only the third function is distinctive of a bill of lading, and CIF sales, string sales afloat, documentary credits and bank pledges all depend on it alone.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks in the singular; the sea waybill comparison answers it with a reason rather than an assertion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an order bill actually transfer?
retrieval_cards.answer: By endorsement and delivery. A special endorsement names the next holder, who must endorse again; a blank endorsement is a bare signature and converts the bill into a bearer bill passing by delivery alone. Bills issue in a set of originals and delivery against any one accomplishes the set.
retrieval_cards.why: The reasons for using an order bill cannot be explained without the mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a bank require an order bill?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it advances money against goods it will never see, and its only security is holding the bill as a pledge so that it can obtain and sell the cargo if it is not repaid. A bill naming the buyer as consignee gives the bank no security at all - the buyer can collect the cargo whether or not he has paid.
retrieval_cards.why: The financing reason is the most important and is usually reduced to 'banks want it'.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the 'right of disposal' and how does an order bill preserve it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The seller's continuing control over goods already shipped. By taking the bill to his own order he keeps the key to delivery, endorses it only when paid or secured, and can sell the cargo to a different buyer if the first defaults.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the reason a seller, as distinct from a bank, wants an order bill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the order bill cost the industry?
retrieval_cards.answer: Documents that arrive after the ship, and the letters of indemnity that follow - outside the contract and forfeiting P&I cover; strict mis-delivery exposure for the full cargo value; fraud through blank endorsements, sets of originals and switch bills; and the stale bill rejected under a credit.
retrieval_cards.why: A discussion of why the order bill is used that reports no cost reads as recited.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the bill NORMALLY only evidence of the contract?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the contract was concluded before the bill existed - space booked, rate agreed, goods delivered; because the bill is signed by the carrier alone; and because it is issued as a consequence of the contract rather than as its formation. Between carrier and shipper it is strong but not conclusive evidence.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) cannot be answered without the general rule being explained first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does the bill become the ACTUAL contract?
retrieval_cards.answer: Principally on transfer to a consignee or endorsee. He was not party to the antecedent bargain, has only the document, and has usually paid on the faith of it - so evidence of any different agreement is not admitted against him, and the bill's terms are the contract between him and the carrier.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the answer the question is looking for and it is the demand with no donor in the corpus.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What else hardens at the moment of transfer?
retrieval_cards.answer: The receipt statements. The description of quantity and of apparent order and condition is prima facie evidence in the carrier's hands but becomes conclusive once the bill is transferred to a third party in good faith. The document hardens as it moves away from the parties who made the bargain.
retrieval_cards.why: Linking the two escalations shows the principle understood rather than two rules memorised.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The charterparty bill - two characters at once.
retrieval_cards.answer: In the charterer's own hands it is a mere receipt, because the contract of carriage between owner and charterer is the charterparty. In an indorsee's hands the same bill is the contract between the owner and that holder, and charterparty terms bind him only so far as effectively incorporated.
retrieval_cards.why: The sharpest available illustration that the character of the document depends on whose hands it is in.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The other three circumstances.
retrieval_cards.answer: Where there was no antecedent agreement at all, so the bill issued on shipment is the only statement of terms. Where the parties agree it shall govern - a booking note subject to the carrier's bill of lading terms. And by statute, through the vesting of rights of suit in the transferee.
retrieval_cards.why: Five circumstances make a complete limb (b); most scripts give one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Its first section vests in the consignee named in the bill, or in the endorsee to whom property passes upon or by reason of the consignment or endorsement, all rights of suit and the same liabilities as if the contract contained in the bill of lading had been made with himself. It also preserves the shipper's own liability for freight.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Bill of lading against sea waybill.
retrieval_cards.answer: Both are receipts and both are evidence of the contract of carriage. The waybill is not a document of title, is not transferable by endorsement, and the goods are released to the named consignee on proof of identity with no document surrendered. It is quick and safe, and it cannot be sold or pledged.
retrieval_cards.why: It isolates the one distinctive function and answers the singular demand.

regulations: Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 (Act 9 of 1856) - IN FORCE at this sitting. Its first section vests in the consignee named in the bill of lading, and in the endorsee to whom property in the goods passes upon or by reason of the consignment or endorsement, all rights of suit and the same liabilities in respect of the goods as if the contract contained in the bill of lading had been made with himself; the shipper's own liability for freight is preserved. REPEALED by the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 with effect from 10 September 2025 - thirty-one months AFTER this sitting.

Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, as amended by the amending Act of 1993 - IN FORCE at this sitting. It is the vehicle by which the HAGUE-VISBY RULES have effect in Indian law, its Schedule setting out the Rules. REPEALED and re-enacted with modifications by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 with effect from 10 September 2025 - thirty-one months AFTER this sitting.

The Hague-Visby Rules as scheduled to the 1925 Act - the carrier's obligation to exercise DUE DILIGENCE BEFORE AND AT THE BEGINNING OF THE VOYAGE to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the cargo spaces fit and safe; the obligation to load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods properly and carefully; the shipper's right to demand a bill showing the leading marks, the number of packages or pieces or the quantity or weight, and the apparent order and condition of the goods, subject to the proviso that the carrier need not state what he has no reasonable means of checking; the escalation of that description from prima facie evidence to conclusive evidence once the bill has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith; the one-year time bar; the package or unit and weight limitation, whose unit of account is the Special Drawing Right; and the nullity of any clause relieving or lessening the carrier's liability otherwise than as the Rules provide. NO ARTICLE OR RULE IS ASSERTED BY NUMBER ANYWHERE IN THIS ANSWER - see unresolved.
Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930 - includes the bill of lading within the definition of a document of title to goods, which is the statutory anchor in Indian law for the document-of-title function.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the governing Indian shipping statute at this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and is THIRTY-SEVEN MONTHS FUTURE.
Hamburg Rules (United Nations Convention on the Carriage of Goods by Sea, 1978) - INDIA IS NOT A PARTY. Not applicable to any Indian bill at this sitting.
Rotterdam Rules (United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Carriage of Goods Wholly or Partly by Sea, 2008) - NOT IN FORCE at this sitting.

PROHIBITED AS FUTURE: the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025) and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), both in force 10 SEPTEMBER 2025, THIRTY-ONE MONTHS after this sitting. questions.short_title: High-Efficiency Propellers - Ducted, Kappel, Contra-Rotating and Azimuth, with Merits and Demerits
questions.text_verbatim: Improving efficiency of propellers is recognized as a growing means to improve energy efficiency of ships. Discuss any three of the following high-efficiency propellers with its merits and demerits: a) Ducted Propellers b) Kappel Propellers c) Cortra rotating Propellers. d) Azimuth Propulsion.

It is preserved in text_verbatim and in the subparts, the device is named correctly as CONTRA-ROTATING once in the answer with a single sentence explaining why, and it is recorded at anchor section 1.4. SECOND DELTA - AND THE ONLY SUBSTANTIVE ONE - THE REGULATORY FRAMING RUNS THE OTHER WAY FROM THE USUAL DIRECTION. Normally a donor asserts something later than the sitting and it must be stripped out. Here BOTH DONORS DELIBERATELY ASSERT NOTHING AT ALL: each carries an EMPTY regulations list, and each records in terms that the MARPOL Annex VI energy efficiency provisions were not read in a licensed consolidated edition, so that no regulation number and no date for EEXI or CII is stated anywhere in either record. THE DIRECTION OF THIS DELTA IS UNUSUAL ENOUGH TO STATE PLAINLY: this is not a case of a later donor over-claiming, but of two earlier records under-claiming relative to what this paper can prove. THIRD DELTA - WHAT THE FRAMING MUST NOT SAY. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy is five months future and is excluded by name; the EU Emissions Trading System extension to maritime is eleven months future and excluded; the IMO Net-Zero Framework is thirty-two months future and excluded. A donor written in October 2025 could say that operators had seen their ratings and were retrofitting in response; that sentence is unavailable here and it is not written. FOURTH DELTA - COVERAGE. MARKS DELTA: neither donor prints mark figures against the four items either, so there is no divergence to record; both carry 16 by rubric as this paper does.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A COMPARATIVE TECHNICAL QUESTION WITH THREE INSTRUCTIONS HIDDEN IN THE STEM, AND CANDIDATES BREAK ALL THREE. First, 'any three of the following' - four devices are printed and three are to be answered. Writing four gives four shallow treatments where three deep ones were wanted, and writing all four is the commonest single error on this question. Second, 'with its merits AND demerits' - both are required, and a device described with advantages only scores about half. Third, the opening sentence is not decoration: 'Improving efficiency of propellers is recognized as a growing means to improve energy efficiency of ships' supplies the framing, and an answer that opens straight into nozzle geometry without saying why any of this is being done has skipped the examiner's own premise. The discriminator is whether the candidate can locate each device against a NAMED LOSS MECHANISM rather than listing features.

The framing is worth including precisely because it is cheap - two short paragraphs - and because it is the part most candidates omit entirely.

Propeller hydrodynamics did not change between this sitting and either donor, and no instrument prescribes a propeller type or design concept, so there is no citation in the technical body that can go out of date. The framing is a different matter: it sits six weeks after the EEXI and CII applicability date and three months after the revised Annex VI entered into force, and five months before a strategy that both donors would treat as current.

technical_ambiguities: Whether the printed 'Cortra rotating Propellers' could be a device other than contra-rotating propellers. It could not. No such device exists, both exact donor instances print 'Contra rotating Propellers' in the same list position with the same three companions, and the corruption is a straightforward transposition. The device is answered as CONTRA-ROTATING and the answer says once, plainly, that the paper prints it otherwise.

Whether a duct always improves efficiency. IT DOES NOT, and this is the most important single discrimination on the question. The duct's benefit rises with THRUST LOADING; on a lightly loaded, fast, fine-form ship the duct's own frictional and form drag exceeds the thrust it generates and the installation is a net loss. An answer that presents the duct as an unqualified improvement has not understood it.

Whether the Kappel propeller is an add-on device. It is not. The tip curvature is INTEGRAL BLADE GEOMETRY, formed in the casting, not a bolted-on end plate or fin. This matters because the whole of its merit case - no added appendage, no added drag, no added maintenance item, straight replacement retrofit - depends on it being integral.

Whether contra-rotation is limited by hydrodynamics or by mechanics. BY MECHANICS. The hydrodynamic case is the strongest of the three, because swirl is the largest single recoverable loss and the after propeller recovers it directly. What has restricted the arrangement in large merchant service is coaxial shafting, the gearing and above all the concentric shaft SEALING arrangement. Saying this shows the candidate knows why a theoretically superior device is rare.

Whether azimuth propulsion belongs in a question about high-efficiency PROPELLERS at all, given that it is a propulsion and steering arrangement rather than a blade or a duct. The stem prints it as one of the four, so the examiner has decided the point. The answer treats it on its own terms - the efficiency gain is real but comes from the clean inflow and the deletion of shafting, struts and rudder, not from the blade - and says so, because a candidate who claims the propeller itself is more efficient has misplaced the mechanism.

Whether any quantified gain can be defended. NOT FROM ANY VERIFIABLE SOURCE. No percentage appears anywhere in this answer and the reason is stated positively, so that a candidate does not supply one.

steps.title: Why propeller efficiency is being pursued - the framing the stem supplies
points: The propeller is the last conversion in the chain and among the least efficient
Revised MARPOL Annex VI in force 1 November 2022; EEXI and CII applicable from 1 January 2023 - six weeks old
A propeller improves both the design index and the operational rating - few measures do both
And unlike slow steaming it costs the operator no time
Operative strategy is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018

steps.title: Where the losses occur - the map the rest of the answer hangs on
points: Propulsive efficiency = hull efficiency × open-water efficiency × relative rotative efficiency
AXIAL loss - kinetic energy left in the accelerated slipstream
ROTATIONAL loss - the race leaves the disc spinning; that swirl is wasted
FRICTIONAL loss - viscous drag on the blade surfaces
TIP VORTEX loss - pressure equalises round the tip and sheds a vortex
Cavitation sets the ceiling on how hard a blade may be loaded
Each device attacks a different loss - that is the organising idea

steps.title: (a) Ducted propellers - an attack on the axial loss
points: An annular aerofoil round the disc; an accelerating duct raises velocity through it and cuts the thrust each blade must make
The duct is itself a lifting surface, so it generates thrust; it also closes the tip gap
Benefit rises with THRUST LOADING - tugs, trawlers, slow full-form ships
MERITS - large thrust augmentation and bollard pull; propeller protection; course stability, or steering with a nozzle
DEMERITS - a net penalty at light loading; fouling, corrosion, debris and ice; internal cavitation erosion; weight, survey and maintenance

steps.title: (b) Kappel propellers - an attack on the tip vortex loss
points: Blade tips curved smoothly towards the suction side as an integrated continuous winglet - not a bolted-on device
Load is carried further outboard while the tip vortex is weakened and displaced; the analogy is the aircraft winglet
MERITS - tip loss cut at the same diameter; no appendage, so no added drag or maintenance item; smoother wake into the rudder, so less vibration; straight replacement retrofit
DEMERITS - modest gain, highly wake-dependent; hull-specific design, CFD and model testing; complex geometry harder to cast, repair and re-pitch; benefit falls away off the design condition

steps.title: (c) Contra-rotating propellers - an attack on the rotational loss
points: Two coaxial propellers turning in opposite directions; the after one recovers the swirl left by the forward one
Swirl is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation

MERITS - highest theoretical gain; thrust split, so lower loading per propeller, less cavitation and vibration; torque reaction largely cancelled; smaller diameter for a given thrust where draught limits it

DEMERITS - limited by mechanics, not hydrodynamics: coaxial shafting and epicyclic gearing, and above all the concentric shaft seal; harder alignment, maintenance and drydocking; little large-merchant service experience

steps.title: (d) Azimuth propulsion - an attack on hull-side and appendage losses
points: A propeller on a unit that rotates through 360°; mechanical Z-drive, or a podded electric unit with the motor in the pod
Efficiency comes from the clean, uniform inflow and the deletion of shafting, struts, brackets and rudder - not from the blade
A pulling unit works in undisturbed water, which is the main gain
MERITS - clean inflow and no appendage drag; full thrust in any direction, so no tunnel thrusters and no rudder; diesel-electric plant flexibility; aft-body freed for cargo

DEMERITS - electrical conversion losses offset part of the gain; high capital cost and complexity; the pod cannot be opened at sea and needs drydocking; slipring, bearing and seal reliability; appendage and structural drag of the pod at high speed

steps.title: Comparative judgement, and the instruction printed in the stem
points: The choice follows thrust loading and operating profile, not fashion
Heavily loaded and slow → the duct earns its drag. Lightly loaded and fast → the duct makes it worse
Moderately loaded single screw, clean wake → Kappel. Large swirl and complexity acceptable → contra-rotating. Manoeuvring-dominated or DP → azimuth
ANSWER THREE, NOT FOUR, and give merits AND demerits for each
Give no percentage figures - they are vendor claims and hull-specific

questions.understand_first: A ship's propeller is the last step in a long chain. Fuel becomes heat, heat becomes shaft power, and shaft power becomes thrust. Each step loses something, but the last step loses the most that can still be recovered, and that is why so much design effort is spent on a piece of bronze that looks unchanged since the nineteenth century. To see where the losses are, it helps to think about what a propeller actually does. It pushes the ship forward by throwing water backwards. That is Newton's third law and there is no way round it - but it means that when the ship has passed, there is a column of water behind it moving astern that was not moving before. Somebody paid for the energy in that moving water, and it is doing nothing useful. That is the axial loss, and the only way to reduce it is to throw a larger mass of water backwards a little more slowly rather than a small mass very fast. That is why large slow-turning propellers are more efficient than small fast ones. But a propeller does not only throw water backwards. It is a rotating device, so it also leaves the water spinning. That spin is pure waste - it contributes nothing to driving the ship - and on a normal installation it is the biggest single loss that could in principle be recovered. Then there is simple friction on the blade surfaces, and finally, because there is high pressure on one side of a blade and low pressure on the other, at the open tip the two sides meet and the water rolls up into a vortex that trails away behind, taking energy with it. Those four losses are the whole story, and once you have them, every device in this question falls into place. The duct is an attack on the axial loss. The Kappel blade is an attack on the tip vortex. Contra-rotating propellers are an attack on the swirl, and they are the most direct attack available - a second propeller turning the other way straightens out the water the first one spun. Azimuth propulsion is different in kind: the propeller itself is not better, but it works in clean undisturbed water instead of in the disturbed wake behind a hull, and all the shafts, struts and rudders that used to drag along behind the ship have been deleted. One warning underlies the whole answer. None of these devices is simply better. Each buys a reduction in one loss by paying something somewhere else - drag, complexity, cost, reliability, or a benefit that only appears if the ship is operated the way the designer assumed. The examiner asks for merits and demerits because that trade is the subject.

blocks.h: 1. Why propeller efficiency is being pursued - the framing the stem supplies

blocks.p: The stem opens by saying that improving propeller efficiency is 'a growing means to improve energy efficiency of ships'. That sentence is the examiner's premise and should be answered before the devices are described, because it explains why any of this is being done.

The engineering reason. The propeller is the last energy conversion in the chain and one of the least efficient. Resistance rises steeply with speed, so a small improvement in propulsive efficiency returns real fuel over a voyage - and unlike slow steaming, which is the other obvious lever, it costs the operator no time.
The regulatory reason at this sitting, which is six weeks old. The position in February 2023 is precise and it is worth stating precisely:

ul: The revised MARPOL Annex VI adopted by resolution MEPC.328(76) entered into force on 1 November 2022 - three months before this sitting.

Its chapter 4 requirements apply from 1 January 2023 - six weeks before this sitting. Existing ships must have an attained EEXI not exceeding the required value under regulations 23 and 25, and ships above the applicable size must determine an annual operational carbon intensity and be rated A to E under regulation 28.
The enhanced SEEMP, including the Part III carbon intensity plan, has been required on board from the same date.
The operative strategy behind all of it is the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, of 2018.

blocks.p: Why this makes propeller work unusually attractive. Most efficiency measures improve one thing or the other. A propeller improves both: it lowers the attained EEXI, which is a design index calculated once, and it lowers fuel per tonne-mile in service, which improves the annual carbon intensity and therefore the rating. Very few retrofits do both, and fewer still do both without costing speed.

An important qualification about the rating, which fixes the answer to this sitting. The first CII reporting year began on 1 January 2023 and the rating is determined only after the calendar year has ended. At the date of this paper no ship holds a CII rating. The pressure is therefore anticipatory - owners are acting on what they expect their rating to be and on the requirement that a ship rated D for three consecutive years or E in any year must submit a corrective action plan - and the answer is written that way rather than as a description of ratings already received.
The EEXI reduction-factor framework itself is treated at Q3 of this paper and is not repeated here.

blocks.h: 2. Where the losses occur - the map the rest of the answer hangs on

blocks.p: The devices cannot be compared unless it is clear what each of them attacks. Overall propulsive efficiency is conventionally decomposed as:
Propulsive efficiency = hull efficiency × open-water (propeller) efficiency × relative rotative efficiency
Three of the four devices in this question attack the middle term; the fourth attacks the first. The open-water efficiency is limited by four loss mechanisms:

rows: Axial
Kinetic energy left in the slipstream, which is accelerated astern and does no further useful work. Reduced by moving a larger mass of water more slowly - hence large, slow-turning propellers
The duct
Rotational (swirl)
The race leaves the disc spinning. That rotation contributes nothing to thrust and is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation
Contra-rotating propellers
Frictional
Viscous drag over the blade surfaces. Reduced by blade area no larger than needed, good section design and a clean, smooth, unfouled surface
Blade design and maintenance
Tip vortex
At the open blade tip the pressure difference between face and back equalises, rolling up into a trailing vortex that carries energy away
The Kappel blade

blocks.p: Two constraints sit over all of them. Cavitation sets the ceiling on how hard a blade may be loaded - push a section too hard and the low-pressure side vaporises, which destroys thrust, erodes the blade and generates noise and vibration. And the propeller does not work in clean water: it works in the ship's wake, which is non-uniform, so each blade passes through a varying inflow once per revolution. That is the source of the pressure pulses felt in the aft accommodation, and it is why a device that works on one hull may do nothing on another.

blocks.h: 3. (a) Ducted propellers - an attack on the axial loss

blocks.p: 3.1 The principle
A ducted propeller runs inside an annular aerofoil - a nozzle, commonly called a Kort nozzle - fitted concentrically around the propeller disc with a small tip clearance.

ul: In the usual accelerating form, the duct's internal section converges towards the propeller plane, so the water velocity through the disc is increased. The propeller therefore has to produce less thrust for the same total, because it is working on a faster stream.

The duct is itself a lifting surface. The flow round its aerofoil section generates a force with a forward component, so the duct contributes thrust of its own - typically a substantial share of the total on a heavily loaded installation.
It also closes the tip gap, so the tip vortex is largely suppressed as a secondary benefit.

A decelerating duct - diverging towards the disc - is used instead where the object is to raise pressure at the propeller and suppress cavitation and radiated noise, at some cost in efficiency. Naval and research vessels use it.

blocks.p: The governing variable is THRUST LOADING - thrust per unit of disc area. The higher it is, the more the duct earns.
3.2 Merits

ul: Large thrust augmentation at high loading. On tugs, trawlers, pushers and slow full-form ships the gain is substantial, and bollard pull in particular improves markedly.
Thrust at low speed and when towing - precisely the conditions in which an open propeller is least efficient.
Protection of the propeller from ropes, nets, floating debris and quay contact.
Course stability with a fixed nozzle; and with a steerable nozzle, a large gain in manoeuvring capability, since the whole jet is directed.
Suppression of the tip vortex, and often reduced propeller-excited hull vibration as a consequence.

blocks.p: 3.3 Demerits

ul: It is a net penalty at light loading, and this is the essential qualification. The duct has its own frictional and form drag, which it carries all the time. On a fast, fine-form, lightly loaded ship that drag exceeds the thrust the duct generates, and fitting one makes the ship worse. A duct is not an improvement in itself; it is an improvement in the right application.

Fouling, corrosion and mechanical damage. The duct is a large wetted surface that fouls, and its internal surface is exposed to debris and ice. Tip clearance is small and critical; a distorted duct can foul the propeller.
Cavitation erosion on the internal surface, in the high-velocity region near the blade tips, is a recognised maintenance problem.
Added weight, structure and support, with the associated survey burden and drydock work.
Poor astern performance in some configurations, since the duct is shaped for one flow direction.

blocks.p: Fit it when: the ship is slow, full-formed and heavily loaded, or does towing or trawling work. Do not fit it when: the ship is fast and lightly loaded.

blocks.h: 4. (b) Kappel propellers - an attack on the tip vortex loss

blocks.p: 4.1 The principle
The Kappel propeller is a conventional propeller whose blade tips are curved smoothly towards the suction side, forming a continuous integrated winglet.

ul: The curvature is part of the blade geometry, cast in. It is not an end plate, fin or cap bolted to a standard blade, and the distinction carries the whole of its merit case.

The aeronautical analogy is exact enough to be worth stating: an aircraft winglet reduces induced drag by weakening and displacing the wing-tip vortex, and the curved propeller tip does the same to the blade-tip vortex.

The effect is to allow load to be carried further outboard - where a blade element is most effective, because it moves fastest - while the vortex that would normally result is weakened and shed further from the blade.

blocks.p: 4.2 Merits

ul: Reduced tip vortex loss at the same diameter. This matters because diameter is very often fixed by draught, aperture or ground clearance, and this device improves efficiency without needing any more of it.
No additional appendage. There is nothing extra in the water, so no added drag, no added structure, no additional item to survey and nothing extra to foul or lose.
A smoother, more uniform wake into the rudder, which reduces hull pressure pulses, vibration and radiated noise - a real benefit on ships where aft accommodation vibration is a complaint.
Retrofittable as a straight replacement. The ship takes a new propeller at a scheduled docking; no hull modification, no shafting change and no change to the machinery.

blocks.p: 4.3 Demerits

ul: The gain is modest compared with the duct at high loading or with contra-rotation, and it is highly dependent on the wake field of the particular hull. It is not a general-purpose improvement.

It requires hull-specific design - wake measurement or computation, CFD and normally model testing - so the design cost is high and cannot be amortised across a class unless the ships are truly identical.
The curved geometry is harder and more expensive to cast, to inspect, to repair after damage and to re-pitch.

The benefit falls away when the ship operates away from the design condition - a different draught, trim or speed than the one the blade was optimised for. A ship whose trading pattern changes may not keep the gain it paid for.

blocks.p: Fit it when: a moderately loaded single-screw ship with a reasonably clean wake needs a gain without a hull change, and the trading pattern is stable.

blocks.h: 5. (c) Contra-rotating propellers - an attack on the rotational loss

blocks.p: A note on the printed word. The paper prints 'Cortra rotating Propellers'. There is no such device; the intended device is the contra-rotating propeller, and it is answered as such. The misprint is noted once and not laboured.
5.1 The principle

ul: Two propellers on the same axis, one behind the other, turning in opposite directions.

The forward propeller leaves its race spinning. The after propeller, turning the other way, is set in that swirling flow and recovers the rotational energy directly, converting it into additional thrust instead of allowing it to be shed astern.

This is the most direct attack available on any of the losses, because rotational loss is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation - typically the biggest item after the unavoidable axial loss.

Mechanically it requires coaxial shafting, an inner shaft running inside a hollow outer shaft, driven through epicyclic gearing that reverses one output; or, in the modern arrangement, a conventional propeller forward with an azimuthing podded unit aft carrying the second.

blocks.p: 5.2 Merits

ul: The highest theoretical gain of the devices in this question, and gained by direct recovery rather than by redistribution.
The total thrust is divided between two propellers, so the loading per propeller falls for the same total thrust.
Lower loading means a reduced cavitation risk, lower blade stresses and reduced propeller-excited vibration.
Torque reaction is very largely cancelled between the two units, which improves course keeping and removes the steady helm bias a single screw induces.
A smaller diameter can deliver a given thrust, which is valuable where draught or aperture limits diameter - exactly the constraint that limits the conventional route to efficiency.

blocks.p: 5.3 Demerits

The limitation is mechanical, not hydrodynamic, and saying so is the point that shows the device is understood. The hydrodynamic case has never been in doubt; what has kept the arrangement rare in large merchant ships is engineering:

ul: Coaxial shafting and the associated epicyclic gearing are complex, heavy and expensive, and they occupy space aft.

The concentric shaft sealing arrangement is a recognised reliability weak point. Two shafts through one gland, one rotating inside the other, is a hard sealing problem and it is the failure that operators fear.
Alignment, bearing loads, maintenance and drydock work are all harder, and a defect on the inner shaft is not a small job.
Limited service experience in large merchant ships, so owner and class confidence is low and residual value is uncertain - a commercial demerit that is as real as the technical ones.
The podded variant substitutes electrical conversion losses and pod maintenance for the gearing problem; it does not remove the complexity, it relocates it.

blocks.p: Fit it when: the rotational loss is large, the diameter is constrained, and the owner can accept the mechanical complexity and the maintenance exposure.

blocks.h: 6. (d) Azimuth propulsion - an attack on hull-side and appendage losses

blocks.p: Only three of the four devices are to be answered. This one is included so that a candidate who chooses it is served, and because the reason it is the least natural choice of the four is itself instructive.
6.1 The principle

ul: A propeller mounted on a unit that rotates through 360° about a vertical axis, so that thrust can be directed in any horizontal direction. There is no rudder.

Two forms: the mechanical Z-drive, in which engine power is taken down through bevel gearing into the rotating unit; and the podded electric drive, in which an electric motor sits inside the submerged pod and drives the propeller directly, with power supplied through sliprings.

The efficiency gain is not in the blade. It comes from two other places, and a candidate who locates it in the propeller has misunderstood the device. First, a pulling unit ahead of its own strut works in clean, undisturbed, largely uniform inflow, instead of in the disturbed and non-uniform wake behind a hull - which raises open-water efficiency and reduces cavitation and vibration. Second, the arrangement deletes the shafting, stern tube, shaft brackets, struts and rudder from the water altogether, and with them their appendage drag.

A secondary and often decisive gain is arrangement freedom: with diesel-electric machinery the prime movers can be sited anywhere and run at their most efficient loading, and the aft body can be shaped for flow rather than for a shaft line.

blocks.p: 6.2 Merits

ul: Clean inflow to the propeller, giving higher open-water efficiency, lower cavitation risk and markedly lower vibration and radiated noise.
No shafting, struts or rudder in the water - a direct reduction in appendage resistance.

Full thrust in any direction. Manoeuvrability is transformed: no rudder is needed, stern thrusters become unnecessary and bow thruster requirements are reduced, and the arrangement is the enabling technology for dynamic positioning.
Machinery arrangement freedom with an electric plant, and the ability to run generators at efficient load and shut down surplus sets.
Hull-form and cargo benefits - the aft body is freed from the shaft line and can be shaped hydrodynamically or used for capacity.

blocks.p: 6.3 Demerits

ul: Electrical conversion losses offset part of the gain. Generator, switchboard, transformer, converter, motor and sliprings each take their share, and on a ship that runs at steady sea speed a direct-drive shaft line remains hard to beat on pure transmission efficiency.
High capital cost and system complexity, and a plant that demands electrical competence on board that a conventional engine room does not.

The pod cannot be opened at sea. A motor, bearing or seal defect inside the pod is a drydocking, not a repair. This is the single most serious operational demerit and it dominates the risk assessment.
Sliprings, steering-gear bearings, thrust bearings and shaft seals in the pod are known maintenance and reliability items, and the sealing of a rotating shaft in a submerged unit is unforgiving.

The pod and its strut are themselves appendages. On a fast, fine ship their drag can consume much of the benefit, which is why the arrangement is common on cruise ships, ferries, icebreakers and offshore vessels and rare on fast cargo liners.
Vulnerability to grounding and ice contact, and a structurally demanding mounting.

blocks.p: Fit it when: manoeuvring, station-keeping, low noise or arrangement flexibility dominate - passenger ships, ferries, icebreakers, offshore and DP vessels. It is the weakest of the four choices for a straight 'high-efficiency propeller' answer, because its gain is a system gain rather than a propeller gain; a candidate choosing it must be able to say so.

blocks.h: 7. Comparative judgement, and the instruction printed in the stem

rows: Ducted
Axial
Slow, full-form, heavily loaded; tugs and trawlers
A net penalty at light loading
Kappel
Tip vortex
Moderately loaded single screw, diameter constrained, stable trading pattern
Modest and wake-specific gain; costly design and casting
Contra-rotating
Rotational (swirl)
Large swirl loss, diameter constrained, complexity acceptable
Mechanical - coaxial shafting, gearing and the concentric seal
Azimuth
Hull-side and appendage; clean inflow
Manoeuvring, DP, low noise, arrangement flexibility
Conversion losses; the pod cannot be opened at sea

blocks.p: The governing principle is that the choice follows the thrust loading and the operating profile, not fashion. The single best test of whether a candidate has understood the subject is whether they can say that a duct on a fast, lightly loaded ship makes the ship worse.

Two instructions printed in the stem must be obeyed. It asks for any three of the four - three treated properly will always outscore four treated superficially, and the natural three are the duct, the Kappel and the contra-rotating arrangement, because each attacks a different named loss and the answer then has a spine. And it asks for merits and demerits: a device presented with advantages only forfeits about half of its marks however well the principle is explained.

Finally, offer no percentage figures. Published gains for ducts, tip-modified blades, contra-rotating arrangements and pods vary widely, depend entirely on hull form, wake field, loading and operating profile, and originate very largely from the manufacturers. A quantified claim cannot be defended in an examination answer, and a mechanistic explanation of why a device gains is worth more than a number that cannot be supported.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks, and the structure is dictated by three instructions printed in the stem that candidates routinely break: answer any three of the four devices, give merits and demerits for each, and take seriously the opening sentence about improving the energy efficiency of ships, which is the examiner's own framing and not decoration.

The organising idea that turns a list into an answer is the loss map. Give propulsive efficiency and the four loss mechanisms first, then locate each device against the loss it attacks. Two short paragraphs at the front make every later paragraph land somewhere.

blocks.h: Three instructions are hidden in the stem, and candidates break all three

ul: 'Any three of the following.' Four are printed; write three. Writing four is the commonest error on this question and it converts three good treatments into four thin ones.
'With its merits and demerits.' Both. A device described with advantages only loses roughly half its marks no matter how well the principle is explained.

The opening sentence is not decoration. 'Improving efficiency of propellers is recognized as a growing means to improve energy efficiency of ships' is the examiner's premise, and two short paragraphs answering it are cheap marks that most scripts leave on the table.

blocks.h: Get the framing right for THIS sitting - it is six weeks old

blocks.p: In February 2023 the position is precise and stating it precisely is worth real credit: the revised MARPOL Annex VI entered into force on 1 November 2022; EEXI and the CII rating requirements apply from 1 January 2023; the enhanced SEEMP including Part III has been required on board since the same date; and the operative strategy is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018.

Do not write that ships have been rated. The first rating year began six weeks before this paper and the rating is determined only after the calendar year ends. No ship holds a CII rating at this sitting. Write the driver as anticipatory - owners acting on the rating they expect, and on the corrective-action-plan consequence of a D-for-three-years or a single E.

Do not write in the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy (five months future), the EU ETS extension to shipping (eleven months future), or anything from the Net-Zero Framework (thirty-two months future). Material written for a 2025 or 2026 sitting on this same question reaches for all three.

blocks.h: Learn the loss map first - it is the spine of the whole answer

blocks.p: Propulsive efficiency = hull efficiency × open-water efficiency × relative rotative efficiency. Then four losses: axial (energy left in the accelerated slipstream), rotational or swirl (the race leaves the disc spinning - the largest single recoverable loss), frictional (viscous drag on the blades), and tip vortex (pressure equalising round the open tip). Cavitation caps how hard a blade may be loaded.

Then say which device attacks which: duct → axial. Kappel → tip vortex. Contra-rotating → swirl. Azimuth → hull-side and appendage losses, plus clean inflow. Once that sentence is on the page the answer has a structure and every later paragraph has somewhere to attach.

blocks.h: The duct - and the qualification that carries the marks

blocks.p: An annular aerofoil round the disc. The accelerating form raises velocity through the propeller so each blade produces less thrust; the duct is a lifting surface so it generates thrust itself; and it closes the tip gap. The decelerating form is for cavitation and noise suppression at some cost in efficiency.

The mark is in the qualification: the duct's benefit rises with THRUST LOADING, and on a fast, lightly loaded, fine-form ship it is a net penalty because its own drag exceeds the thrust it makes. If you write one qualifying sentence in this whole answer, write that one.

blocks.h: Kappel - insist that the curvature is integral

blocks.p: Tips curved smoothly towards the suction side as a continuous integrated winglet, cast into the blade. It is not a bolted-on end plate, and the whole merit case depends on that: no appendage, no added drag, nothing extra to survey, and a drop-in retrofit at a scheduled docking.

Its honest weaknesses: the gain is modest, it is specific to the hull's wake field, it needs CFD and model testing so the design cost is high, the geometry is dearer to cast and repair, and the benefit falls away if the ship trades away from its design draught and speed.

blocks.h: Contra-rotating - say why a better device is rare

blocks.p: Two coaxial propellers turning opposite ways; the after one recovers the swirl left by the forward one. Since swirl is the largest recoverable loss, this is the most direct attack available, and it also splits the thrust between two propellers - so lower loading, less cavitation, less vibration, cancelled torque reaction, and a smaller diameter for a given thrust.

Then make the point that separates the scripts: the constraint is mechanical, not hydrodynamic. Coaxial shafting, epicyclic gearing, and above all the concentric shaft seal, which is the recognised reliability weak point. Add the commercial demerit - little large-merchant service experience, so owners and class are cautious. That is why a theoretically superior arrangement is uncommon.
The paper prints 'Cortra'. It is a misprint for contra. Name the device correctly, note the misprint in one clause, and move on - it shows you know the subject rather than the page.

blocks.h: Azimuth - if you choose it, locate the gain correctly

blocks.p: A propeller on a unit rotating through 360°, either a mechanical Z-drive or a podded electric unit with the motor in the pod. The gain is not in the blade. It comes from the clean undisturbed inflow to a pulling unit and from deleting the shafting, struts and rudder from the water. Say that explicitly; a candidate who claims the propeller itself is more efficient has misplaced the mechanism and it shows.

Demerits worth having: electrical conversion losses eat part of the gain; capital cost and complexity; the pod is an appendage in its own right and its drag can consume the benefit on a fast ship; and the operational one that dominates every risk assessment - a defect inside the pod cannot be repaired at sea and means drydocking.

This is the weakest of the four for a 'high-efficiency propeller' answer, because its gain is a system gain. Prefer the duct, the Kappel and the contra-rotating arrangement as your three - they attack three different named losses, which gives the answer a spine.

blocks.h: Close with a judgement, not a summary

blocks.p: The choice follows thrust loading and operating profile, not fashion. Heavily loaded and slow, the duct earns its drag; lightly loaded and fast, it makes matters worse. Moderately loaded single screw with a clean wake, a tip-modified blade. Large swirl and complexity acceptable, contra-rotating. Manoeuvring or station-keeping dominant, azimuth. A short closing paragraph of that kind is worth more than a restatement of what has already been said.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Do not answer all four devices. Three, properly.
Do not give a percentage efficiency gain for anything. The published figures are hull-specific and largely vendor-sourced, and none can be defended in an examination.
Do not name a manufacturer's product, or claim how many ships carry a device.
Do not present the duct as an unqualified improvement.
Do not describe the Kappel tip as a fitted or bolted-on winglet.
Do not attribute contra-rotation's rarity to hydrodynamic doubt. It is mechanical.
Do not import the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, EU ETS or any Net-Zero Framework content - all are future at this sitting.
Do not say ships have been rated A to E. None had been at this date.
Do not repeat the EEXI reduction-factor detail from Q3 of this paper; refer to it and get on with the propellers.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Does a duct always improve efficiency?" No. Its benefit rises with thrust loading; on a fast, fine, lightly loaded ship its own drag exceeds the thrust it makes and the ship is worse.
"Is the Kappel tip a fitted winglet?" No - it is integral cast blade geometry. The whole merit case depends on it: no appendage, no added drag, nothing extra to survey, drop-in retrofit.
"Why are contra-rotating propellers rare?" Mechanics, not hydrodynamics - coaxial shafting, epicyclic gearing, and above all the concentric shaft seal.
"Where does a pod's efficiency gain come from?" Not from the blade - from clean, undisturbed inflow to a pulling unit and from deleting shafting, struts and rudder.
"What is the worst operational demerit of a pod?" It cannot be opened at sea. A defect inside means drydocking.
"Which loss is the largest recoverable one?" Rotational - the swirl left in the race.
"How much will a duct save?" Give no percentage. Published figures are hull-specific and largely vendor-sourced.

"What is the regulatory driver at this sitting?" EEXI and the CII rating, applicable six weeks ago, under the revised Annex VI in force since 1 November 2022 and the Initial GHG Strategy of 2018 - and no ship has been rated yet.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your ship has a fixed-pitch propeller and a fouled hull. Which do you clean first, and why?
How would you know, from the ship's own data, whether a propeller polish had paid for itself?
What would you inspect on a nozzle at drydocking?
Why is cavitation erosion worse on the inside of a duct than on the blade?
What would you tell an owner asking whether to fit a pod to an existing cargo ship?
How does a propeller change affect the EEXI Technical File?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Framing, loss map, then the devices, then the judgement. FRAMING (1): revised Annex VI in force 1 Nov 2022, EEXI and CII applicable 1 Jan 2023, Initial GHG Strategy 2018, no ship rated yet. LOSS MAP (2): axial · rotational (largest recoverable) · frictional · tip vortex, with cavitation capping blade loading. Then one device per loss: DUCT (3) → axial; KAPPEL (4) → tip vortex; CONTRA-ROTATING (5) → swirl; AZIMUTH (6) → hull-side and appendage. JUDGEMENT (7): the choice follows thrust loading and operating profile. Anchor: one loss each - and answer three, not four.

Both exact instances of this stem carry an empty regulations list, and each records expressly that MARPOL Annex VI was not read in a licensed consolidated edition, so neither asserts any regulation number or any date for EEXI or CII. It does not bind this paper, because this paper holds the primary material for a different question - Q3 reads MEPC.328(76) at source and the paper consumes the corpus's canonical Annex VI regulation records - so the framing here is stated at P1 provenance.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI as revised by resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. Chapter 4 applies from 1 January 2023: regulations 23 and 25 require an existing ship's attained EEXI not to exceed the required EEXI, and regulation 28 requires the annual operational carbon intensity indicator to be determined and rated A to E, with a corrective action plan where a ship is rated D for three consecutive years or E in any year. The operative policy instrument is the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, 2018 - NOT the 2023 Strategy, which is five months future at this sitting. No instrument prescribes any propeller type or design concept; the regulations create the driver, not the design.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering all four devices when the stem asks for any three, and giving merits only when it asks for merits and demerits. On the engineering, the trap is presenting the ducted propeller as an unqualified improvement: its benefit rises with thrust loading and on a fast, lightly loaded ship the duct's own drag makes the ship worse. On the framing, the trap is importing later law - the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy (five months future), the EU ETS extension to shipping (eleven months future) and any Net-Zero Framework material (thirty-two months future) - and, subtler, writing that ships have been rated A to E when at this sitting the first rating year was six weeks old and no ship held a rating at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the high-efficiency propeller question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the regulatory and commercial framing at this sitting. 2 the loss map - propulsive efficiency decomposed, and the four losses. 3 to 6 the four printed devices with principle, merits and demerits. 7 the comparative judgement and the instruction to answer three, not four.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem hides three instructions and the framing paragraph is the part most scripts omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The four loss mechanisms, and which device attacks each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Axial - energy left in the slipstream - attacked by the duct. Rotational or swirl, the largest recoverable loss - attacked by contra-rotating propellers. Frictional - blade surface drag. Tip vortex - attacked by the Kappel blade. Azimuth propulsion attacks hull-side and appendage losses instead.
retrieval_cards.why: This single mapping is the spine of the whole answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is propulsive efficiency decomposed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Propulsive efficiency = hull efficiency x open-water efficiency x relative rotative efficiency. Three of the four devices attack the open-water term; azimuth propulsion attacks the hull and appendage side.
retrieval_cards.why: It locates every device precisely instead of leaving them as a list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a duct actually gain?
retrieval_cards.answer: An accelerating annular aerofoil raises the velocity through the disc, so each blade produces less thrust; the duct is itself a lifting surface and generates thrust of its own; and it closes the tip gap, suppressing the tip vortex.
retrieval_cards.why: Three distinct mechanisms - most scripts give only the first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does a duct make a ship WORSE?
retrieval_cards.answer: On a fast, fine-form, lightly loaded ship. The duct carries its own frictional and form drag all the time, and at low thrust loading that drag exceeds the thrust it generates. The benefit rises with thrust loading, which is why tugs and trawlers gain and fast liners do not.
retrieval_cards.why: The single best test of whether thrust loading is understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Accelerating against decelerating duct.
retrieval_cards.answer: Accelerating - converging towards the disc, raising velocity through it, used for efficiency at high thrust loading. Decelerating - diverging, raising pressure at the propeller to suppress cavitation and radiated noise, at some cost in efficiency. Naval and research vessels.
retrieval_cards.why: Shows the duct is understood as an aerofoil rather than as a ring.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the Kappel tip a fitted device?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The curvature towards the suction side is integral blade geometry, cast in as a continuous winglet - not an end plate or fin bolted to a standard blade. Its whole merit case depends on that: no appendage, no added drag, nothing extra to survey, and a straight replacement retrofit.
retrieval_cards.why: Describing it as an add-on destroys the reasoning behind every one of its merits.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the Kappel gain matter more than its size suggests?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it reduces tip vortex loss at the SAME diameter, and diameter is very often fixed by draught, aperture or ground clearance. It improves efficiency where the conventional route - a bigger, slower propeller - is unavailable.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why a modest gain is worth paying for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do contra-rotating propellers gain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two coaxial propellers turn in opposite directions; the after propeller sits in the swirling race of the forward one and recovers the rotational energy directly as thrust. Rotational loss is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most direct attack available on any of the four losses.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are contra-rotating propellers rare in large merchant ships?
retrieval_cards.answer: For mechanical, not hydrodynamic, reasons. Coaxial shafting and epicyclic gearing are complex, heavy and costly; the concentric shaft sealing arrangement is a recognised reliability weak point; alignment, maintenance and drydocking are all harder; and limited service experience keeps owner and class confidence low.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying the constraint is mechanical is the point that separates the scripts.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does azimuth propulsion's efficiency gain actually come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not from the blade. From the clean, undisturbed, largely uniform inflow to a pulling unit ahead of its own strut, and from deleting the shafting, stern tube, struts and rudder - and their appendage drag - from the water altogether.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who claims the propeller itself is more efficient has misplaced the mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The demerit of a pod that dominates the risk assessment.
retrieval_cards.answer: The pod cannot be opened at sea. A motor, bearing, slipring or seal defect inside the submerged unit means drydocking, not a repair. Electrical conversion losses through generator, converter and motor also offset part of the hydrodynamic gain.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the operator's real objection, and it is more convincing than a list of components.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which device for which ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: Slow, full-formed, heavily loaded, or towing - a duct. Moderately loaded single screw with a clean wake and a stable trade - Kappel. Large swirl loss, constrained diameter, complexity acceptable - contra-rotating. Manoeuvring, DP, low noise or arrangement flexibility - azimuth.
retrieval_cards.why: The closing judgement is worth more than a summary of what has already been said.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the regulatory driver at February 2023, exactly?
retrieval_cards.answer: Revised MARPOL Annex VI in force since 1 November 2022; EEXI and the CII rating applicable from 1 January 2023, six weeks earlier; enhanced SEEMP including Part III required on board from the same date; and the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018 as the operative strategy. No ship yet holds a CII rating.
retrieval_cards.why: Precise dating earns credit and keeps later strategy and EU ETS material out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the stem instruct that candidates ignore?
retrieval_cards.answer: Answer ANY THREE of the four printed devices, not all four; and give MERITS AND DEMERITS for each, not advantages alone. Three treated properly outscores four treated superficially, and a device given without demerits loses about half its marks.
retrieval_cards.why: Both are printed instructions and both are routinely broken.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The paper prints 'Cortra rotating Propellers'. What is it?
retrieval_cards.answer: A misprint for CONTRA-ROTATING propellers. No device of that name exists, and both other corpus instances of this identical stem print 'Contra'. Name the device correctly, note the misprint once, and answer it.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming it correctly shows the subject is known rather than the page copied.

questions.short_title: MLC 2006 - Flag and Port State Responsibilities, Complaint Procedures, Detainable Deficiencies, and Indian Grievance Redressal
questions.text_verbatim: Referring to the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) 2006, discuss: a) Flag State & Port State responsibilities. b) On-board & On-shore Compliant Procedures. c) Detainable deficiencies. d) Grievance Redressal Mechanisms for Indian seafarers.

subparts.text: Grievance Redressal Mechanisms for Indian seafarers.

questions.subpart_marks_note: FOUR limbs, printed a) to d), and no mark figure is printed against any of them, or against the question, or anywhere on this paper; 16 is derived from the rubric. Four limbs against sixteen derived marks gives four each if they are read as equal, and that reading is taken, but the limbs are NOT of equal size: limb a) alone is the whole of a sixteen-mark question elsewhere in the corpus, while limb c) is a single concept. The practical consequence is that limb a) must be compressed hard and limbs c) and d) must not be treated as afterthoughts, which is the opposite of what a candidate's instinct will be.

QP2406-Q6 (June 2024) prints four limbs, but FOUR DIFFERENT ONES: minimum requirements, conditions of employment, compliance and enforcement, and abandonment.
