decomposition: Limb a): the flag State's responsibilities under Title 5 - the inspection and certification system, recognized organizations, the certificate and the DMLC, inspection and enforcement - AND the port State's, which is a different mechanism with different limits, compressed into one limb

Limb b): the ON-BOARD complaint procedure, and separately the ONSHORE complaint-handling procedure. The printed word is 'Compliant' and it is a misprint for 'Complaint' - the question cannot be answered at all until that is resolved
Limb c): detainable deficiencies - the two grounds on which a ship may be detained under this Convention, and what in practice falls under each

Limb d): grievance redressal for INDIAN seafarers - which requires the Convention's own escalation route AND the Indian statutory architecture, and which is the limb with no donor and no held Indian source
The structural point that runs through the whole question: India is both a flag State and, for most Indian seafarers, a LABOUR-SUPPLYING State, and the two engage different parts of Title 5
The edition question, which decides what may be asserted at all: which set of amendments is in force at this sitting
The relationship between limbs b) and d) - the Convention's complaint route IS the first part of the answer to the Indian grievance question, and joining them is what makes limb d) answerable
reuse_evidence: DERIVED at this baseline against 297 built questions across 33 papers - the 31 integrated on main at 124dfbe plus QP2309 and QP2303 read from their pushed branches. Not read from any frozen field. The highest lexical score against any corpus question was 0.26, and the family was established by READING the printed stems of every MLC question in the solved set.

NO EXACT DONOR EXISTS FOR THIS QUESTION. That is a finding, not a gap in the search: the printed stems of every MLC question in the corpus were read, and no solved question prints this four-limb combination.

FAMILY, PARTIAL OVERLAP - PREFERRED DONOR. QP2407-Q6 (July 2024, +17 months) prints TWO limbs with printed marks - flag State obligations (8) and port State obligations (8). Both printed stems were read in full. IT CORRESPONDS TO LIMB a) OF THIS QUESTION AND TO NOTHING ELSE, and it gives that material sixteen marks where this paper gives it about four. It is the strongest donor record on this paper by evidence class: twenty-six P1 primary-verified sources and an EMPTY unresolved list.

SECOND FAMILY INSTANCE, REJECTED AS DONOR AND USED AS A CROSS-CHECK: QP2406-Q6 (June 2024, +16 months) prints four limbs, but four DIFFERENT limbs - minimum requirements, conditions of employment, compliance and enforcement, and abandonment. Only its limb (c) touches this question, and it covers ground QP2407-Q6 covers better. It was read in full for the Convention's architecture - the Articles, Regulations, Part A Standards and Part B Guidelines; the five Titles; the Article XIII amendment route through the ILO Special Tripartite Committee; Article V(7) no more favourable treatment; and Article VI substantial equivalence.

WHAT IS REUSED FOR LIMB a): the flag State's system of inspection and certification; the authorization of recognized organizations and the rule that the flag State remains fully responsible; the Maritime Labour Certificate and the DMLC with Part I by the competent authority and Part II by the shipowner; the certification threshold and periodicity; the inspection interval; and on the port State side the prima facie evidence rule, the four triggers for a more detailed inspection, and the limitation of any inspection to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code.

WHAT IS REUSED FOR LIMBS b) AND c): the on-board complaint procedure and the onshore complaint-handling procedure, which the donor treats inside its two limbs rather than as subjects in their own right; and the two detention grounds. In this paper both become limbs of their own and are expanded well beyond the donor's treatment of them.

WHAT HAS NO DONOR AT ALL: limb d). NO QUESTION IN THE SOLVED CORPUS HAS PREVIOUSLY ASKED ABOUT GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL FOR INDIAN SEAFARERS, and no Indian instrument on the subject is held by the corpus. It is authored from the Convention's own architecture and from the Indian statutory frame, and asserts no circular, no named office and no named forum. See unresolved.

WHAT IS NOT REUSED: the donor's sitting-relative framing. Its whole temporal argument is built on a FIVE-MONTH margin to 23 December 2024; here the margin is TWENTY-TWO MONTHS. The conclusion is the same and the reasoning is re-derived rather than carried.
questions.question_delta: THE DELTA IS LARGE IN THREE DIFFERENT DIRECTIONS, AND THE FIRST OF THEM DECIDES WHAT THE QUESTION EVEN ASKS. FIRST - THE MISPRINT, AND IT IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL ON THE PAPER. The stem prints 'On-board & On-shore COMPLIANT Procedures'. The word is COMPLAINT. There is no instrument, procedure or concept in MLC 2006 called a compliant procedure; what the Convention provides is an ON-BOARD COMPLAINT PROCEDURE and an ONSHORE SEAFARER COMPLAINT-HANDLING PROCEDURE, and the pairing of 'on-board' with 'on-shore' in the printed limb maps exactly onto that pair and onto nothing else. The misprint is preserved in text_verbatim and in the subparts and is recorded at anchor section 1.4; the answer names the correct term once, states plainly that the paper prints it otherwise, and then answers what the Convention actually contains. ANSWERING A 'COMPLIANT PROCEDURE' WOULD BE ANSWERING NOTHING. It is worth recording that this same question recurs at QP2307-Q4 in July 2023, five months later, where the word is PRINTED CORRECTLY - which independently confirms the reading. SECOND - THE STRUCTURAL DELTA, WHICH IS SEVERE AND RUNS THE OPPOSITE WAY FROM A CANDIDATE'S INSTINCT. QP2407-Q6 devotes a full sixteen-mark question, with eight printed marks each, to flag State obligations and port State obligations. HERE THAT ENTIRE SUBJECT IS LIMB a) AND IS WORTH ABOUT FOUR. Meanwhile the complaint procedures, which the donor treats as one step inside each of its limbs, become a limb of their own; detainable deficiencies, which the donor treats as two sentences on detention grounds, become a limb of their own; and the Indian grievance layer, which the donor does not touch at all, becomes a fourth. THE COMMONEST WAY TO FAIL THIS QUESTION IS TO WRITE THE DONOR'S ANSWER: a full and accurate account of Title 5 that consumes the whole time and leaves three limbs unanswered. The answer is therefore built with limb a) deliberately compressed to its load-bearing structure. THIRD - THE TEMPORAL DELTA, WHICH IS THE SAME CONCLUSION REACHED WITH A MUCH LARGER MARGIN. The donor sits at July 2024 and excludes the 2022 amendments because they enter into force on 23 December 2024, five months later. This paper sits at February 2023 and excludes them for the same reason with a TWENTY-TWO MONTH margin. The operative text at both sittings is MLC 2006 AS AMENDED THROUGH THE 2018 SET. The reasoning is re-derived rather than inherited, and the larger margin is stated because it changes the confidence: at five months a reader might wonder whether an early-adopting flag had anticipated the amendments; at twenty-two months, before the amendments had even been through their acceptance period, the question does not arise. FOURTH AND SMALLER - THE INDIAN ADMINISTRATION. At this sitting the maritime administration is the DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF SHIPPING, under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The rename to the Directorate General of Maritime Administration followed the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 and took effect in 2026, THIRTY-SEVEN MONTHS AFTER THIS SITTING. known_traps.md Entry 6 is expressly INVERTED for point-in-time examination content, exactly as it was for QP2304: the renamed body is named ONLY as the excluded future position and never as the operative administration.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: FOUR LIMBS OF VERY UNEQUAL NATURAL SIZE, AND ONE OF THEM CANNOT BE READ AS PRINTED. Limb a) is, elsewhere in this corpus, an entire sixteen-mark question in its own right; here it is a quarter of one. Limb b) prints 'Compliant' where it means 'Complaint', and a candidate who does not resolve that has nothing to write. Limb c) is a single concept that must be tied to the Convention's own two grounds rather than recited as a list. Limb d) leaves the Convention altogether and asks about India. The examiner is testing breadth across the compliance and enforcement Title and then testing whether the candidate can connect it to the seafarer's own practical position - which is what limbs b) and d) together are really about. The discriminator is TIME MANAGEMENT: this question rewards four adequate limbs far more than one excellent one.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 by rubric. NO MARKS ARE PRINTED against any limb, or anywhere on this paper. Instruction 2 states all questions carry equal marks, six answered questions are required, and the paper prints Total Marks - 100. Four printed limbs are read as approximately four marks each. The internal discipline that follows is the important part: limb a) must be COMPRESSED, because its natural size is four times its allocation here, and limbs c) and d) must be given their full share, because their natural size is smaller than their allocation and the temptation is to hurry them.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The flag State and port State mechanisms distinguished correctly - the flag State certifies and inspects its own ships continuously, the port State checks documents on a foreign ship and may go further only on defined triggers - with the certificate and DMLC, the split of DMLC Parts I and II, and the prima facie evidence rule all correct; the complaint procedures given as TWO distinct procedures with the on-board one exhausted first and the onshore one available in port, with the protection against victimization stated; detention tied to the Convention's own two grounds rather than to a recited list of faults; and for India, a route that starts with the Convention's own escalation, identifies India's position as both flag State and labour-supplying State, and names the domestic statutory frame without inventing circulars or forums.
primary_source_plan: Answer limbs a), b) and c) from MLC 2006 Title 5 as established by the MIW verification record for QP2407-Q6, which worked with the held consolidated text at P1 and carries an empty unresolved list.
THE OPERATIVE EDITION IS MLC 2006 AS AMENDED THROUGH THE 2018 AMENDMENTS. State it expressly.

THE 2022 AMENDMENTS ARE ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - in force 23 December 2024, TWENTY-TWO MONTHS after this sitting. Nothing from that set may be presented as an obligation. Say 'adopted but not in force' in those words.
THE 2025 AMENDMENTS DO NOT EXIST AT THIS SITTING - approved by the 113th International Labour Conference in June 2025, twenty-eight months later. Never cited.
The 2014, 2016 and 2018 amendment sets ARE in force and their content may be stated as law.
DO NOT REPRODUCE ANY PROVISION OF THE CONVENTION VERBATIM. Regulations and Standards are cited by number, as house discipline, and their effect is stated.
ASSERT NO RATIFICATION COUNT AND NO TONNAGE PERCENTAGE. The corpus figure is dated well after this sitting and cannot be carried back. Say that ratification is very wide, without a number.
ASSERT NO INSPECTION, DETENTION OR DEFICIENCY STATISTIC, and name no regional port State control memorandum of understanding, because none is held.
FOR LIMB d): NO CIRCULAR NUMBER, NO NAMED OFFICE OR CELL, AND NO NAMED FORUM OR TRIBUNAL. Anchor section 5.2 item 3. The limb is answered to statutory and institutional ARCHITECTURE only.

THE INDIAN STATUTE IS THE MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 AND THE ADMINISTRATION IS THE DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF SHIPPING. The 2025 Act and the DGMA rename are thirty-seven months future. known_traps.md Entry 6 is inverted for this sitting. No section of the 1958 Act is cited by number.
DO NOT CITE ANY CASE AUTHORITY OR ANY COURT DECISION. None is held.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - AND FOR A REASON THAT IS PHYSICAL RATHER THAN THEORETICAL. The corpus holds TWO consolidated texts of this Convention in the same folder: one carrying the amendments through 2018, and one carrying the amendments approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session in 2022. The second is present, readable, and INAPPLICABLE at this sitting. It is the specific circumstance in which a wrong-edition answer is written without anyone noticing, and it is why the risk is recorded as high even though the margin here is twenty-two months rather than the donor's five.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: HIGH, AND CONCENTRATED IN LIMB d). Limbs a) to c) are international and carry no Indian content. Limb d) is entirely Indian, has no donor, and rests on a statutory frame - the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - that was replaced by the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 on 15 March 2026, thirty-seven months after this sitting, with the maritime administration renamed at the same time. The risk is compounded because no Indian instrument on seafarer grievance redressal is held by the corpus at all, so the limb must be answered to architecture and the absence of sources must be visible rather than papered over.
technical_ambiguities: Whether 'Compliant Procedures' could mean something other than complaint procedures. IT COULD NOT. No instrument, procedure or defined term in MLC 2006 is called a compliant procedure. The Convention provides an ON-BOARD COMPLAINT PROCEDURE at Regulation 5.1.5 and an ONSHORE SEAFARER COMPLAINT-HANDLING PROCEDURE at Regulation 5.2.2, and the printed pairing of 'On-board' with 'On-shore' maps onto that pair exactly. The reading is confirmed independently by QP2307-Q4, five months later, which prints the same question with the word spelled correctly.

Whether limb a) is one limb or two. It is printed as one - 'Flag State & Port State responsibilities' - and it must be answered as one, but the two mechanisms are genuinely different and the answer must show that it knows they are. It is written as one limb in two clearly separated parts.

Whether 'detainable deficiencies' is a term of art in the Convention. IT IS NOT, and this matters. The Convention does not publish a list of detainable deficiencies; it provides TWO GROUNDS on which a ship may be detained. The published lists that circulate belong to regional port State control regimes and to industry guidance, not to the Convention. The answer therefore states the two grounds as the law and gives illustrations of what falls under each as illustrations, saying so.

Whether limb c) overlaps limb a) so far as to be redundant. It does not, but it is close enough that the answer must be organised to avoid saying the same thing twice: limb a) states the port State's INSPECTION powers and the triggers for going further, and limb c) states what a more detailed inspection may find that justifies DETENTION.

Whether limb d) should be answered on the Convention or on Indian law. On BOTH, and in that order. The Convention supplies the route every seafarer has, and the Indian layer supplies the domestic machinery. Answering only the Indian layer misses that the Convention's own escalation is itself a grievance mechanism available to an Indian seafarer, and answering only the Convention ignores the word 'Indian' in the printed limb.

Whether India's relevant capacity in limb d) is as a flag State. FOR MOST INDIAN SEAFARERS IT IS NOT. The great majority serve on foreign-flag ships, so India's obligations towards them arise principally under the LABOUR-SUPPLYING responsibilities of Regulation 5.3 and under its regulation of recruitment and placement services, not under its flag State responsibilities. This is the structural insight that makes the limb answerable without inventing Indian sources, and it is Convention architecture rather than an assertion about India.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Six sections. Section 1 fixes the edition and the architecture of the Convention in a short paragraph, because nothing else can be asserted safely until the edition is settled. Section 2 answers limb a) in two compressed parts, flag State then port State. Section 3 opens limb b) by resolving the misprint, then gives the on-board procedure and the onshore procedure as two distinct mechanisms. Section 4 answers limb c) on the Convention's two detention grounds, with illustrations identified as illustrations. Section 5 answers limb d) in three layers - the Convention's own route, India's capacity as flag State and as labour-supplying State, and the domestic statutory architecture - and states expressly what is not asserted. Section 6 is a short closing observation joining limbs b) and d).

steps.title: Which edition applies, and how the Convention is built
points: ILO instrument, in force 20 August 2013 - the 'fourth pillar' alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW
Articles · Regulations · Code Part A Standards (mandatory) · Code Part B Guidelines (guidance)
Five Titles; Title 5 is compliance and enforcement and splits into flag State, port State and labour-supplying responsibilities
At this sitting: as amended through the 2018 set. The 2022 amendments are ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - 23 December 2024, twenty-two months away

steps.title: Limb a) - Flag State and Port State responsibilities
points: FLAG: an effective system of inspection and certification; may authorise recognized organizations but remains fully responsible
Maritime Labour Certificate + DMLC at 500 GT on international voyages; 5 years, intermediate inspection between the 2nd and 3rd anniversaries; interim 6 months
DMLC Part I by the competent authority, Part II by the SHIPOWNER - the classic trap
Inspection interval shall in no case exceed three years; inspectors may prohibit sailing
PORT: any foreign ship may be inspected; the certificate and DMLC must be accepted as prima facie evidence, so the ordinary inspection is a document review
Inspection limited to the Articles, Regulations and Part A only of the Code
Article V(7) no more favourable treatment - a non-ratifying flag gains no advantage

steps.title: Limb b) - the on-board and onshore COMPLAINT procedures
points: ON-BOARD - Regulation 5.1.5. Fair, effective and expeditious; resolution at the lowest level, but direct access to the master and to external authorities preserved
A copy of the procedure to every seafarer, with contacts and the name of an impartial adviser on board
Victimization is PROHIBITED AND PENALIZED - the provision that makes the rest usable
ONSHORE - Regulation 5.2.2. Complaint to an authorized officer in port; seek resolution on board first
Unresolved → notify the flag State for advice and a corrective plan; still unresolved → report to the Director-General of the ILO
Confidentiality of the source is safeguarded throughout

steps.title: Limb c) - detainable deficiencies
points: The Convention publishes no list. It gives TWO GROUNDS
(1) Conditions clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers
(2) A serious or repeated breach of the requirements, including seafarers' rights
Reached only through a more detailed inspection, opened on one of four triggers: documents missing or invalid; clear grounds; flag changed to avoid compliance; or a complaint
Then: rectification, or an accepted plan of action; the flag State is notified forthwith; compensation for undue detention

steps.title: Limb d) - grievance redressal mechanisms for Indian seafarers
points: Layer 1 - the Convention's own route, which every Indian seafarer has: on board → master → flag State → authorized officer in port → Director-General of the ILO

Layer 2 - India's capacity. Flag State for Indian ships; but for most Indian seafarers, who serve on foreign flags, the operative head is LABOUR-SUPPLYING responsibility, Regulation 5.3, plus Regulation 1.4 licensing of recruitment and placement services and the no-fees rule
Layer 3 - the domestic frame. Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the shipping master for engagement, discharge and wage disputes; the Directorate General of Shipping as the maritime administration
Practical actors, not law: seafarers' unions and the ITF inspectorate
NOT ASSERTED: no circular number, no named office or cell, no named forum or tribunal, no section number

steps.title: Closing - the thread that joins limbs b) and d)
points: Flag State certifies and port State verifies - and both can be satisfied while a seafarer sits unpaid on a certified ship
What closes that gap is the complaint - which is why a complaint is also one of the four triggers
Limb d) is the same thread followed to its Indian end: regulate the agent who is within reach, because the foreign owner is not

questions.understand_first: Almost every other maritime convention protects something other than the people on board. SOLAS protects the ship and the lives in an emergency, MARPOL protects the sea, STCW makes sure the crew are competent. The Maritime Labour Convention is the one that protects the seafarer as a worker - his wages, his hours, his food, his accommodation, his right to go home - and that difference in subject creates a difference in enforcement that is the whole point of this question. The difficulty is obvious once stated. A safety defect can be seen: a corroded hatch cover is a corroded hatch cover whoever looks at it. A labour breach usually cannot. Whether a seafarer has been paid, whether his rest hours are genuine or manufactured, whether he signed his employment agreement freely or was told to sign it - none of that is visible to an inspector walking round the deck, and the only person who knows is the one with the most to lose by saying so. So the Convention builds enforcement in three layers, and the four limbs of this question are three of those layers plus India. The first layer is the flag State, which certifies the ship, inspects her regularly, and issues a certificate saying that conditions on board meet the standards. The second is the port State, which cannot inspect every foreign ship from scratch - it would be unworkable - so it starts by accepting the flag State's certificate at face value and looks no further unless something gives it a reason to. The third layer exists because the first two can both be satisfied on paper while the seafarer is still unpaid: the complaint procedures, which give the seafarer himself a route, first on board and then ashore. That third layer is why the misprinted limb of this question matters so much. The paper prints 'Compliant Procedures'. The word is Complaint, and it is not a detail - the complaint procedures are the mechanism by which the person who actually knows what is happening can make it visible. Everything else in Title 5 depends on somebody telling somebody. And that also explains the last limb. An Indian seafarer's problem is usually not that no rule exists; it is that the ship is under a foreign flag, the owner is a company he has never met in a country he has never visited, and the person who hired him was an agent in Mumbai. So the useful question is not 'what does the Convention say' but 'who, in practice, can he go to' - and the answer runs through India not as the flag State, which it usually is not, but as the country that supplied the labour and licensed the agent.
questions.memory_cue: FOUR LIMBS, FOUR MARKS EACH - COMPRESS LIMB a), IT IS A WHOLE QUESTION ELSEWHERE. EDITION: MLC 2006 in force 20 Aug 2013, as amended through the 2018 set. 2022 amendments = ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE (23 Dec 2024, +22 months). Structure: Articles · Regulations · Part A mandatory · Part B guidance; Title 5 = flag / port / labour-supplying. a) FLAG: effective inspection and certification system; may authorise ROs but stays fully responsible; MLC + DMLC at 500 GT international, 5 yrs, intermediate between 2nd and 3rd anniversary, interim 6 months; DMLC Part I = authority, Part II = SHIPOWNER; inspection interval never more than 3 years; power to prohibit sailing. PORT: certificate + DMLC = PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE, so ordinary inspection = document check; limited to Articles, Regulations, Part A only; Art V(7) no more favourable treatment. b) COMPLAINT (paper prints 'Compliant'): ON-BOARD reg 5.1.5 - fair, effective, expeditious; lowest level first but direct access to master and to external authorities; copy to every seafarer + contacts + impartial adviser on board; VICTIMIZATION PROHIBITED AND PENALIZED. ONSHORE reg 5.2.2 - authorized officer in port; try on board first → notify flag State for a corrective plan → still unresolved → Director-General of the ILO; source kept confidential. c) DETAINABLE: the Convention has NO list - it has TWO GROUNDS: (1) conditions clearly hazardous to safety, health or security; (2) serious or repeated breach incl. seafarers' rights. Reached via a more detailed inspection on four triggers: bad/missing documents · clear grounds · flag changed to avoid compliance · a complaint. Then rectify or accepted plan of action, flag State notified forthwith, compensation for undue detention. d) INDIA - THREE LAYERS: (1) the Convention's own route above; (2) India is usually NOT the flag State - most Indian seafarers are on foreign flags, so the head is reg 5.3 LABOUR-SUPPLYING + reg 1.4 licensing of recruitment and placement services and the NO-FEES rule; (3) MS Act 1958, the shipping master, the Directorate General of Shipping. Unions and ITF = practical, not law. NO circular, NO named office, NO named forum, NO section number. Administration is DG Shipping - DGMA is 37 months future.

blocks.h: 1. Which edition applies, and how the Convention is built

blocks.p: Nothing in this question can be asserted safely until the edition is fixed, so it is fixed first and briefly.

The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is an International Labour Organization instrument, not an IMO one, adopted at the International Labour Conference in 2006 and in force since 20 August 2013. It is commonly called the fourth pillar of international maritime regulation, alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW.

ul: It is built in three levels: the Articles, the Regulations, and the Code, which is in two parts - Part A Standards, which are mandatory, and Part B Guidelines, which are guidance.

It has five Titles: minimum requirements; conditions of employment; accommodation, recreation, food and catering; health protection, medical care, welfare and social security; and Title 5, compliance and enforcement, which is where the whole of this question lives.

Title 5 divides into three, and the third is the one candidates forget: flag State responsibilities, port State responsibilities, and labour-supplying responsibilities. Limb d) of this question turns on the third.
The Code is amended not by IMO tacit acceptance but by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII.

One structural rule is worth stating because it stiffens the whole Title: the substantial equivalence permitted by Article VI, by which a Member may implement Part A by substantially equivalent measures, does not apply to Part A of the Code within Title 5. The compliance machinery itself must be implemented as written.

blocks.p: The edition operative at this sitting is MLC 2006 as amended through the 2018 amendments. The 2014 set, which introduced the abandonment and financial security provisions, the 2016 set on harassment and bullying, and the 2018 set on wages while held captive are all in force. The amendments approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session in 2022 are ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE: they enter into force on 23 December 2024, twenty-two months after this paper, and nothing from that set may be presented as an obligation here.

blocks.h: 2. Limb a) - Flag State and Port State responsibilities

blocks.p: This limb is printed as one, and it is worth about four marks - but it is a complete sixteen-mark question elsewhere. It must therefore be compressed to its structure. The single sentence that organises it: the flag State builds and certifies the system; the port State checks the certificate, and looks behind it only when it has a reason to.
2.1 Flag State responsibilities

rows: Reg 5.1.1 general principles

Responsible for implementation on ships that fly its flag, and for maintaining an effective system of inspection and certification so that conditions meet and continue to meet the standards. A copy of the Convention is kept on board
Reg 5.1.2 recognized organizations

It may authorise ROs to inspect and certify on its behalf, having satisfied itself of their competence and independence - but it remains fully responsible. The current list is provided to the ILO and made public
Reg 5.1.3 certification

A Maritime Labour Certificate and a Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance for ships of 500 gross tonnage and over on international voyages or operating from or between foreign ports; others on the shipowner's request. Valid for five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates; an interim certificate runs for six months
The DMLC

Part I is drawn up by the competent authority and lists the national requirements; Part II is drawn up by the SHIPOWNER and sets out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance. This split is the classic examination trap
Reg 5.1.4 inspection and enforcement

Regular inspections at an interval that shall in no case exceed three years, by qualified and independent inspectors with power to board, examine, require rectification and prohibit the ship from sailing. Rights of appeal, confidentiality of the complaint source, no conflict of interest, reports to the authority and the master and posted on board, an annual report, and adequate penalties
Reg 5.1.6 casualties
An official inquiry into any serious marine casualty causing injury or loss of life

blocks.p: 2.2 Port State responsibilities
The port State's role is different in kind. It is not certifying anything; it is verifying, on a foreign ship, and its powers are deliberately bounded:

ol: Any foreign ship calling at a port of a Member may be inspected, on the basis provided by Article V(4).

The Maritime Labour Certificate and the DMLC must be ACCEPTED as prima facie evidence of compliance. The ordinary inspection is therefore a review of those documents and nothing more. This is what makes the system workable at the scale of world shipping.
Any inspection is limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code. Part B, being guidance, is not an enforcement standard.

A more detailed inspection may be carried out on any of four triggers: the required documents are not produced or are not maintained or are falsely maintained; there are clear grounds for believing conditions do not conform; there are grounds to believe the ship has changed flag to avoid compliance; or there is a complaint. It is mandatory where conditions could be clearly hazardous or where there is a serious or repeated breach.

Article V(7) - no more favourable treatment. Ships of States that have not ratified receive no advantage from that fact. Without this the Convention could be escaped by choosing a flag, and with it the port State's inspection reaches every ship.

blocks.p: The third leg of Title 5, labour-supplying responsibilities under Regulation 5.3, should be named here in a sentence even though the printed limb does not ask for it, because limb d) depends on it.

blocks.h: 3. Limb b) - the on-board and onshore COMPLAINT procedures

blocks.p: A necessary correction before the limb can be answered. The paper prints 'On-board & On-shore Compliant Procedures'. The word is COMPLAINT. There is no instrument, procedure or defined term in MLC 2006 called a compliant procedure; what the Convention provides is an on-board complaint procedure and an onshore seafarer complaint-handling procedure, and the printed pairing of 'on-board' with 'on-shore' maps onto that pair and onto nothing else. The limb is answered accordingly, and this is noted once and not laboured.
These are two distinct procedures with different owners, different audiences and different escalation routes. Treating them as one is the commonest error on this limb.
3.1 The on-board complaint procedure - Regulation 5.1.5
Every ship must have procedures for the fair, effective and expeditious handling of seafarer complaints alleging breaches of the Convention, including seafarers' rights.

ul: The complaint should be resolved at the lowest level possible. That is the design intention - most matters are best settled by the head of department or the master before they become anything else.

But the seafarer's right to complain directly to the master is preserved, and so is his right to complain directly to the appropriate external authorities - the flag State administration or an authority in the port - without first exhausting the on-board route. The lowest-level principle is a preference, not a precondition, and stating that distinction correctly is where the mark is.

Every seafarer is given a copy of the on-board complaint procedures applicable on the ship, in a language he understands, together with the contact information for the competent authority in the flag State and in his country of residence, and the name of a person on board who can advise him impartially on the procedure.
The seafarer may be accompanied or represented during the procedure.

blocks.p: The provision that makes all of it usable: victimization is prohibited and penalized. Any form of victimization of a seafarer for having filed a complaint is forbidden and must be penalized under national law. Without that protection the procedure would be worthless, because the person best placed to complain is also the person most easily dismissed at the next port, and an answer that omits it has missed the point of the mechanism.
3.2 The onshore complaint-handling procedure - Regulation 5.2.2
This is the port State's procedure, and it exists so that a seafarer on a foreign ship in a foreign port has somewhere to go that is not his own employer.

ol: A seafarer - or a representative, or an organisation acting for him - may make a complaint to an authorized officer in the port at which the ship has called, alleging a breach of the Convention.
The officer undertakes an initial investigation to establish whether the complaint is well-founded.
Resolution is sought at ship level first. Where appropriate the officer promotes settlement on board, which is a deliberate mirror of the on-board principle.
If it cannot be resolved on board, the flag State is notified and asked for advice and a corrective plan of action, with a deadline.
If it still cannot be resolved, a copy of the report is sent to the Director-General of the ILO, and the appropriate seafarers' and shipowners' organisations in the port State are informed.

The confidentiality of the source of the complaint is safeguarded throughout, and steps are taken to avoid the seafarer being identified. This mirrors the anti-victimization rule on the on-board side.

blocks.p: The connection worth drawing, because it is the reason both exist: a complaint is also one of the four triggers for a more detailed port State inspection. So the complaint procedure is not only a remedy for the individual seafarer; it is one of the principal ways the enforcement machinery of limb c) is set in motion at all.

blocks.h: 4. Limb c) - detainable deficiencies

blocks.p: An important preliminary: the Convention publishes no list of detainable deficiencies. Lists of that kind circulate, and they are useful, but they belong to regional port State control regimes and to industry guidance rather than to the Convention. What the Convention provides is TWO GROUNDS for detention, and an answer built on the two grounds is both correct and more durable than one built on a recited list.
4.1 How the ship gets there

Detention is the end of a sequence, not a first step. The ordinary port State inspection is the document review described at section 2.2. It becomes a more detailed inspection only on one of the four triggers - documents not produced, not maintained or falsely maintained; clear grounds for believing conditions do not conform; grounds to believe the flag was changed to avoid compliance; or a complaint. The scope of that more detailed inspection is drawn from the Convention's own appendix listing the areas to be examined, which are essentially the subject matter of Titles 1 to 4.
4.2 The two grounds

rows: 1. Conditions on board are clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers
The defect creates a real and present danger to the people on board - as distinct from a paperwork failure or a breach that is serious but not dangerous
2. There is a serious or repeated breach of the requirements of the Convention, including seafarers' rights

The breach need not endanger anyone. Its gravity, or its repetition, is what justifies detention - and 'including seafarers' rights' makes clear that a purely contractual or financial wrong can detain a ship

blocks.p: Those two grounds are the answer to this limb. The second is the one most often missed, and it is the more remarkable of the two: this is a Convention under which a ship may be detained because seafarers have not been paid, with nothing whatever wrong with the ship.
4.3 What in practice falls under them - given as illustration, not as a list from the Convention

ul: Documentary: no valid Maritime Labour Certificate or DMLC, or a certificate that no longer reflects the conditions found.
Employment: seafarers serving without a signed seafarers' employment agreement, or on terms they had no opportunity to examine.
Wages: substantial wages long unpaid - which also touches the abandonment provisions.
Age and fitness: a seafarer below the minimum age, or serving without a valid medical certificate.
Hours: serious or systematic breach of the hours of work and rest limits, particularly where the records appear to have been manufactured.
Food and water: insufficient or unfit food, or insufficient drinking water.
Accommodation and health: grossly unsanitary or unsafe accommodation, or an absence of the required medical care.

Repatriation and abandonment: failure to repatriate, or the absence of the financial security certificate that the 2014 amendments require - and here the ship may be detained precisely because the seafarers cannot get home.

blocks.p: These are illustrations of the two grounds and are identified as such, because presenting them as the Convention's own list would be wrong.
4.4 What follows a detention

ul: The ship is detained until the deficiencies are rectified, or until the officer has accepted a plan of action to rectify them and is satisfied it will be carried out promptly.
The flag State is notified forthwith, and is invited to be present. The seafarers' and shipowners' organisations in the port State may be informed.

Compensation is payable for any loss or damage suffered as a result of a ship being unduly detained or delayed. The power is real and so is the check on it; an answer that gives the power without the check has given half of it.
Every effort is made to avoid the ship being unduly detained or delayed in the first place - the object is rectification, not punishment.

blocks.h: 5. Limb d) - grievance redressal mechanisms for Indian seafarers

blocks.p: This limb leaves the Convention and asks about India, and it should be answered in three layers, in this order. What is deliberately not done here is as important as what is: no circular, no named office or cell, and no named forum or tribunal is asserted, because no held source supports one. The limb is answered to architecture.
5.1 Layer one - the route the Convention itself gives every Indian seafarer
The first and most practically useful answer is that an Indian seafarer already has the escalation described at section 3, and it is available to him wherever he is and whatever flag he serves under:

ol: The on-board complaint procedure, with the right to go directly to the master, the right to an impartial adviser on board, and protection against victimization.
Direct complaint to the flag State administration, without exhausting the on-board route.
Complaint to an authorized officer in the port of call, wherever in the world that is, under the onshore procedure - with the source kept confidential.
Escalation by that officer to the flag State for a corrective plan of action, and ultimately to the Director-General of the ILO.

And where the complaint is about repatriation, unpaid wages or abandonment, direct access to the financial security provider under the 2014 amendments - a claim that does not go through the shipowner, who is by definition the party who has failed.

blocks.p: 5.2 Layer two - India's capacity, which is usually not the one candidates assume
This is the structural insight that makes the limb answerable, and it is Convention architecture rather than an assertion about India.

rows: Flag State
Indian-flagged ships
The whole of the flag State machinery at section 2.1 - certification, inspection, the power to prohibit sailing, and the obligation to respond to an onshore complaint referred by a foreign port State
Port State
Any foreign ship in an Indian port
The onshore complaint-handling procedure and the inspection and detention powers at sections 3.2 and 4
Labour-supplying State
The great majority of Indian seafarers, who serve on foreign-flag ships

Regulation 5.3 labour-supplying responsibilities, and Regulation 1.4 - the licensing and regulation of recruitment and placement services operating in the territory, the requirement that they keep registers and verify employment agreements, the prohibition on charging fees to the seafarer, and the requirement that they operate a system of protection to compensate the seafarer for monetary loss arising from the service's failure to meet its obligations

blocks.p: The point to make explicitly: for most Indian seafarers the flag State is not India, so the operative Indian head is the labour-supplying one. It is also the most useful in practice, because the recruitment and placement service is in India, is licensed in India, and can be reached in India - which the foreign shipowner very often cannot. The regulation of the agent is the enforceable end of the chain.
5.3 Layer three - the Indian statutory and institutional architecture

ul: The governing statute at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. It is the vehicle through which India's obligations as flag State, port State and labour-supplying State are given domestic effect.

The maritime administration is the Directorate General of Shipping, which acts as the competent authority for the purposes of the Convention - drawing up DMLC Part I, authorising recognized organizations, appointing inspectors and authorized officers, and licensing recruitment and placement services.

The shipping master is the statutory officer through whom seafarers are engaged and discharged and before whom wage and discharge disputes have historically been brought. That office is the traditional first domestic point of redress for a seafarer's claim against a ship.

The ordinary courts remain available for a contractual claim for wages, and a maritime claim may found an action in rem against the ship in the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts - which is often the only effective remedy against a foreign owner, because it proceeds against an asset within the jurisdiction rather than against a person outside it.

Practical actors that are not law but matter enormously: the seafarers' unions, and the inspectorate of the International Transport Workers' Federation, which boards ships, pursues wage claims and arranges food and repatriation. They are named as industry mechanisms and not as legal machinery.

blocks.p: What is expressly not asserted. No administrative circular is cited by number; no grievance cell, committee or office is named; no tribunal or forum is named; and no section of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is cited by number. No held source supports any of them for this date, and inventing one would be worse than the gap. And the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 does not exist at this sitting - it commenced on 15 March 2026, thirty-seven months later - so the administration is the Directorate General of Shipping and not the renamed body that followed it.

blocks.h: 6. Closing - the thread that joins limbs b) and d)

blocks.p: The four limbs look like four separate topics and they are not. The flag State certifies, the port State verifies, and both can be entirely satisfied while a seafarer sits unpaid on a certified ship. What closes that gap is the complaint - which is why the Convention gives the seafarer two procedures, protects him from victimization for using them, keeps his identity confidential, and makes a complaint one of the four triggers that opens a detailed inspection and can end in detention.

Limb d) is the same thread followed to its Indian end. An Indian seafarer's practical difficulty is not the absence of a rule but the distance to the person who owes him the money. The Convention's answer is to give him a route that runs through whichever port he is in rather than through the owner's country; India's answer is to regulate, licence and hold responsible the agent who recruited him, because that is the link in the chain that is physically within reach.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks across four printed limbs of very unequal natural size, and the structure decides the mark more than the content does. Limb a) is a complete sixteen-mark question elsewhere in this corpus; here it is worth about four. Limbs c) and d) are smaller subjects than their allocation and will be hurried if the candidate follows instinct.

So the discipline is: compress limb a) deliberately, and protect the time for c) and d). The commonest way to fail this question is to write a superb account of Title 5 that consumes the paper and leaves three limbs unanswered. Four adequate limbs beat one excellent one by a wide margin.

blocks.h: First: the misprint, because the limb is unanswerable without resolving it

blocks.p: The paper prints 'On-board & On-shore Compliant Procedures'. It means COMPLAINT. There is no such thing in MLC 2006 as a 'compliant procedure'; the Convention has an on-board complaint procedure (Regulation 5.1.5) and an onshore seafarer complaint-handling procedure (Regulation 5.2.2), and the printed pairing of on-board with on-shore matches that pair exactly.

Say so in one clause - 'the printed word appears to be a misprint for complaint procedures, which are dealt with at Regulations 5.1.5 and 5.2.2' - and then answer the Convention. Do not spend a paragraph on it and do not silently ignore it.

blocks.h: Second: manage the time, because the limb sizes are wildly uneven

blocks.p: Limb a) - flag State and port State responsibilities - is a complete sixteen-mark question in other papers of this corpus. Here it is one of four limbs and worth about four. The single commonest way to fail this question is to write a superb limb a) and leave b), c) and d) unwritten.
Compress limb a) to its skeleton and spend the time you save on limbs c) and d), whose natural size is smaller than their allocation. Your instinct will be exactly the wrong way round.

blocks.h: Fix the edition in one sentence and get a mark for it

blocks.p: MLC 2006, in force 20 August 2013, as amended through the 2018 amendments. The 2014 (abandonment and financial security), 2016 (harassment and bullying) and 2018 (wages while held captive) sets are all in force.

The 2022 amendments are adopted but NOT in force - they come into force on 23 December 2024, nearly two years after this paper. Do not write in appropriately sized PPE, free drinking water as an amendment obligation, social connectivity and internet access, or repatriation of the remains of a deceased seafarer. Consolidated texts carrying the 2022 set are in circulation and read as current; using one is the specific way this question is failed.

blocks.h: Limb a) - the skeleton that carries the marks

blocks.p: Flag State: build and certify. An effective system of inspection and certification; recognized organizations may be authorised but the flag State remains fully responsible; the Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC at 500 GT on international voyages, five years, intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversaries; DMLC Part I by the competent authority, Part II by the shipowner - get this the right way round, it is the classic trap; inspection interval never more than three years; inspectors may prohibit sailing.

Port State: check, and look behind only with a reason. The certificate and DMLC must be accepted as prima facie evidence, so the ordinary inspection is a document review; inspection is limited to the Articles, Regulations and Part A only; a more detailed inspection follows on four triggers - bad or missing documents, clear grounds, flag changed to avoid compliance, or a complaint; and Article V(7) no more favourable treatment stops a ship escaping by choosing a flag.
Name the third leg - Regulation 5.3 labour-supplying responsibilities - in one sentence. It is not asked in limb a), but limb d) depends on it and naming it early makes the last limb look planned.

blocks.h: Limb b) - two procedures, not one, and one provision that carries the mark

blocks.p: On board (5.1.5): fair, effective and expeditious; resolution at the lowest level is the preference, but the right of direct access to the master and to external authorities is preserved and is not conditional on exhausting the on-board route. Every seafarer gets a copy of the procedure with contacts and the name of an impartial adviser on board, and may be accompanied or represented.

Then the sentence that must not be omitted: victimization for filing a complaint is prohibited and must be penalized. Without it the procedure is worthless, because the person best placed to complain is the person most easily dismissed at the next port.

Onshore (5.2.2): complaint to an authorized officer in the port; initial investigation; resolution sought on board first; if unresolved, the flag State is notified and asked for a corrective plan of action; if still unresolved, a report goes to the Director-General of the ILO; and the source is kept confidential throughout.

Then make the link that shows the system understood: a complaint is one of the four triggers for a more detailed inspection, so the complaint procedure is not just a remedy - it is how the enforcement machinery of limb c) starts.

blocks.h: Limb c) - resist the urge to recite a list

blocks.p: The Convention publishes no list of detainable deficiencies. It gives two grounds: conditions clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers; or a serious or repeated breach of the requirements, including seafarers' rights.

The second ground is the one worth dwelling on. It does not require danger. A ship may be detained under this Convention because seafarers have not been paid, with nothing at all wrong with the ship - and that is genuinely unusual in maritime enforcement. Say it.

Then give examples - unpaid wages, no valid certificate or DMLC, no employment agreements, under-age or medically uncertificated seafarers, manufactured rest-hour records, insufficient food or drinking water, unsanitary accommodation, failure to repatriate, no financial security certificate - but introduce them as illustrations of the two grounds, not as the Convention's list.

Finish the limb properly: detention runs until rectification or an accepted plan of action; the flag State is notified forthwith; and compensation is payable for undue detention or delay. Giving the power without the check gives half the answer.

blocks.h: Limb d) - the insight that makes it answerable

blocks.p: Answer in three layers. First, the Convention's own route, which every Indian seafarer already has - on board, direct to the master, direct to the flag State, to an authorized officer in any port, up to the Director-General of the ILO, and direct to the financial security provider in an abandonment.

Second, and this is the point that lifts the limb: for most Indian seafarers India is NOT the flag State. They serve on foreign-flag ships. So India's operative head is labour-supplying responsibility under Regulation 5.3, together with Regulation 1.4 - the licensing and regulation of recruitment and placement services, the requirement that they verify employment agreements, the prohibition on charging fees to the seafarer, and the required system of protection to compensate monetary loss. This is also the practically useful answer: the agent is in India and can be reached; the foreign owner usually cannot.

Third, the domestic architecture: the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the Directorate General of Shipping as the maritime administration and competent authority; the shipping master as the statutory officer for engagement, discharge and wage disputes; the ordinary courts, and the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts for an action in rem against the ship, which is often the only effective remedy against a foreign owner. Then the practical actors that are not law - the seafarers' unions and the ITF inspectorate.

Do not invent Indian detail. No circular number, no named grievance cell, no named tribunal or forum, no section number of the 1958 Act. An architecture stated accurately is worth far more than a citation that is wrong, and the examiner will know.

blocks.h: Get the Indian statute and the administration right for THIS sitting

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced on 15 March 2026 - thirty-seven months after this paper - and the maritime administration was renamed at that point. At this sitting the administration is the Directorate General of Shipping. Material written for a 2026 sitting uses the new name and the new Act; both are wrong here.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Do not write the 2022 amendments in as obligations. They are adopted but not in force at this sitting.
Do not give a ratification count or a percentage of world tonnage. The figures in circulation are far later than this sitting and cannot be carried back.
Do not give any inspection, detention or deficiency statistic, and do not name a regional port State control memorandum of understanding.
Do not reproduce any provision of the Convention word for word. Cite the Regulation or Standard and state its effect.
Do not reverse DMLC Parts I and II.
Do not present a detainable-deficiency list as though the Convention published it.
Do not invent an Indian circular, cell, committee, forum or section number.
Do not cite the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 or the renamed administration.
Do not cite case authority. None is held.
Above all, do not spend half the paper on limb a).

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "The paper says Compliant Procedures. What is being asked?" COMPLAINT procedures. MLC 2006 contains no such thing as a compliant procedure - it has an on-board complaint procedure (5.1.5) and an onshore complaint-handling procedure (5.2.2).
"Which edition applies?" As amended through the 2018 set. The 2022 amendments are adopted but not in force - 23 December 2024, twenty-two months away.
"Who draws up DMLC Part II?" The shipowner. Part I is the competent authority's. Reversing them is the classic error.
"Must a seafarer exhaust the on-board procedure first?" No. Lowest-level resolution is the design preference; direct access to the master and to external authorities is expressly preserved.

"On what grounds may a ship be detained?" Two - conditions clearly hazardous to safety, health or security, or a serious or repeated breach including seafarers' rights. The Convention publishes no list.
"Can a ship be detained with nothing wrong with the ship?" Yes - unpaid wages will do it, under the second ground.
"What protects the seafarer who complains?" Victimization is prohibited and must be penalized, and the source of an onshore complaint is kept confidential.
"In what capacity does India engage for most Indian seafarers?" As a labour-supplying State under Regulation 5.3, not as the flag State - most serve under foreign flags.
"What is the Indian maritime administration at this sitting?" The Directorate General of Shipping. The rename followed the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 in 2026, thirty-seven months later.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Where is the on-board complaint procedure kept on your ship, and who is the impartial adviser named in it?
A rating tells you he has not been paid for two months. What do you do, in order?
Your ship is in a foreign port and an inspector asks for the DMLC. Which part do you produce, and who wrote it?
What would you expect a port State inspector to look at first under the MLC?
What is the financial security certificate on your notice board for?
An Indian seafarer on a foreign-flag ship has a wage claim against an agent in India. Where can he go?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Edition first, then the four printed limbs. EDITION (1): through the 2018 set; 2022 amendments adopted but NOT in force; Articles · Regulations · Part A mandatory · Part B guidance; Title 5 = flag / port / labour-supplying. LIMB a) (2): flag builds and certifies - DMLC I authority, II shipowner, five years, never more than three; port checks - prima facie evidence, Part A only, four triggers. LIMB b) (3): on-board 5.1.5 - lowest level but direct access preserved, victimization prohibited; onshore 5.2.2 - port officer → flag State → Director-General of the ILO. LIMB c) (4): two grounds, not a list - clearly hazardous, or serious or repeated breach. LIMB d) (5): Convention route · labour-supplying, reg 5.3 and 1.4 · MS Act 1958, shipping master, DG Shipping. CLOSE (6): the complaint is what closes the gap.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, the wrong-edition hazard, and the Indian evidence gap

blocks.p: Temporal risk is HIGH here for a physical reason rather than a theoretical one. The corpus holds two consolidated texts of this Convention in the same folder - one through the 2018 amendments and one carrying the amendments approved in 2022. The second is present, readable and inapplicable at this sitting, and that is precisely the circumstance in which a wrong-edition answer is written without anyone noticing. The operative text is MLC 2006 as amended through the 2018 set, and the twenty-two month margin to 23 December 2024 makes the exclusion robust.

Limb d) has no donor anywhere in the corpus and no held Indian source, and the answer says so. No administrative circular is cited by number, no grievance cell, committee or office is named, no tribunal or forum is named, and no section of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is cited by number. The limb is answered to statutory and institutional architecture, and the organising insight - that for most Indian seafarers India is not the flag State but the labour-supplying State - is Convention architecture rather than a claim about India.

No ratification count and no tonnage percentage is asserted. The corpus figure is dated thirty-one months after this sitting; it is a live example of a fact that is true for the present and would be a false assertion here. No inspection, detention or deficiency statistic is given, and no regional port State control memorandum is named, so the practical examples in limb c) are expressly identified as illustrations of the two grounds rather than as any published list.

No provision of the Convention is reproduced verbatim - Regulations and Standards are cited by number and their effect stated - and no case authority is cited, because none is held. The Title 5 material is INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED rather than P1: the Convention text was not re-read at source this session.

quick_revision.recall_15s: FOUR LIMBS ≈ 4 MARKS EACH. COMPRESS LIMB a) - IT IS A WHOLE 16-MARK QUESTION ELSEWHERE. PRINTED 'Compliant' = COMPLAINT. EDITION: MLC 2006, ILO, in force 20 Aug 2013, as amended through the 2018 set; 2014/2016/2018 in force; 2022 amendments ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - 23 Dec 2024, +22 months. Build: Articles · Regulations · Part A Standards MANDATORY · Part B Guidelines guidance; five Titles; Title 5 = flag / port / LABOUR-SUPPLYING; substantial equivalence does NOT apply to Part A within Title 5. a) FLAG (build + certify): effective inspection and certification system (5.1.1); ROs may be authorised but flag remains FULLY responsible (5.1.2); Maritime Labour Certificate + DMLC at 500 GT international (5.1.3), 5 years, intermediate inspection between 2nd and 3rd anniversary, interim 6 months; DMLC Part I = competent authority, Part II = SHIPOWNER; inspection interval never exceeds 3 years (5.1.4), inspectors may prohibit sailing; 5.1.6 casualty inquiry. PORT (check): certificate + DMLC = PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE → ordinary inspection is a document review; limited to Articles, Regulations, Part A ONLY; Art V(7) NO MORE FAVOURABLE TREATMENT. b) COMPLAINT PROCEDURES - TWO, NOT ONE. ON-BOARD 5.1.5: fair, effective, expeditious; lowest level is a PREFERENCE not a precondition - direct access to the master and to external authorities is preserved; copy to every seafarer + contacts + impartial adviser on board; may be accompanied; VICTIMIZATION PROHIBITED AND PENALIZED. ONSHORE 5.2.2: authorized officer in port → initial investigation → resolve on board first → notify FLAG STATE for a corrective plan → Director-General of the ILO; source confidential. Link: a complaint is one of the four triggers for a more detailed inspection. c) DETAINABLE - NO LIST IN THE CONVENTION, TWO GROUNDS: (1) conditions CLEARLY HAZARDOUS to safety, health or security; (2) SERIOUS OR REPEATED BREACH incl. seafarers' rights - no danger needed; unpaid wages can detain a perfectly sound ship. Reached via more detailed inspection on four triggers: documents bad/missing · clear grounds · flag changed to avoid compliance · complaint. After: rectify or accepted plan of action; flag State notified forthwith; compensation for undue detention. d) INDIA - THREE LAYERS: (1) the Convention's route above + direct access to the financial security provider (2014 amendments); (2) India is usually NOT the flag State → the head is reg 5.3 LABOUR-SUPPLYING + reg 1.4 licensed recruitment and placement, NO FEES to the seafarer, system of protection for monetary loss; (3) MS Act 1958 · Directorate General of Shipping · shipping master · courts and High Court admiralty in rem; unions and ITF = practical not law. NO circular, NO named cell, NO named forum, NO section number, NO ratification figure, NO detention statistic. DG Shipping, NOT DGMA - the rename is 37 months future.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MLC 2006 Title 5, compliance and enforcement, as amended through the 2018 amendments. Regulation 5.1.1 general principles and the flag State's system of inspection and certification; 5.1.2 authorization of recognized organizations with the flag State remaining fully responsible; 5.1.3 the Maritime Labour Certificate and the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance, Part I by the competent authority and Part II by the shipowner; 5.1.4 inspection and enforcement, with an interval that shall in no case exceed three years and the power to prohibit sailing; 5.1.5 on-board complaint procedures with the prohibition on victimization; 5.1.6 marine casualties. Regulation 5.2.1 inspections in port, with the certificate and DMLC accepted as prima facie evidence, the four triggers for a more detailed inspection, and the two grounds for detention - conditions clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers, or a serious or repeated breach of the requirements including seafarers' rights. Regulation 5.2.2 onshore seafarer complaint-handling procedures escalating to the flag State and to the Director-General of the ILO. Regulation 5.3 labour-supplying responsibilities, with Regulation 1.4 on recruitment and placement services. Article V(4) as the basis for inspecting a foreign ship, Article V(7) no more favourable treatment, and Article VI, whose substantial equivalence does NOT extend to Part A of the Code within Title 5.
quick_revision.major_trap: Two traps, and the first is fatal to the limb. Reading limb b) as printed. The paper prints 'Compliant Procedures'; the word is COMPLAINT, and MLC 2006 contains no such thing as a compliant procedure. Answering the printed word is answering nothing; the limb is Regulations 5.1.5 and 5.2.2. The second is temporal: writing the answer from the 2022 amendments. They are adopted but not in force at this sitting - 23 December 2024, twenty-two months away - and consolidated texts carrying them are in circulation and read as current. Appropriately sized PPE, drinking water as an amendment obligation, social connectivity, and repatriation of the remains of a deceased seafarer are all from that set and none is an obligation here. Two smaller traps: reversing DMLC Parts I and II (Part I is the authority's, Part II is the shipowner's), and spending half the paper on limb a), which is a complete sixteen-mark question elsewhere but is worth about four here.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the MLC four-limb question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 0 fix the edition. 1 limb a) compressed - flag State builds and certifies, port State checks and may detain. 2 limb b) resolve the misprint, then the on-board procedure and the onshore procedure as two distinct mechanisms. 3 limb c) the two detention grounds, with illustrations identified as illustrations. 4 limb d) the Convention's route, India's capacity, the domestic architecture.
retrieval_cards.why: Four limbs of very unequal natural size; the failure mode is a superb limb a) and three unwritten ones.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The paper prints 'On-board & On-shore Compliant Procedures'. What is being asked?
retrieval_cards.answer: COMPLAINT procedures. MLC 2006 has no concept called a compliant procedure. It provides an on-board complaint procedure at Regulation 5.1.5 and an onshore seafarer complaint-handling procedure at Regulation 5.2.2, and the printed on-board / on-shore pairing maps onto that pair exactly.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most consequential misprint on this paper; answering the printed word answers nothing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which edition of the MLC applies at February 2023?
retrieval_cards.answer: MLC 2006 as amended through the 2018 amendments. The 2014, 2016 and 2018 sets are in force. The 2022 amendments are ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - they enter into force on 23 December 2024, twenty-two months after this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: A consolidated text carrying the 2022 set is in circulation and reads as current; using it is how this question is failed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the Convention built, and what are the three legs of Title 5?
retrieval_cards.answer: Articles, Regulations, and the Code in two parts - Part A Standards mandatory, Part B Guidelines guidance. Five Titles. Title 5 divides into flag State, port State and LABOUR-SUPPLYING responsibilities. Substantial equivalence under Article VI does not apply to Part A within Title 5.
retrieval_cards.why: The third leg is the one candidates forget, and limb d) depends on it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who draws up DMLC Part I and Part II?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I is drawn up by the COMPETENT AUTHORITY and lists the national requirements. Part II is drawn up by the SHIPOWNER and sets out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance.
retrieval_cards.why: The classic examination trap on this Convention, and it is routinely reversed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The flag State's certification and inspection numbers.
retrieval_cards.answer: Certificate and DMLC for ships of 500 GT and over on international voyages or operating from or between foreign ports. Valid five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates; interim certificate six months. Inspection interval shall in no case exceed three years.
retrieval_cards.why: Precise numbers are cheap marks and are the part most often approximated.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the port State's ordinary inspection only a document review?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the Maritime Labour Certificate and the DMLC must be ACCEPTED as prima facie evidence of compliance. Inspection is limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code, and goes further only on one of the four triggers.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what makes the scheme workable across world shipping, and it explains why the triggers matter.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The four triggers for a more detailed inspection.
retrieval_cards.answer: Required documents not produced, not maintained or falsely maintained; clear grounds for believing conditions do not conform; grounds to believe the ship changed flag to avoid compliance; or a complaint. It is mandatory where conditions could be clearly hazardous or where there is a serious or repeated breach.
retrieval_cards.why: They connect limb b) to limb c) - a complaint is one of them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes the on-board complaint procedure usable at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: The prohibition on victimization. Any victimization of a seafarer for having filed a complaint is forbidden and must be penalized under national law. Without it the procedure is worthless, because the person best placed to complain is the one most easily dismissed at the next port.
retrieval_cards.why: Omitting it misses the entire point of the mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the seafarer obliged to exhaust the on-board procedure first?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Resolution at the lowest level is the design PREFERENCE, but the right to complain directly to the master, and directly to the appropriate external authorities including the flag State and an authority in the port, is expressly preserved.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating it as a precondition rather than a preference is the error on this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The onshore complaint-handling escalation.
retrieval_cards.answer: Complaint to an authorized officer in the port of call; initial investigation; resolution sought on board first; if unresolved, the flag State is notified and asked for advice and a corrective plan of action; if still unresolved, a report goes to the Director-General of the ILO. The source of the complaint is kept confidential throughout.
retrieval_cards.why: A five-step escalation with a named endpoint is worth far more than 'he can complain ashore'.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what grounds may a ship be detained under the MLC?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two. Conditions on board are clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers; OR there is a serious or repeated breach of the requirements, including seafarers' rights. The Convention publishes no list of detainable deficiencies - the lists in circulation are regional PSC and industry material.
retrieval_cards.why: An answer built on the two grounds is correct and durable; a recited list is neither.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is remarkable about the second detention ground?
retrieval_cards.answer: It requires no danger. A ship may be detained under this Convention because seafarers have not been paid, with nothing at all wrong with the ship. Gravity, or repetition, is what justifies detention, and 'including seafarers' rights' makes the purely contractual wrong sufficient.
retrieval_cards.why: It is unusual in maritime enforcement and it shows the Convention's subject is the worker, not the ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What follows a detention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Detention until the deficiencies are rectified or an accepted plan of action is in place; the flag State notified forthwith and invited to be present; seafarers' and shipowners' organisations informed; and compensation payable for any loss or damage from undue detention or delay.
retrieval_cards.why: Giving the power without the check on it gives half the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what capacity does India engage for MOST Indian seafarers?
retrieval_cards.answer: As a LABOUR-SUPPLYING State, not as the flag State - most Indian seafarers serve on foreign-flag ships. That engages Regulation 5.3 labour-supplying responsibilities and Regulation 1.4 on recruitment and placement services: licensing, verification of employment agreements, the prohibition on charging fees to the seafarer, and a system of protection to compensate monetary loss.
retrieval_cards.why: The structural insight that makes limb d) answerable without inventing Indian sources, and the practically useful one - the agent is reachable, the foreign owner is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The Indian domestic architecture at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the Directorate General of Shipping as maritime administration and competent authority; the shipping master as the statutory officer for engagement, discharge and wage disputes; the ordinary courts, and the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts for an action in rem against the ship. Unions and the ITF inspectorate are practical actors, not law.
retrieval_cards.why: An accurate architecture beats an invented citation, and the in rem route is often the only effective remedy against a foreign owner.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Indian statute and administration at February 2023?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and the Directorate General of Shipping. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 - thirty-seven months later - and the administration was renamed at that point. Neither the 2025 Act nor the renamed body may appear.
retrieval_cards.why: The standing statute trap for the whole 2023 batch, and the corpus register records the later position.

regulations: Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 (ILO) - IN FORCE 20 AUGUST 2013. AT THIS SITTING THE OPERATIVE TEXT IS THE CONVENTION AS AMENDED THROUGH THE 2018 AMENDMENTS. The 2014 amendments (abandonment and financial security), the 2016 amendments (harassment and bullying, effective 8 January 2019) and the 2018 amendments (wages while held captive, effective 26 December 2020) are all in force.

MLC 2006 Article VI - the Regulations and Part A of the Code are mandatory, Part B contains Guidelines; substantial equivalence is permitted for Part A, BUT NOT for Part A of the Code within Title 5, whose compliance machinery must be implemented as written.

MLC 2006 Article V paragraph 4 - the basis on which a foreign ship may be inspected in the port of any Member. Article V paragraph 7 - NO MORE FAVOURABLE TREATMENT for ships of States that have not ratified.
MLC 2006 Article XIII - the Code is amended by the ILO Special Tripartite Committee, not by IMO tacit acceptance.
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.1 and Standard A5.1.1 - flag State general principles; the effective system of inspection and certification; a copy of the Convention on board.
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.2 and Standard A5.1.2 - authorization of recognized organizations, with the flag State remaining FULLY RESPONSIBLE and the current list provided to the ILO and made public.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.3 and Standard A5.1.3 - the Maritime Labour Certificate and the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance. Ships of 500 gross tonnage and over on international voyages or operating from or between foreign ports; others on request. Five years' validity with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates; interim certificate six months. DMLC PART I BY THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY, PART II BY THE SHIPOWNER.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.4 and Standard A5.1.4 - inspection and enforcement. The interval between inspections SHALL IN NO CASE EXCEED THREE YEARS. Qualified, independent inspectors with power to board, examine, require rectification and PROHIBIT THE SHIP FROM SAILING; rights of appeal; confidentiality of the source of any complaint; no conflict of interest; reports to the authority and the master and posted on board; an annual report; adequate penalties.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.5 and Standard A5.1.5 - ON-BOARD COMPLAINT PROCEDURES. Fair, effective and expeditious handling; resolution at the lowest level as the design preference, WITHOUT prejudice to the right to complain directly to the master or to external authorities; a copy of the procedures to every seafarer with contact information and the name of an impartial adviser on board; the right to be accompanied or represented; and the PROHIBITION AND PENALIZATION OF VICTIMIZATION for filing a complaint.
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.6 - an official inquiry into any serious marine casualty causing injury or loss of life.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.2.1 and Standard A5.2.1 - inspections in port. The certificate and DMLC ACCEPTED AS PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE; inspection limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code; FOUR TRIGGERS for a more detailed inspection; and TWO GROUNDS FOR DETENTION - conditions clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers, or a serious or repeated breach of the requirements including seafarers' rights. Rectification or an accepted plan of action; the flag State notified forthwith; COMPENSATION FOR UNDUE DETENTION OR DELAY.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.2.2 and Standard A5.2.2 - ONSHORE SEAFARER COMPLAINT-HANDLING PROCEDURES. Complaint to an authorized officer in port; initial investigation; resolution sought at ship level; notification to the flag State for advice and a corrective plan of action; escalation to the Director-General of the ILO; confidentiality of the source safeguarded.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.3 and Standard A5.3 - LABOUR-SUPPLYING RESPONSIBILITIES, with Regulation 1.4 and Standard A1.4 on recruitment and placement services: licensing and regulation, registers, verification of employment agreements, the PROHIBITION ON CHARGING FEES TO THE SEAFARER save for the statutory medical, seafarer's book and passport, and a SYSTEM OF PROTECTION to compensate the seafarer for monetary loss arising from the service's failure.

MLC 2006 Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2 - abandonment and financial security, introduced by the 2014 amendments and IN FORCE at this sitting: a certificate posted on board, direct access by the seafarer, and cover for outstanding wages, repatriation and essential needs.

ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE: the amendments approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session in 2022 - IN FORCE 23 DECEMBER 2024, TWENTY-TWO MONTHS AFTER THIS SITTING. Nothing from that set is presented as an obligation.
PROHIBITED AS FUTURE: the amendments approved by the 113th International Labour Conference in June 2025 - twenty-eight months after this sitting. Never cited.

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) - THE DOMESTIC STATUTE IN FORCE AT THIS SITTING, and the vehicle for India's flag State, port State and labour-supplying obligations. The maritime administration is the DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF SHIPPING. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 - THIRTY-SEVEN MONTHS FUTURE - and the administration was renamed at that point; neither appears in this answer. NO SECTION OF THE 1958 ACT IS CITED BY NUMBER.
